entries.name: A Bugesera king flees
entries.place_and_era: Bugesera to Rwanda. The source sets this in the late seventeenth century.
entries.attested: The chapter says the Baganwa rose against Bugesera. King Nsoro Nyabarega had to flee to Rwanda.
entries.unknown: It names a king, not a whole court or people in flight. The source keeps two ruler names open and says less is known of Burundi.
entries.next_step: This is a source lead. Resolve the land or home-loss unit before any case assessment.

entries.name: A chief and the rule of a district in the Udayendiram charter
entries.place_and_era: South Asia. The text names the district as Vishnuraja. The date of the event remains unknown.
entries.attested: The charter reports the defeat of a chief and an order to leave. It also reports Pallava rule over the district.
entries.unknown: An order does not show that the chief left. The fate and rights of residents and the duration of rule remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Check how the atlas shows this case with an unknown date.

entries.name: A claim of captives at site 1Pi61
entries.place_and_era: Pickens County, Alabama. Dye places the burials in the Late Woodland period. Exact dates remain unknown.
entries.attested: Dye reports that other researchers read the burial treatment as a sign of captives. Their view concerns people buried at this site.
entries.unknown: Burials alone do not show where these people came from or how they reached this site. The report does not establish slave status or forced labor.
entries.next_step: Define the captive claim and the control over people that it implies. Keep this view distinct from proof of transport.

entries.name: A disputed model of moves into New York
entries.place_and_era: New York and central Pennsylvania. One model placed the move around 900. A later version put it before the sixth century. Neither is an adopted event date.
entries.attested: Keener reports a model by Snow. In it, groups moved north, fought and drove earlier residents away. He also describes a view that the people developed there. He gives evidence that changed the proposed dates.
entries.unknown: The migration and forced moves remain disputed. Pots and village patterns do not settle who moved or why. We have not read the original debate papers.
entries.next_step: Check the move and land claims against the cited studies and the view that people developed there.

entries.name: A grant in Sylhet
entries.place_and_era: Sylhet, seventh century CE in this account. The issuer and exact year remain unnamed.
entries.attested: The chapter describes a land gift meant to extend cultivation into a forest tract.
entries.unknown: The forest claim does not prove that no one used the land. The exact recipients and actual effects remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Find prior use and the effect of this grant. Keep it apart from the later Chandra grant.

entries.name: A mountain town: defeat and later departure
entries.place_and_era: North America, in the source account. The date and exact place are unknown.
entries.attested: The 1896 English account by Cushing says warriors defeated a mountain town. They spared some people from cellars and took them into Black Corn kin. Those people later left with the southern group.
entries.unknown: The account does not prove that these acts took place. It gives no firm date or modern site. It does not show if people had to join the later journey or lost their homes for good. Its Black people label does not set a modern racial identity.
entries.next_step: Find evidence for the time, place and later journey. Keep the cause of that journey unknown.

entries.name: A report of brief loss of rule at Pandua
entries.place_and_era: Pandua in Bengal. Eaton gives 1353 as context for this invasion. Exact dates for the loss of rule remain unknown.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that Firuz Tughluq drove Shams al-Din Ilyas Shah from Pandua for a time. He failed to annex Bengal.
entries.unknown: The text does not establish removal of civilians or long-term control. The later invasion is a separate question.
entries.next_step: Define the brief change in control at Pandua. Keep it distinct from the later invasion and from the coin traces at Chhota Pandua.

entries.name: A report of new rule in Kamata and Kamrup
entries.place_and_era: Kamata and western Assam (Kamrup). Eaton gives 1494 as campaign context. Exact dates and bounds remain unknown.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that Husain Shah invaded and annexed these tracts. The claim concerns a change of rule.
entries.unknown: The report does not establish civilian removal or resettlement. The length of control remains unclear. It does not define all of modern Assam.
entries.next_step: Define the tracts and the change in control in this report. Keep this process distinct from Tai-Ahom settlement.
source_citations: N. G. Rhodes, “Husain Shah of Bengal and his victory over Kamata,” Oriental Numismatic Society Newsletter 66 (June 1980), PDF page 4; printed page number unverified.

entries.name: A report of the removal of Ho-Chunk in Wisconsin
entries.place_and_era: The Wisconsin Driftless Area. The authors report removal in the 1840s. The exact dates remain unknown.
entries.attested: Theler and Boszhardt report the removal of many Ho-Chunk. This question concerns their loss of residence.
entries.unknown: The text leaves each affected group and its next place unclear. The agents and the separate moves remain unknown. The old records that the authors cite remain unverified here.
entries.next_step: Define the affected tracts and the link to the broader Old Northwest case. Keep the reported removal as an open question.

entries.name: A royal report about the town of Pithumda
entries.place_and_era: South Asia. The reported act has no fixed calendar date.
entries.attested: A translated royal text says the king ploughed down a named town with asses.
entries.unknown: The act and its effects remain unverified. The fate of residents, land rights and length of control are unknown.
entries.next_step: The source assessment is saved and an atlas draft is next, with the reported act and unknown outcomes kept distinct.

entries.name: Abok loses rule
entries.place_and_era: Koc. The source gives no exact date for the overthrow.
entries.attested: Jonam traditions in the chapter say Luo under Daca overthrew Abok. Koc split into three states.
entries.unknown: The chapter gives a political outcome. It does not establish eviction or an exact act date. A named tradition adds no second witness here.
entries.next_step: This is a candidate for study. Resolve the unit and its limits before any case assessment.

entries.name: Afghan refugees received lands and towns in Bengal
entries.place_and_era: Bengal after the defeat by Babur in 1526. That defeat is date context. Exact dates for refuge and grants remain unknown.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that Nasir al-Din Nusrat Shah gave refuge to defeated Afghans. His cited note reports lands and towns endowed to these refugees.
entries.unknown: The report does not name each grant or its bounds. It does not establish harm to prior residents. Modern Afghan or Pashtun labels do not identify this group.
entries.next_step: Define the refugee group and the lands and towns in the report. Keep the grants and refuge as one open question.

entries.name: Afrin occupation and property loss
entries.place_and_era: Afrin, northern Syria; from 2018
entries.attested: Located reports concern property abuses and forced changes in the local population.
entries.unknown: The project has not yet reviewed a bounded event in full.
entries.next_step: Review the reports and keep other northern Syrian operations separate.

entries.name: Ahom loss and return of rule
entries.place_and_era: The later Ahom realm. The account reports defeat in 1662 and a return to rule a few years later.
entries.attested: Terwiel reports an Ahom defeat in 1662. Muslim invaders defeated them. Ahom rule resumed a few years later.
entries.unknown: The exact tract, resident groups and interval remain unknown. The account does not establish a forced move. Later recovery does not erase the earlier loss of control.
entries.next_step: Trace effects on residents and the extent of the changed rule. Keep this later sequence distinct from early conquests.

entries.name: Akjoujt copper-centre decline
entries.place_and_era: Akjoujt; early historic context, decline date unknown
entries.attested: A regional history describes the decline of this copper centre.
entries.unknown: The end of copper work does not show that people were forced out.
entries.next_step: Review the site layers for a cause of departure and a land outcome.

entries.name: Alaungpaya-era captive removal
entries.place_and_era: Manipur to Burma; ruler-period context before 1819, exact dates unknown
entries.attested: The source reports captive removal and forced resettlement under the named ruler.
entries.unknown: The short account does not settle if one program or several caused the moves.
entries.next_step: Define the process and complete its event and overlap review.

entries.name: Ali Burghul’s control of Tripoli
entries.place_and_era: Tripoli; source reports 1793
entries.attested: A regional history reports entry into the city and rulers driven from power.
entries.unknown: The text does not show that the whole family left or who supported the action.
entries.next_step: Distinguish loss of power from removal of people.

entries.name: Alwa and Soba pasture control
entries.place_and_era: Alwa and Soba areas, Sudan; fifteenth-century context
entries.attested: The source describes pasture control, new settlers and marriages between groups.
entries.unknown: This does not yet prove a specific forced loss of land or homes.
entries.next_step: Find a forced land process distinct from pasture use and settlement.

entries.name: Amda Seyon’s Hadiya captives
entries.place_and_era: Hadiya; medieval chronicle context, event date unknown
entries.attested: A royal chronicle describes deaths and captives taken from Hadiya to the royal city.
entries.unknown: The account does not show the exact destination, full affected group, or later return.
entries.next_step: Review the links to other attacks before this becomes a separate case.

entries.name: An order to move people to Lakhnauti
entries.place_and_era: Near Lakhnauti in Bengal. The order dates to the reign of Jalal al-Din Khalaji. Its exact date remains unknown.
entries.attested: Jalal al-Din Khalaji ordered boats to take people to this area, Eaton reports. He ordered them to live there, away from Delhi.
entries.unknown: The text calls them thugs or criminals. These are its labels. Arrival and compliance with the order remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Resolve the group and tract. Examine what the order changed in residence there. Keep the order distinct from proof of its execution.

entries.name: Andalusi Christian deportation
entries.place_and_era: Andalusia to Morocco; autumn 1126
entries.attested: The sources report forced removal of Christian families and church leaders.
entries.unknown: The sources do not prove that all Christians lost their homes or land.
entries.next_step: This case is in the atlas; its open source questions still need review.

entries.name: Angolan forced exile to Congo
entries.place_and_era: Northwestern Angola to Congo; 1961
entries.attested: The chapter says state repression forced people from northwest Angola to Congo.
entries.unknown: Each home tract, later fate and return remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Resolve links to other Angola cases before atlas use.

entries.name: Awatovi violence and residence question
entries.place_and_era: Awatovi; source reports a 1700 account
entries.attested: An article recounts a reported oral history of men trapped in kivas and fires.
entries.unknown: The reviewed text does not show where captives went or a defined land outcome.
entries.next_step: Review the cited account for lost homes and distinguish deaths from outward movement.

entries.name: Awdighust conquest and local Zanata killing
entries.place_and_era: Awdighust; within a 1054–1059 campaign account, exact attack date unknown
entries.attested: The source says conquerors killed local Zanata residents.
entries.unknown: The source retains later market life and does not prove death of all residents.
entries.next_step: Review the open source questions before any further atlas change.

entries.name: Balbus and Garamantian towns
entries.place_and_era: Garamantian oasis towns; ancient Roman context
entries.attested: Pliny reports that Roman forces captured named oasis towns.
entries.unknown: His report does not show resident removal or later land ownership.
entries.next_step: Review links with the broader campaign before a separate atlas case.

entries.name: Bamiléké-associated village expulsion
entries.place_and_era: Bamum-country tract, Cameroon; tentative seventeenth-century context
entries.attested: The sources describe village expulsion while some residents stayed and joined Bamum society.
entries.unknown: The exact phase and its link to the kingdom conquest remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Resolve the related events before the case assessment.

entries.name: Batwa evictions from Kahuzi-Biega
entries.place_and_era: Kahuzi-Biega, DRC; park changes in 1970 and 1975
entries.attested: A rights decision records eviction complaints and finds exclusion from the park contrary to state duties.
entries.unknown: The decision does not show that its remedies brought return or restored land rights.
entries.next_step: Review the affected groups and links with broader park evictions before atlas review.

entries.name: Bedde residence retreat
entries.place_and_era: Komadugu Yobe area; gradual process, chronology unknown
entries.attested: The author links gradual retreat from prior homes to Kanuri advance.
entries.unknown: The dates and identity of the affected group in each source remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Review each source and define a bounded loss of homes.

entries.name: Bornu royal complaint of slave raids
entries.place_and_era: Bornu; letter dated 1391, attack dates unknown
entries.attested: The chapter reports a royal complaint of attacks and captive sales.
entries.unknown: The attack dates, origin tracts and affected subgroups remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Define separate attacks and their links to loss of homes.

entries.name: Brahmans settle in Bengal
entries.place_and_era: Bengal, from at least the fifth century CE in this account.
entries.attested: The chapter describes Brahman migrants and changes in farms and social life.
entries.unknown: Prior land rights and the effects on village residents remain unknown. The Assam comparison does not establish a Bengal land loss.
entries.next_step: Find the tract, prior rights and the effect of a bounded act.

entries.name: Brooke acquisition of occupied Iban districts
entries.place_and_era: Sarawak river districts; 1850s–1860s context, exact cession dates unresolved
entries.attested: The source describes acquisition of occupied Iban river districts.
entries.unknown: Formal state consent does not prove resident consent or complete village clearance.
entries.next_step: Review the open source questions before any further atlas change.

entries.name: Brooke-era settlement in Baram and Limbang
entries.place_and_era: Baram and Limbang, Sarawak; late nineteenth-century policy context
entries.attested: The article says the state approved Sea Dayak and Chinese settlement in acquired districts.
entries.unknown: The loss of land for prior residents remains unclear.
entries.next_step: Trace the policy in practice and the prior land rights.

entries.name: Brunei worker deportation
entries.place_and_era: Brunei to Sarawak; postwar employment context, deportation date unknown
entries.attested: The article reports government deportation of a roads worker to Sarawak.
entries.unknown: The reason, precise home tract and later fate remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Assess the bounded removal and its links to prior cases.

entries.name: Buryat flight from Baikal
entries.place_and_era: The author places this flight near Baikal in the 1650s to 1670s.
entries.attested: Rubtsova reports flight from troops, loss of goods and homes, and later refuge.
entries.unknown: The student essay retells stories with few source details. A separate event from the broad case remains unproved.
entries.next_step: Define the flight account and its link to the current Baikal case.

entries.name: Camp moves in response to raids
entries.place_and_era: Northeast North America. Dye sets the camp moves in the late 1500s and early 1600s. The local bounds remain open.
entries.attested: Dye links moves of summer camps from major rivers to small tributaries with raids. These are changes in where people stayed.
entries.unknown: The source does not bound each group or river reach. It does not prove that each move was forced or final. Algonquian is a broad language label here. It does not name one Algonquin people. Dye cites work that we did not read.
entries.next_step: Trace the groups or river reaches and the raids tied to these moves. Keep seasonal use and forced loss distinct.

entries.name: Captive clans from Niani
entries.place_and_era: Niani to Songhay; Sonni dynasty context, event date unknown
entries.attested: The reference work reports an account of captive clans brought from Niani.
entries.unknown: Their prior homes and forced-transfer process remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Trace the account and define the groups and removal process.

entries.name: Captives from Sabr al-Din’s city
entries.place_and_era: Ifat; medieval chronicle context, event date unknown
entries.attested: A royal chronicle reports a ruined city and survivors led away as captives.
entries.unknown: The text does not show where they went or how long they were held.
entries.next_step: Review shared people and actions with the other campaign episodes before atlas review.

entries.name: Castle Rock Pueblo violence question
entries.place_and_era: Castle Rock Pueblo; late thirteenth-century source context
entries.attested: An article discusses victims and a theory that a household group was affected.
entries.unknown: The reviewed text does not show lost homes or where captives went at this site.
entries.next_step: Review the cited site evidence for a specific process and land outcome.

entries.name: Cave 7 burial and violence question
entries.place_and_era: Cave 7; Basketmaker II context, event date unknown
entries.attested: A later study rejects a single-event massacre and discusses violence and selective burial.
entries.unknown: The conclusion does not show a defined land or home loss, or prove that nothing happened.
entries.next_step: Keep the lead open and seek a new residence question beyond this closed source review.

entries.name: Central Plains and Middle Missouri movement
entries.place_and_era: Central Plains and Middle Missouri; occupation-phase context, event date unknown
entries.attested: A state site guide describes moves into the valley that displaced earlier groups.
entries.unknown: The text does not show one defined removal or the fate of a specific occupied tract.
entries.next_step: Identify a specific process and group without one event guessed from the regional pattern.

entries.name: Chandra grants in Sylhet
entries.place_and_era: Sylhet, tenth century CE. Sircar places Sricandra's charter at about 930 CE. This date is an estimate.
entries.attested: Eaton reports land grants and settlement. Sircar describes land and revenue rights granted to religious bodies and Brahmans. The charter directs cultivators to pay the recipients. It excludes Buddhist holdings and land attached to a boat station.
entries.unknown: The charter does not show who enforced the change or whether cultivators lost earlier rights. The stated number of beneficiaries is not a count of arrivals or displaced people.
entries.next_step: Trace the earlier rights and the effects of the transfer. Keep the stated settlement and the excluded holdings in view.
source_citations: Richard M. Eaton, The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, 1204–1760, chapter 1, “Before the Turkish Conquest,” archive section s1.1.3 and note 54; printed pagination unverified.

D. C. Sircar, Epigraphic Discoveries in East Pakistan (1973), Lecture II, “Paschimbhag Plate of Sricandra, Regnal Year 5,” printed pages 19–40 (PDF pages 36–57); consulted edition discussion, not independently verified inscription transcription.

entries.name: Chilula and Wiyot land question
entries.place_and_era: Lower Mad River near Blue Lake, California; local date unknown
entries.attested: Golla reports encroachment on Wiyot land by Chilula groups. He says the language boundary moved west.
entries.unknown: The local effect on homes or land control is unknown. How the wider account of land loss fits this place is unknown.
entries.next_step: Find what the local encroachment changed in land use or control.

entries.name: Clans and shrines in Busoga
entries.place_and_era: Busoga. The source gives several paths to rule, not one act date.
entries.attested: The chapter says Owiny and Wakoli became clans in power. Some migrants took over shrines and founded states. Marriage and old rites also shaped this process.
entries.unknown: The units and land effects remain unclear. A new clan in power does not itself prove that residents lost homes or all left.
entries.next_step: This is a source lead. Resolve the land or home-loss unit before any case assessment.

entries.name: Coins and a question of Deva rule in Bengal
entries.place_and_era: The south and east Bengal delta. The text and note give different date contexts. Exact dates for a change of rule remain unknown.
entries.attested: Eaton uses coins to trace brief Deva rule and a return of sultanate rule. Mint names and place names remain disputed.
entries.unknown: These traces leave the process and tract unclear. Chhota Pandua and Hazrat Pandua are distinct places. The report does not establish moves by residents.
entries.next_step: Resolve which tract and change in rule these traces support. Coin evidence can support a case when it bounds the process.

entries.name: Contested use at Mulberry Creek
entries.place_and_era: Mulberry Creek in northwest Alabama. Dye places the site in the late Middle Archaic. Exact dates for the dispute remain unknown.
entries.attested: Dye reports a dispute over shellfish, tool manufacture, and burial use at this site. He links the burial evidence to raids and feuds.
entries.unknown: The account does not establish who lost access to the site or homes there. A dispute alone does not show a change in control.
entries.next_step: Define the disputed uses and any change in access or control at this site.

entries.name: Cottonwood Wash archaeological comparison
entries.place_and_era: Cottonwood Wash; early Pueblo I context, event date unknown
entries.attested: An article cites this site among examples discussed in relation to violence.
entries.unknown: The reviewed text does not show forced departure or a land outcome here.
entries.next_step: Review the cited site evidence for a specific process that affected homes.

entries.name: Court grants of farmland
entries.place_and_era: Northern and western Bengal, tenth to twelfth centuries in this account.
entries.attested: The chapter describes royal grants of fields to Brahmans with court ties. It notes a different pattern in Samatata.
entries.unknown: Prior rights and effects on residents remain unknown. This group of grants can overlap with the named gift and western tax grants.
entries.next_step: Find which rights changed and how. Link the related grants to avoid a double count.

entries.name: Crow Creek attack and residence loss
entries.place_and_era: Crow Creek. The source places village life in the 1300s. The date of the attack remains unknown.
entries.attested: Willey describes an attack at Crow Creek. He links burned lodges to the loss of village life, homes and defense. He considers that some people escaped. He proposes that escaped villagers returned, or people with ties to them came, to bury the dead. He also reports later ceremonies at the site.
entries.unknown: The attackers and the fates of all survivors remain unknown. Willey does not fix the dates of each fire or prove later village residence. He gives two possible causes for the upper bone layer. The detailed methods behind his summaries remain unread.
entries.next_step: Keep this source account with the same Crow Creek record. Retain the unknown fire dates, later village use and survivor destinations.

entries.name: Daur removal from the Amur
entries.place_and_era: Amur region and Nonni valley; source reports 1653–1654
entries.attested: A book reports a state order to destroy homes and crops, then Daur flight to the Nonni valley.
entries.unknown: The text does not show if all ordered fires occurred or which homes they affected.
entries.next_step: Review how this removal relates to other Amur histories before a separate atlas case.

entries.name: Denbigh change: did people have to leave?
entries.place_and_era: Alaska, near the Bering Sea and Arctic coasts. The source gives broad age ranges, not a firm event date.
entries.attested:
A 2018 state report says a migration with Denbigh culture displaced or replaced earlier people. It leaves that choice open. It also describes later continuity with Choris.

The Raghavan study supports continuity among some sampled groups in Canada and Greenland. Its results do not resolve this Denbigh claim.

Anderson reports Ipiutak homes and camps at Cape Krusenstern. He says that people later left those houses. This does not settle the earlier Denbigh claim.
entries.unknown: The report does not link a human act to a loss of homes or land. Changes in tools or DNA do not prove that people had to leave.
entries.next_step: Selected Cape chapters now give context. They cover chronology, Birnirk and Ipiutak, with figures and plates. They do not settle the earlier Denbigh claim. The Oxford chapter remains unread because access is blocked. Seek evidence that links a human act to loss of homes, land use or control.

entries.name: Did these groups merge or leave?
entries.place_and_era: Okii and Iteso-Iworopom homelands south of Apule. The source sets this near the 1820s and 1830s.
entries.attested: The chapter says proto-Karimojong entered these homelands. They either absorbed the groups or forced them to leave.
entries.unknown: The account leaves both outcomes open. It does not show that all people left. Drought and mixed group ties remain part of the account.
entries.next_step: This is a candidate for study. Resolve the unit and its limits before any case assessment.

entries.name: Djerba taken in the source account
entries.place_and_era: Djerba; source reports 1558, date not independently verified
entries.attested: A regional history reports the capture of the island and states a year.
entries.unknown: The text does not show forced departures or a verified event date.
entries.next_step: Keep the date attributed and prepare the capture account with its limits.

entries.name: Djiganyai and Bou Khzama settlement changes
entries.place_and_era: Dhar Néma; ancient and later occupation phases
entries.attested: A site study describes renewed and repeated use of these settlements.
entries.unknown: Repeated use does not show that new groups forced earlier residents off the land.
entries.next_step: Compare the dated layers to distinguish site reuse from a specific takeover.

entries.name: Dogon expulsion from Yatenga
entries.place_and_era: Yatenga toward Bandiagara; medieval context, campaign dates unknown
entries.attested: The reference work reports expulsion toward the cliffs.
entries.unknown: The exact campaign, affected groups and later land outcome remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Trace the account and define the affected tract and process.

entries.name: Driftless villages and moves to new settlements
entries.place_and_era: The Driftless Area, with Fred Edwards and Hartley Fort, and later sites at Apple River and Red Wing. Around 950 to 1200 CE is source context. The time of a specific human process remains unknown.
entries.attested: The authors propose that scarce deer and wood led people to leave. They describe walled villages and suggest that groups later joined at new sites. They favor war as part of this change.
entries.unknown: The text leaves open how people moved and how land use or control changed. The figures and table layouts remain unread. The links between named cultures are the authors' views.
entries.next_step: Keep this as a research lead. Define a human process and its effect on residence or land control. A tract can bound the inquiry.

entries.name: Duckfoot: burned homes and departure
entries.place_and_era: Southwest North America. The reports suggest departure by about 880 CE. They do not date a forced move.
entries.attested: The reports link burned roofs to the end of use of the site. The author argues that someone burned the homes on purpose. He proposes that residents did this, then left with no plan to return.
entries.unknown: The cause remains unresolved. The report considers disease, famine and violence. It does not establish forced departure or new control of land.
entries.next_step: Find evidence that links the end of residence to a forced move or loss of land.

entries.name: Dunkula seizure and royal flight
entries.place_and_era: Dunkula to al-Daw, Sudan; 1365–1366
entries.attested: The chapter reports new control of the city and flight of the king.
entries.unknown: Other resident fates and the extent of destruction remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Review the open source questions before any further atlas change.

entries.name: Dâô and Nindien land seizure
entries.place_and_era: Dâô and Nindien, New Caledonia; decree dated 1899
entries.attested: A study reports seizure of land and part of a reservation.
entries.unknown: The account does not show that residents left or identify the full affected group.
entries.next_step: Define the seized tract and its links with other cases before atlas review.

entries.name: Earlier retaliation in Ifat
entries.place_and_era: Ifat; medieval chronicle context, event date unknown
entries.attested: A royal speech recounts an earlier raid, burned towns, and captives.
entries.unknown: The text does not show that these captives left the area or where they went.
entries.next_step: Keep this raid distinct and check its links with the later campaign.

entries.name: Earlier Taranaki pressure and southward residence
entries.place_and_era: Taranaki and southern North Island; 1820s
entries.attested: The sources describe war pressure and southward moves before the later atlas case.
entries.unknown: The force behind each early move and the links to later migrants remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Review each early move and link it to the narrower departure case.

entries.name: Early Ahom conquest in the valley
entries.place_and_era: A small part of the Brahmaputra Valley. The account places this act at the start of the thirteenth century.
entries.attested: Terwiel reports an early Ahom conquest. Newcomers who spoke Tai took control of a small part of the valley.
entries.unknown: The earlier residents and exact bounds remain unknown. The account does not establish a forced move. A separate event from the broad Ahom account is not established.
entries.next_step: Add the early control report to the current Ahom case. Define how this conquest relates to the longer account. Keep later conquests separate.

entries.name: Early settlement in the Hadley and McCraney valleys
entries.place_and_era: Western Illinois; occupation context about 600 to 1000 CE, event dates unknown
entries.attested: The report locates occupied sites and describes possible repeated use.
entries.unknown: The report does not show forced departure, land loss or who lived at each site.
entries.next_step: Find evidence of a forced departure from a defined place or the loss of land rights.

entries.name: Elara takes the realm
entries.place_and_era: Sri Lanka. The account gives no firm calendar date.
entries.attested: The chronicle says Elara came from the Cola country and took the realm from Asela. It calls his rule just.
entries.unknown: The account does not show who left their homes or lost rights to land. The wider effects on residents are unknown.
entries.next_step: Assess this reported takeover as a distinct case. Keep its just rule and unknown resident outcomes in view.

entries.name: Enslaved people recruited to serve in Bengal
entries.place_and_era: Bengal. Eaton places recruitment in the 1460s and 1470s. Exact arrival dates and sites remain unknown.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that Bengal rulers recruited or imported enslaved people from East Africa. They were to serve in army and state posts. His source uses the label habashi.

entries.name: New homes and moves in the American Bottom
entries.place_and_era: The American Bottom in Illinois. Dye uses AD 650 to 900 for one phase. His next phase spans AD 900 to 1050. The field report adds AD 400 to 650 as earlier context. Dates for local moves remain unknown.
entries.attested: Dye suggests that some settlers came from nearby areas. He later describes moves from uplands to river plains and larger villages. The field report records repeated use of homes. At Sprague, soil in one house pit predates a fire. The report suggests a return to homes and food stores.
entries.unknown: The causes of the moves and earlier land use remain open. Fire does not prove that someone drove people from their homes. Wasps can nest in homes that people still use. The proposed return does not establish who returned. Some tables in the report conflict.
entries.next_step: The selected report sections are complete. Keep both Dye phases distinct. Keep earlier land use as a separate open question. Revisit local causes or loss of homes with new evidence.

entries.place_and_era: Clay places Peter Village in Fayette County, Kentucky, in the Early Woodland period. Dye places the Peter enclosure in northwestern Ohio. This place conflict remains unresolved. Early Woodland is context, not a date for forced removal.
entries.attested: Clay reports post holes, burned wood, a ditch, and an inner bank. He interprets a stockade before the ditch. He reports unfinished mineral weights and small human skull fragments. Defense and sacred use remain possible. His small sample does not establish the uses of the whole site.
entries.unknown: The cause of the fire and the later use of the site remain unknown. Clay also considers decay or post removal. The skull fragments do not establish a violent death. No forced departure or loss of access follows from these traces alone.
entries.next_step: Keep both place accounts explicit. Seek evidence about site use and any imposed change in access or control.

entries.name: Velvikudi grant-rights loss
entries.place_and_era: Velvikudi; earlier loss and later renewal, calendar dates unknown
entries.attested: A charter account reports lost village grant-rights and later legal renewal.
entries.unknown: The text does not show eviction or full recovery of rights and homes after renewal.
entries.next_step: Keep the earlier loss and later legal phases distinct, with the final outcome unknown.

entries.name: Viet captive transfer at Drang Lai
entries.place_and_era: Land of the Viets to an unresolved destination; attested by 1409/1410, transfer date unknown
entries.attested: The text says its authority captured Viets, moved them and assigned them to Milady the Mother.
entries.unknown: Their prior homes, exact destination and service status remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Resolve the actors and the captives' links to the affected land.

entries.name: Vijaya and Kuvanna chronicle narratives
entries.place_and_era: Sri Lanka; ancient narrative context, historical event dates unknown
entries.attested: A chronicle tells separate stories of city deaths, household exclusion, child refuge, and new families.
entries.unknown: The text does not show which human groups lost which land in these stories.
entries.next_step: Review each story and its land outcome without guessed links to people alive today.

entries.name: Village land rights in a royal charter from Udayendiram
entries.place_and_era: South Asia. The text names the village as Udayachandramangalam. The date of the event remains unknown.
entries.attested: The charter reports loss of prior holders' land rights for a royal grant.
entries.unknown: The exact rights, later possession and loss of homes remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Check how the atlas shows this case with an unknown date.

entries.name: Violent deaths at Cherry
entries.place_and_era: Cherry in the Lower Tennessee Valley. Dye places the site in the Archaic period. Exact dates remain unknown.
entries.attested: Dye discusses a possible massacre and violent deaths at Cherry. He links the pattern to a possible dispute over resources.
entries.unknown: The account does not establish a change in land access, control, or homes. Windover is a separate site and question.
entries.next_step: Define any link between the violence and a change in use of the site or homes.

entries.name: Virgin Lands settlement
entries.place_and_era: Northern Kazakhstan; program began in 1954, later bounds unknown
entries.attested: The sources describe state-led farm settlement and use of pasture for crops.
entries.unknown: This does not prove that the land was empty or all local people left.
entries.next_step: Resolve links to other steppe and deportation cases before atlas use.

entries.name: War captives in Songhay farming settlements
entries.place_and_era: Songhay; Askiya Muhammad’s reign, 1493–1529
entries.attested: The reference work describes farm settlements for people enslaved in war.
entries.unknown: Their origin tracts and specific destination settlements remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Find a bounded capture and settlement process in the sources.

entries.name: War splits Buzinza
entries.place_and_era: Buzinza, Rusubi and the coast. The source sets the split at the start of the nineteenth century.
entries.attested: The chapter says a war for the throne split Buzinza. Rusubi and the coast broke away under named rulers.
entries.unknown: This was an internal struggle. The account does not establish foreign conquest or household flight. Kakaraza had earlier fought off attacks.
entries.next_step: This is a candidate for study. Resolve the unit and its limits before any case assessment.

entries.name: Western grants redirect taxes
entries.place_and_era: In the west, along the Bhagirathi-Hooghly basin. The chapter sets these grants after the ninth century.
entries.attested: The chapter says villagers had to pay the land donees in cash and kind. The fields were already in use.
entries.unknown: The chapter does not report eviction. It leaves open whether former users lost rights or whether tax claims changed hands.
entries.next_step: Define the grant group and the rights that changed. A fiscal change alone does not settle a land loss.

entries.name: What befell the Poet people?
entries.place_and_era: The Kapoeta river, in the 1820s as the source tells it.
entries.attested: The chapter says Korwakol and Jie Rengen joined to destroy a Poet farm community.
entries.unknown: The fate of its people and homes remains unclear. Destruction alone does not tell us who died or left.
entries.next_step: This is a source lead. Resolve the land or home-loss unit before any case assessment.

entries.name: What links Ipiutak warfare and later change?
entries.place_and_era: Northern and western Alaska. The source gives broad age ranges, not a firm event date.
entries.attested:
The 2018 report describes violent injuries. It also reports later population replacement. It does not link those injuries to one forced loss of homes or land.

Anderson reports houses, camps and later house abandonment at Cape Krusenstern. He also describes resource use. House 30 burned. Three partly burned skeletons lay beneath the fallen wood.

Anderson reports a possible earlier wound in one adult. He interprets the positions of the children as possible attempts to dig down and escape.
entries.unknown:
The report also notes trade and some intermarriage. Ipiutak is an archaeological label, not proof of one modern people. Dates and the causes of change remain unclear.

The cause of the fire is unknown. The chapter does not establish an attack, a forced move or the fate of the whole community.

Raghavan discusses Dorset and Thule farther east. That text reports no massacre evidence. It does not rule out the Ipiutak injuries.
entries.next_step: Keep the house fire and later replacement claim separate. Ask whether a source links a human act to loss of homes, land use or control. The Ipiutak chapter and its figures and plates give context. They do not resolve that link.

entries.name: Where did Jaki extend his rule?
entries.place_and_era: Madi country. The source gives no exact date for the extension.
entries.attested: The chapter says Jaki and his sons extended their rule. In Terego, Madi elders accepted Banale as chief.
entries.unknown: The account does not state how Jaki gained rule. The elders accepted Banale. The idea that they sought to avoid Jaki remains open.
entries.next_step: This is a candidate for study. Resolve the unit and its limits before any case assessment.

entries.name: Whistling Elk burned lodges
entries.place_and_era: Whistling Elk; departure date unknown
entries.attested: Excavators found a burned inner roof and a mostly unburned outer roof. Pots and tools lay on the floor. The authors infer a hasty departure and propose an attack as one possible cause.
entries.unknown: The cause, forced departure and later control of the land remain unknown. The finds do not prove an attack.
entries.next_step: Find evidence for the cause of departure and any loss of homes or land.
source_citations: Larry J. Zimmerman, Initial Coalescent: A Blending of Cultures, South Dakota Archaeology, Educational Series 8, PDF page 3; publication year and printed pagination unverified.

Dennis L. Toom and Kenneth L. Kvamme, “The ‘Big House’ At Whistling Elk Village (39HU242): Geophysical Findings and Archaeological Truths,” Plains Anthropologist 47(180) (2002), printed pages 5–16 (PDF pages 2–13).

Kenneth L. Kvamme, “Archaeological prospecting in fortified Great Plains villages: new insights through data fusion, visualization and testing,” Archaeological Prospection: 4th International Conference on Archaeological Prospection (2001), printed pages 141–143 (PDF pages 1–3); additional publication, not an established independent witness.

entries.name: Who sought refuge by the Nile?
entries.place_and_era: Pakwac-Pawir and lands west of Cwa. The source gives drought and refuge context.
entries.attested: The chapter says the influx apparently weakened the Paluo position. It describes a control dispute and Nyipir and Tifool followers who moved west.
entries.unknown: The famine, refuge influx and control conflict need distinct units. The axe is part of a tradition. Drought alone does not prove a forced land loss.
entries.next_step: This is a source lead. Resolve the land or home-loss unit before any case assessment.

entries.name: Who split the lands of Bugesera?
entries.place_and_era: Bugesera. The source gives both the end of the eighteenth century and the start of the nineteenth.
entries.attested: The chapter says Rwanda and Burundi split Bugesera between them. It describes a loss of rule over a named land.
entries.unknown: The exact boundary and local rights remain unknown. The source does not report blanket eviction. An earlier king fled in a separate episode.
entries.next_step: This is a candidate for study. Resolve the unit and its limits before any case assessment.

entries.name: Who took rule in Mubari?
entries.place_and_era: Mubari. The source sets the occupation in the eighteenth century.
entries.attested: The chapter says Rwanda occupied Mubari. It also describes Kivu shore settlements and other states that retreated or broke up.
entries.unknown: Those outcomes differ. Some old powers kept their independence under a kind of protectorate. The account does not prove one shared tract or mass home loss.
entries.next_step: This is a candidate for study. Resolve the unit and its limits before any case assessment.

entries.name: Who took the Bongera lands?
entries.place_and_era: Bongera lands in Rwanda. The source gives no date for this annexation.
entries.attested: The chapter says Cyirima Rugwe annexed the Bongera lands.
entries.unknown: The early origin of the principality does not date this act. The local rights and residents remain unknown. Lack of an exact year does not rule it out.
entries.next_step: This is a candidate for study. Resolve its scope; an exact year is not a rule for entry.

entries.name: Why did kings choose the island?
entries.place_and_era: Bukerebe. The source places the account in its eighteenth-century narrative.
entries.attested: The chapter says the Tatoga threat forced the kings to put their capital on the island. It does not name a former site.
entries.unknown: The former site and affected residents remain unknown. This does not prove that all people on the peninsula left or that Tatoga conquered it.
entries.next_step: This is a source lead. Resolve the land or home-loss unit before any case assessment.

entries.name: Why did people leave Buganda?
entries.place_and_era: Buganda to nearby states. The chapter describes a long process with no single act date.
entries.attested: The chapter links royal control to long rebellions and violence. It says more people went into exile in nearby states.
entries.unknown: The account does not identify one purge, one ruler or one group of exiles. Exact homes, destinations and dates remain unclear.
entries.next_step: This is a source lead. Resolve the land or home-loss unit before any case assessment.

entries.name: Winter clans enter a valley and settle
entries.place_and_era: North America, in the source account. The Snow-water valley and its springs have no exact modern map location. The date is unknown.
entries.attested: The 1896 English account by Cushing says the People of Winter fought into Snow-water valley. They first settled at springs that gave out mud.
entries.unknown: The account does not prove that these acts took place. It does not name prior residents or say that they lost homes. The date, exact site and length of the stay are unknown.
entries.next_step: Find evidence for the time, place and prior residents. Keep their fate unknown.

entries.name: Wintuan and Maiduan movement question
entries.place_and_era: California; source’s approximate relative date remains unverified
entries.attested: A study suggests southward moves. Golla adds a possible Wintuan spread based on language patterns.
entries.unknown: The link to a forced move or land loss is unknown. The excerpt is cut short; a Maiduan claim remains unverified.
entries.next_step: Find the rest of the section. Keep the two groups and their land questions distinct.

entries.name: Wolof expulsion in Koly’s conquests
entries.place_and_era: Futa Toro river valleys; early sixteenth-century context
entries.attested: The reference work reports a tradition of conquest and expulsion from river valleys.
entries.unknown: The exact campaigns, groups and land outcomes remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Review the tradition and identify a bounded affected tract.

entries.name: Woodland violence and settlement in the Illinois valley
entries.place_and_era: Lower and central Illinois River valley; Late Woodland period, event dates unknown
entries.attested: Wilson reports skeletal injuries and interprets changes in settlements as partly due to hostilities.
entries.unknown: The chapter does not establish a forced departure from a defined place or the loss of land rights.
entries.next_step: Read the cited field reports for evidence of who left, why they left and what happened to their land.

entries.name: Young men leave elders
entries.place_and_era: The chapter describes several societies. It gives no one local episode or act date.
entries.attested: The chapter says some young men left to escape elders' control. The elders controlled cattle and marriage. They kept young men dependent.
entries.unknown: The local society and episode remain unclear. Pressure and movement need a clear land or home-loss unit. A lack of names or numbers does not rule it out.
entries.next_step: This is a source lead. Resolve the land or home-loss unit before any case assessment.

entries.name: Yuan removal in the Sayan-Altai
entries.place_and_era: Sayan-Altai; source places the account near 1293
entries.attested: A scholar says Kublai removed local residents and settled other people there.
entries.unknown: The text does not show the exact date, full scope, or long-term result.
entries.next_step: Review which people and actions overlap with the related Yuan removals.

entries.name: Zhalanash violence during return
entries.place_and_era: Zhalanash; return-period context, incident date unknown
entries.attested: A study reports hostility and deaths near a Cossack allotment.
entries.unknown: The passage does not show a defined land seizure or removal process.
entries.next_step: Identify the affected people and a direct land or residence outcome.

entries.name: Beal reports a loss of rule at Pushkalavati
entries.place_and_era: A city in Gandhara, as named by Beal. The exact site and date remain unknown.
entries.attested: Beal gives this report in a note to his translation. He says Alexander besieged and took the city from Astes or Hasti. He says Alexander put Sangaeus or Sanjaya in charge.
entries.unknown: The note does not establish the fate of the people in this city or the former ruler. The date, exact site and length of new rule remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Seek evidence for the date and effects on residents. Keep this reported capture separate from claims about forced moves.

entries.name: Bhir lane walls and public access
entries.place_and_era: Small lanes at Bhir Mound, Taxila, with the west end of Lane 2 as an example. The date remains unknown.
entries.attested: Marshall says cross-walls closed some small lanes and stopped public shortcuts. He thought those lanes seemed to belong to the houses beside them.
entries.unknown: The prior public right and any change in that right remain unknown. The account does not name who put up the walls or establish force, conflict or loss of homes.
entries.next_step: Assess whether the lane barrier took a prior right of public access. Keep the described barrier distinct from a proved loss of rights. The cause of the closure remains unknown.

entries.name: Bhir sack and possible loss of use
entries.place_and_era: The West Group at Bhir Mound, Taxila. Marshall places the sack in the early second century BCE. The date remains unassigned here.
entries.attested: Marshall reports that Bactrian Greeks sacked the city. He thinks the West Group buildings probably burnt at that time. He saw no sign of later buildings there.
entries.unknown: The link between the sack and fire remains uncertain. Fire alone does not show who caused it or what happened to residents. The end of use does not prove permanent loss.
entries.next_step: Keep this reported sack and probable end of use as a separate research record. Seek evidence about the date and residents.

entries.name: Reported loss of Murrelet-point fort
entries.place_and_era: Murrelet-point fort in a Tlingit oral account. Its modern site and the date of the attack remain unknown.
entries.attested: The account says a southern war party destroyed the fort and captured women there. A captive woman then named another town. That next attack is a separate event.
entries.unknown: The account includes spirit stories. The modern groups and the number of captives remain unknown. It does not show a permanent loss of land or a change in title.
entries.next_step: Assess this reported fort loss as one event. Keep the other war events separate. Preserve the unknown date and the limits of the oral account.

entries.name: Reported loss of village rights in Sonpur
entries.place_and_era: 12 villages in Sonpur. The date of the loss remains unknown. The 1831 grievances give context, not an exact date.
entries.attested: Dalton reports that a royal grant holder gave the 12 villages to Sikh farmers. Singrai Manki lost his village rights and control.
entries.unknown: The source does not establish that all residents left. The full village list, land title and duration of the loss remain unknown. The original deposition remains unread.
entries.next_step: Keep this reported loss of village rights as one research record. Seek evidence about the date and effects on residents.

entries.name: Reported loss of homes in eastern Wisconsin
entries.place_and_era: Eastern Wisconsin. The source gives regional dates up to AD 1300. Dates for each act remain unknown.
entries.attested: Dye reports that Oneota groups drove local groups out or absorbed them. He reports later Oneota control of eastern Wisconsin.
entries.unknown: The cause of the Aztalan departure remains uncertain. The account does not establish the fate of each group.
entries.next_step: Keep the reported loss of homes or control as one research record. Seek evidence about the dates and each group's fate.

entries.name: Flight and return at Norris Farms
entries.place_and_era: Norris Farms 36 in the Illinois River valley. The source places village life around AD 1300. Dates of each attack remain unknown.
entries.attested: Dye reports repeated attacks, flight and later return. Tubbs describes newer evidence that Oneota and Middle Mississippian people lived together at Morton Village. Her account retains both violence and cooperation.
entries.unknown: The place of each attack, the attackers and the burial party remain unclear. Newer, preliminary finds do not support an earlier theory of restricted access to food. This does not rule out brief flight or prove permanent loss of the village.
entries.next_step: Keep the flight and return account distinct from the theory of restricted access to food. Check the original attack studies.
source_citations: David H. Dye, War Paths, Peace Paths (2009), chapter 8, printed pages 130–131 (PDF pages 151–152); consulted synthesis, cited originals unread.

Ryan Maureen Tubbs, Ethnic Identity and Diet in the Central Illinois River Valley (Michigan State University doctoral dissertation, 2013), sections 3.4–3.5, printed pages 44–58 (PDF pages 63–77); these sections only, full dissertation and isotope results unread.

entries.name: Etowah: violent loss and later use
entries.place_and_era: Etowah, northern Georgia. The 2024 study places its violent collapse around 1325-1375 and later use by about 1400.
entries.attested: Dye gives an attack as one possible cause of abandonment. Sullivan and coauthors report a violent attack and loss of the town's former political role. They also report later use of the site.
entries.unknown: The attackers, the number affected and the fate of those who left remain unknown. Later use does not prove that the former residents returned. Both accounts draw on King, so they do not give two independent checks.
entries.next_step: Assess the form of the attack and loss of residence at Etowah. Keep that loss separate from later use of the site.
source_citations: David H. Dye (2009), War Paths, Peace Paths, chapter 9, pp. 153-154 (PDF pp. 174-175).

Lynne P. Sullivan, Kevin E. Smith, Scott C. Meeks and Shawn M. Patch (2024), "Tracking Mississippian Migrations from the Central Mississippi Valley to the Ridge and Valley with a Unified Absolute Chronology," American Antiquity 89(2): 221-237. DOI: 10.1017/aaq.2024.1. Relevant pages: 223, 225, 227, 229 and 232.

entries.name: Sri Lanka: proposed Naga arrival in the Iron Age
entries.place_and_era: Sri Lanka. The Iron Age is source context. The time and place of any land loss remain unknown.
entries.attested: Deraniyagala proposes that people he links to the Nagas moved into land used by Yakka hunter-gatherers. This is a model.
entries.unknown: The people, route and land effects remain unresolved. The source also allows diffusion, local descent, shared ancestry, gene flow and drift.
entries.next_step: Assess who moved and what happened to prior land use. Keep the source model and its alternatives open.

entries.name: Sri Lanka: wet-rice growth and pressure on Yakka/Vadda life
entries.place_and_era: Sri Lanka. The early rice and town context gives no date or mapped area for this process.
entries.attested: Deraniyagala offers a model of Sinhalese wet-rice town growth. In his model, this growth forced Yakka/Vadda groups into a relict state. He also describes partial symbiosis. The groups kept their identity.
entries.unknown: The bounded people, place and land-use effects remain unresolved. This claim of pressure is a model, not an observed expulsion.
entries.next_step: Assess the claimed pressure and its land-use effects. Keep partial symbiosis and retained identity in view.

entries.name: Vijitanagara: the text says people fled from the river bank to this city
entries.place_and_era: Sri Lanka. The chronicle places this refuge in its ancient past. The date and exact route remain unknown.
entries.attested: The Mahavamsa says people on the river bank escaped death and sought protection in Vijitanagara. It calls them Damilas. This is a source term, with no fixed modern ethnic match.
entries.unknown: The people were soldiers, other residents, or both. Their mix remains unknown. Their number, homes and later fate also remain unknown. The later siege does not settle their fate. The chapter joins religious claims that devalue the dead with grief and a final adverse view of deaths from greed.
entries.next_step: Assess who moved and what happened to their homes or land. Keep refuge and military retreat open as possible parts of this movement.

entries.name: Vijitanagara: the text says the king took the city in a siege
entries.place_and_era: Sri Lanka. The chronicle places this siege in its ancient past. The date and exact site remain unknown.
entries.attested: The Mahavamsa reports that Dutthagamani took the fortified city after a siege. It describes deaths at the gates and in the streets. The narrator says he destroyed the city.
entries.unknown: The scope of the damage and the fate of residents remain unknown. The account does not establish total loss of life or a new resident group. Religious speech devalues the dead. The chapter also gives grief, restraint and rites for Elara. Its last verse condemns deaths from greed. Its large totals lack a verified count.
entries.next_step: Keep the reported siege as one research record. Its effects on residents remain unknown.

entries.name: Los Angeles land and water purchases in Owens Valley
entries.place_and_era: Owens Valley, California, in the early twentieth century and the 1920s. Exact process dates remain unknown.
entries.attested: The Commission describes City land and water purchases, water export and groundwater use. It says settlers lost land and Paiute people lost ranch jobs.
entries.unknown: The account does not define which Native land uses or homes these purchases displaced. Job loss alone does not prove land seizure. The later land exchange is a separate process.
entries.next_step: Trace Native land and water use through the purchases. Distinguish forced loss from ordinary sales and the later exchange.

entries.name: Owens Valley Paiute land exchange in the 1930s
entries.place_and_era: Bishop, Big Pine and Lone Pine, Owens Valley, California. The source gives both 1937 and 1939 for the exchange.
entries.attested: The Commission describes a federal and City land exchange. It reports a smaller occupied land base afterward. A plan named three valley reservations. Water export was one of several motives.
entries.unknown: Reports proposed moves outside the valley; a later plan named sites within it. The extent of actual moves remains unknown. Consent and force remain unresolved. Acreages and current water rights remain unverified.
entries.next_step: Define the affected people, former tracts and land loss. Keep proposals distinct from actual land change. Resolve dates without an exact date rule.

entries.name: Owens Valley Paiute removal to Fort Tejon and return
entries.place_and_era: Owens Valley and Fort Tejon in California. Settler entry dates to the 1800s in this account. Removal and return dates remain unknown.
entries.attested: The Owens Valley Indian Water Commission describes forced removal to Fort Tejon after conflict and massacres. Ancestors returned. They faced loss of land access and few choices beyond ranch labor.
entries.unknown: The number removed, return routes and full land loss remain unknown. The people continued to live in the valley. This question overlaps the broad California settler case.
entries.next_step: Keep this forced removal and return as one research record. The death toll and terms of labor remain unknown.

entries.name: Western Mono settlement inferred from shared speech
entries.place_and_era: Western Sierra Nevada, near the upper San Joaquin, Kings and Kaweah rivers. The date is unknown.
entries.attested: Kroeber infers a recent western Mono settlement from similar speech across the Sierra. He names western groups and their neighbors.
entries.unknown: The account gives no arrival date or land seizure. Earlier residents and land outcomes remain unknown. Kroeber leaves group ties and boundaries unclear. His account includes colonial bias and continued Mono presence.
entries.next_step: Define the people and land in this question. Compare it with the broad Numic spread case; do not assign its dates or victims.

entries.name: Mayurasarman: a reported grant of land
entries.place_and_era: The poem names land from the western sea to Prehara. The Prehara boundary and the dates of the acts remain unknown.
entries.attested: The translated praise poem says Pallava rulers made Mayurasarman a friend. He served them, then received land under a pact against entry by others.
entries.unknown: This grant does not establish that people lost their homes. The prior rights, scope of control, and length of the grant remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Keep the reported land grant as one research record. Its use on the ground and effects on prior users remain unknown.

entries.name: Mayurasarman and the base he made in a forest
entries.place_and_era: The poem names a forest near Sriparvata. Kielhorn links that place to Srisaila. The dates and the bounds remain unknown.
entries.attested: The translated praise poem says Mayurasarman defeated Pallava frontier guards and made a base in the forest. It also praises his raids.
entries.unknown: A base alone does not establish a loss of land or access. The forest is not known to match the later grant.
entries.next_step: Determine whether the forest base caused loss of land or access. Keep that question separate from the later grant.

entries.name: Kakustha and kin who sought a place of refuge
entries.place_and_era: The poem places refuge in Kakustha territory. The dates, the home tracts, and the bounds remain unknown.
entries.attested: The translated praise poem says stronger parties harassed relatives. The relatives entered his land with their belongings and found shelter.
entries.unknown: Shelter does not establish a forced move or the loss of a home. It does not establish a loss for earlier residents.
entries.next_step: Trace the pressure at the place of origin and any loss of homes. Assess any loss of land at the place of shelter on its own.

entries.name: Burned sites and violent deaths in Gallina
entries.place_and_era: Gallina, New Mexico; medieval source context. Dates for each event remain unknown.
entries.attested: Authors report burned structures at home sites, often with food stores. Some contexts include unburied people who died from violence.
entries.unknown: Fire causes and the loss of specific homes remain unresolved. Captivity is a theory. The source does not prove one forced regional departure.
entries.next_step: Review the reported sites to define each process and its effect on homes or stores. Keep other fire causes in view.

entries.name: A field grant at Nasik
entries.place_and_era: Near Nasik in western India; ancient period.
entries.attested: A royal order grants a named field to monks. It names a man who held the field before.
entries.unknown: The text does not explain the fate of people who used the field.
entries.next_step: Check whether the grant took away earlier rights to the field.

entries.name: Home loss in Embobut Forest
entries.place_and_era: Kenya, from late 2017. The report dates to 2018.
entries.attested: The rights commission reports forced evictions and burned homes. Its account uses interviews and site visits.
entries.unknown: The report gives no end date for the forced moves. It does not state where all affected people went.
entries.next_step: Prepare this reviewed case for the atlas. Keep its unknown scale and later outcome clear.

entries.name: Changes at coastal shell rings
entries.place_and_era: The report covers the southeast coast of North America. It concerns sites before written records.
entries.attested: The report reviews ring sites and changes in their use. It weighs sea rise, resource shifts and possible conflict.
entries.unknown: Possible conflict is a theory in this report. That theory does not establish a forced move or loss of land.
entries.next_step: Trace the claims to site studies. Look for human acts that caused loss of homes or land use.

entries.name: Forced move from the northern Kurils
entries.place_and_era: The move was from the northern Kurils to Shikotan. It took place in 1884.
entries.attested: A university page reports a forced move in 1884. The government of Japan forced the move. The page names northern Kuril Ainu as the people moved. It names Shikotan as their new home.
entries.unknown: This is a later summary, not an account from 1884. The route, length of stay and terms of return are unknown. Later population decline does not show a death count or its cause.
entries.next_step: Prepare this reviewed case for the atlas. Keep its scale and later history unknown.

entries.name: The exile of Anwar
entries.place_and_era: Sonargaon in Bengal. The year is not known.
entries.attested: Eaton reports an exile. Raja Ganesh sent Anwar to Sonargaon.
entries.unknown: The source names Anwar. It does not name people who went with him. Whether this claim fits a case stays open.
entries.next_step: Review the named exile under the case rule. Keep any wider group unknown.

entries.name: The exile and return of Ala al-Haq
entries.place_and_era: From the capital to Sonargaon. The year is not known.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that Sultan Sikandar sent Ala al-Haq into exile. He states that the exile ended after several years. Ala al-Haq was then free to return.
entries.unknown: Eaton cites a Sufi text for this claim. The exile names one man. Whether this claim fits a case stays open.
entries.next_step: Review the exile and return as one claim. Keep the later return in view.

entries.name: The forced move of Tawwama
entries.place_and_era: From Delhi to Sonargaon. The year is not known.
entries.attested: A note in Eaton reports an exile. The Delhi court sent Tawwama to Sonargaon.
entries.unknown: The note names Tawwama, not his followers. It gives no year for the exile or return. Whether this claim fits a case stays open.
entries.next_step: Review the named exile under the case rule. Keep the earlier move from Bukhara separate.

entries.name: The capture of Sylhet
entries.place_and_era: Sylhet town in Bengal.
entries.attested: Eaton cites a stone text for this claim. It names Sikandar Khan Ghazi as the conqueror. It puts the capture in 1303 or 1304.
entries.unknown: Ibn Battuta saw Shah Jalal much later. This visit does not attest to the earlier capture. The first site of the stone is not clear.
entries.next_step: Review the town control claim on its own. Keep the saint and the conqueror separate.

entries.name: A temple site in Deva Mahal
entries.place_and_era: Deva Mahal, a port in Bengal.
entries.attested: A late account names Jalal al-Din Tabrizi. It says that he pulled down a temple. It says that a Sufi rest house took its place.
entries.unknown: Eaton sees a later model of conquest in this account. The exact year is not known. Land bought for a kitchen is a separate claim.
entries.next_step: Review the claim and its source limits. Keep the temple site and bought land separate.

entries.name: A question about Shah Jalal and his followers
entries.place_and_era: Sylhet and the Bengal frontier.
entries.attested: Eaton cites a later account of Shah Jalal and his followers. It reports shares and leave to marry. Eaton links these to homes and local ties.
entries.unknown: The people and their rights remain unclear. Marriage or a new home does not prove forced removal. The town capture is a related but separate claim.
entries.next_step: Trace the people and the rights in the account. Keep any link to the town capture open.

entries.name: A crop levy near Habiganj
entries.place_and_era: Near Habiganj in Bengal.
entries.attested: Eaton cites a report by Ibn Battuta. It describes local people who grew crops. The report calls them non-Muslims under protection. A levy took a share of their crop.
entries.unknown: This is a tax report. It does not state a loss of land or homes. Any change in local rights stays open.
entries.next_step: Review the local rights and the levy. Keep a tax claim apart from land loss.

entries.name: Kaikaus and southeast Bengal
entries.place_and_era: Southeast Bengal. The report dates the conquest to 1291.
entries.attested: Eaton reports a conquest under Kaikaus and a change in rule.
entries.unknown: The local rights and the fate of the people remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Prepare this case for the atlas. Its local effects and later history stay unknown.

entries.name: A conquest at Sonargaon
entries.place_and_era: Sonargaon in Bengal. The report concerns a medieval reign.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that Fakhr al-Din took control of Sonargaon.
entries.unknown: The date of the act and its effect on local people remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Define the tract and the change in control.

entries.name: A conquest in Kamrup
entries.place_and_era: Kamrup. The report dates the conquest to 1358.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that Sikandar took control of Kamrup.
entries.unknown: The local rights and the fate of the people remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Keep this conquest apart from the later report under Husain Shah.

entries.name: New rule in east Bengal
entries.place_and_era: East Bengal. The report dates the new conquest to 1420.
entries.attested: Eaton reports a new conquest after a revolt. He names Jalal al-Din Muhammad as the ruler.
entries.unknown: The tract and its link to the Deva revolt remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Define the tract and the change in control. Keep the two reports apart.

entries.name: Nobles and homes in the capital
entries.place_and_era: Bengal. The date of the residence rule is unknown.
entries.attested: Eaton states that nobles had to keep homes in the capital.
entries.unknown: The report does not state how this rule changed their other homes.
entries.next_step: Define the residence rule and its effect on homes.

entries.name: Property after a noble died
entries.place_and_era: Bengal. The date of the property rule is unknown.
entries.attested: Eaton describes a rule that gave half the property to the crown when a noble died.
entries.unknown: The report does not state which rights or land this rule affected.
entries.next_step: Define the property rights and the effect of the rule.

entries.name: Homes and fields at Hirakud
entries.place_and_era: Near Sambalpur, India. The book gives figures for 1954-55 and a summer 1955 start.
entries.attested: The book reports state-led moves as water covered homes and fields near Sambalpur. The book also reports plans to flood some land in Madhya Pradesh. Some buyers got less land as prices rose.
entries.unknown: The last move dates and later returns remain unclear. The book does not show full payment or new land for all people. Land rights for each person remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Prepare this case for the atlas. Its final move dates and later outcomes stay unclear.

entries.name: Ban on cutting trees
entries.place_and_era: Seraikella State, India. The start date is unknown; fieldwork took place in 1925.
entries.attested: The authors say the State did not allow the Ho to cut trees. They link the lack of firewood to a change from cremation to burial.
entries.unknown: The start date, reach and enforcement of the ban are unknown here. The account does not establish eviction or loss of homes.
entries.next_step: Assess the loss of resource use as a separate unit. Keep the ban report apart from its stated link to funeral rites.

entries.name: Burial ban at Paharpur
entries.place_and_era: Seraikella area, India. The event date is unknown; fieldwork took place in 1925.
entries.attested: The authors use kili as a term for clan. The authors say the Mundri kili took control of a burial ground once linked to the Haiburu kili. They say the site no longer allowed Haiburu burial.
entries.unknown: The source does not state how or when the site changed hands. It does not establish force, deaths or loss of homes.
entries.next_step: Assess the loss of burial use under the atlas rules. Keep dates, force and effects on residents unknown unless supported.

entries.name: Homes at Hulas
entries.place_and_era: Hulas, northern India. The report describes homes from Harappan times and later periods. Dates remain uncertain.
entries.attested: Excavators found homes, hearths and rebuilt floors. The report places later homes north of an earlier settlement.
entries.unknown: The report does not state why the earlier settlement ended. It does not state whether anyone forced people out or where they went.
entries.next_step: Examine why use of the old homes ended. Examine how later people came to use nearby land.

entries.name: Sirsukh foundation and land control
entries.place_and_era: Near Taxila, now in Pakistan. Ancient era; the event year is unknown.
entries.attested: Marshall says Kushan rulers left Sirkap and built a new walled city at Sirsukh.
entries.unknown: The account does not establish a loss of prior land use or control. Forced moves from Sirkap also remain unproven.
entries.next_step: Find whether the new city caused or secured a loss of prior land use or control.

entries.name: Breaks in use at Volivoli II
entries.place_and_era: Volivoli II shelter, Viti Levu, Fiji. The dates of the breaks are unknown.
entries.attested: Anderson and Clark infer repeated use of this shelter, with breaks when people left it.
entries.unknown: The deposits do not show why use stopped or whether people lost access.
entries.next_step: Find whether an act caused people to lose use of, or access to, this shelter.

entries.name: Ugaga land gift
entries.place_and_era: Ugaga is an island in Fiji. The gift dates to around 1830. The account notes later claims in 1997.
entries.attested: The account says Ugaga was a gift to the Vunivalu of Serua. The gift paid for the defence of Naceva against Rukua.
entries.unknown: The account does not establish which prior rights changed. Claims noted in 1997 do not settle rights today.
entries.next_step: Find which prior rights to land, use or access changed through this gift.

entries.name: Huron villages forced to move
entries.place_and_era: Huron villages in northeast North America. A report from 1615 describes a retreat before that year.
entries.attested: Keener reports that Onondaga attacks forced Huron villages to move. The former sites are not known.
entries.unknown: The move year, routes and later fate of all those who moved remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Keep this retreat apart from the later Huron and Petun defeats.

entries.name: A fort burned at Stadocona
entries.place_and_era: Stadocona, in the St. Lawrence area. The source dates the attack to 1533.
entries.attested: Keener reports that Toudamans attacked and burned a fort. People were driven from it and killed as they came out.
entries.unknown: This attack does not fix the later fate of all St. Lawrence peoples. The source uses more than one way to state the losses.
entries.next_step: Keep this fort attack apart from the wider loss of St. Lawrence towns.

entries.name: Loss of a Mohawk village
entries.place_and_era: A Mohawk village. Keener dates its loss to 1626 but does not name the site.
entries.attested: Keener reports that Mahican forces destroyed this village.
entries.unknown: The source does not fix where all its people went, or when a return was possible.
entries.next_step: Trace later use of the village site. Do not assume that all Mohawk people left.

entries.name: Capture of a Fire Nation village
entries.place_and_era: A walled Fire Nation village. The source dates the siege to 1642.
entries.attested: Keener reports that Neutral forces took the village after a siege. The account reports deaths and captives.
entries.unknown: The exact site and later fate of all captives remain unknown. Fire Nation is the source name.
entries.next_step: Keep the capture apart from later attacks on Neutral villages.

entries.name: A lost village of the Susquehannock people
entries.place_and_era: A Susquehannock village. The source dates its loss to July 1652 and marks the place as uncertain.
entries.attested: Keener lists the village as destroyed. The entry also reports captives and Iroquois deaths.
entries.unknown: The exact site, later use and fate of all residents remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Keep this loss apart from the reported move into Maryland in 1675.

entries.name: Loss of a Seneca village
entries.place_and_era: A Seneca village. The source dates this loss to June 1654.
entries.attested: Keener reports its destruction in a clash between Iroquois and Erie forces. The entry says Seneca warriors lost.
entries.unknown: The order of the group names does not fix who attacked. Later use of the site remains unknown.
entries.next_step: Keep this loss apart from later attacks on Erie places.

entries.name: Assault on a defended place in 1660
entries.place_and_era: A place held by a French force. Keener dates the assault to 1660 but does not name the site here.
entries.attested: Keener reports that attackers used shields and broke into the walled place. Its defenders were killed or captured.
entries.unknown: This does not prove that a whole town was forced out. A table entry has a possible link to this clash. That link is not settled.
entries.next_step: Keep the place use and the possible table link distinct.

entries.name: A lost village of the Abenaki people
entries.place_and_era: An Abenaki village in New England. The source dates its loss to late 1661.
entries.attested: Keener lists the village as destroyed.
entries.unknown: The exact site, later use and fate of all residents remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Trace this village loss. Do not treat it as the fate of all Abenaki people.

entries.name: Mohawk villages destroyed after people left
entries.place_and_era: Mohawk villages in Iroquoia. The source dates the French attack to 1666.
entries.attested: Keener reports that French forces destroyed villages after their people left. His table lists four villages.
