entries.unknown: The attack does not explain why people first left. Whether a return was possible remains open.
entries.next_step: Keep the destruction and the cause of the earlier departure separate.

entries.name: A Fox village destroyed
entries.place_and_era: A Fox village in the Great Lakes area. The source dates its loss to March 1670.
entries.attested: Keener reports that Seneca forces destroyed the village. He also reports captives and deaths.
entries.unknown: The exact site, later use and fate of all residents remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Keep this village loss apart from later settler expansion in the region.

entries.name: Damage to property held by the French
entries.place_and_era: The source dates this clash to July 1688. It does not give a full account of the French property.
entries.attested: Keener reports extensive damage to French property in a clash.
entries.unknown: The account does not say which homes, land or other property were harmed. The link to loss of place use remains open.
entries.next_step: Find what property was harmed and what use of a place was lost.

entries.name: French settlements burned near Montreal
entries.place_and_era: French settlements near Montreal. The source dates this attack to November 1689.
entries.attested: Keener reports that settlements were burned.
entries.unknown: The exact bounds, later use and fate of all residents remain unknown. This is not the same claim as French farm expansion.
entries.next_step: Trace later use of these places. Do not assume that all residents left.

entries.name: Recovery of lands in the 1680s
entries.place_and_era: Some lands once taken by Iroquois forces. Keener describes their recovery by the 1680s.
entries.attested: Keener reports that their opponents won back some lands.
entries.unknown: He does not name the tracts or set out a full return of former residents.
entries.next_step: Find which lands and changes in control this report describes.

entries.name: Barrie village formation and earlier land use
entries.place_and_era: Simcoe County, Ontario. Sutton places the village at about 1280 to 1330 CE. A test on maize gave a later date.
entries.attested: Sutton reports houses, middens and evidence of crops and food use. He argues that migrants founded a permanent village and kept links to groups farther south.
entries.unknown: The report does not identify the exact source community. The rights and fate of earlier users remain unclear. It does not establish a forced move. The final abandonment of the village is also unclear.
entries.next_step: Trace earlier use and the later history of the same village tract. Keep the date conflict and gaps in local rights evidence visible.

entries.name: How life in the hilltop villages at Sanganakallu changed
entries.place_and_era: These hill sites lie in south India. Use declined from about 1400 to 1200 BCE. Some activity lasted later.
entries.attested: The study finds that hilltop villages and craft sites fell out of use. Its authors link the change to water access and social choices. People still used nearby plains and a rock shelter.
entries.unknown: The study does not settle whether people moved away or their numbers fell. It does not establish forced removal or loss of land access.
entries.next_step: Trace how residence and land use changed. Abandonment alone does not show forced removal.

entries.name: Water access and shared places in southern India
entries.place_and_era: The study covers the Tungabhadra and Krishna river regions in south India. It looks at changes from about 1200 BCE.
entries.attested: The authors discuss elite use of once-shared places and control of water access. They link these changes to new social relations.
entries.unknown: Which uses and access changed in each place, and how this affected people, remain open.
entries.next_step: Study changes in shared use and water access apart from changes in hilltop life.

entries.name: Later homes near Horseshoe Lake
entries.place_and_era: This study concerns Horseshoe Lake in Illinois. The lake is near Cahokia. It traces later use from about 1400 to 1700.
entries.attested: The study finds renewed Indigenous use by about 1500. It points to growth toward about 1650. In the authors' view, hunts are one possible use.
entries.unknown: The lake evidence does not name each group or explain each move. The roles of climate, disease and human movement remain unclear. It does not by itself show forced removal.
entries.next_step: Study changes in local homes and land use. Keep earlier lake users distinct from later named groups.

entries.name: A pressured move to Horseshoe Lake
entries.place_and_era: This question concerns a reported move in 1735 from a mission near Cahokia to Horseshoe Lake. Later questions concern 1752 and the first half of the 1800s.
entries.attested: White and colleagues report a move by Cahokia group members in 1735. They link it to tensions with French colonists. They also report forced moves to Oklahoma in the first half of the 1800s. This later account concerns former local residents and their descendants.
entries.unknown: The source leaves the pressure on each household and terms of land use unclear. A possible departure in 1752 and later land uses remain separate questions. The Oklahoma report is not yet matched to one removal episode.
entries.next_step: Trace the pressured move and changes in home and land use. Keep later departure and forced removal questions open and distinct.

entries.name: Failed western advance and divided return
entries.place_and_era: Westward country and the Red River, glossed as the Colorado, then a return journey. The cold Ocean People country is unknown. North America; the event date and era are unknown. Smith told the account, and Allison translated it. It was written down in 1935.
entries.attested:
Smith describes a force that went west and destroyed groups it met. It then failed against Ocean People who defended houses in a cold country. The Wooshkam met and chose to withdraw to avoid the loss of their people.

On the way back, kin followed a child toward the far bank of the river. The water closed and split them from the others. Siuuhu told them to make homes there and become kin of the Yumas. He told the others to return to won land. He also called for Wooshkam and Hohokam to work together.
entries.unknown: The cold country, full route, place where water boiled and modern identities of the Ocean People and separated kin remain unclear. The call for Yuma kinship is not a full ancestry record. The won land has no exact bounds here. Failed attack, earlier destruction and divided homes are different outcomes. Attempts to cross and pauses do not fix an event calendar.
entries.next_step: Keep the destructive advance, failed attack, retreat and different homes on return distinct. Use those different outcomes to define the movement.

entries.name: Great-house losses, captives and survivors
entries.place_and_era: Casa Grande, Casa Blanca, Snaketown and other named homes in what is now Arizona. Some site links are uncertain. The event date and era are unknown. Smith told the account, and Allison translated it. It was written down in 1935 and edited by Bahr in 1994.
entries.attested:
Smith gives different fates for homes and people. Casa Grande residents fled to a mountain, where they were killed; battle did not wreck the house. Casa Blanca defenders shot through holes in the walls before the house fell. Some Snaketown people fled west; others stayed before its houses were destroyed. At the house with an ocotillo base, some people were killed and the rest captured.

Another house near Guadalupe was destroyed. At Pueblo Grande a leader kept his own people inside a house that seemed to be stone. The house was later destroyed. The account links this to the fall of another house at La Ciudad.

The force captured people, debated their deaths, guarded them and sent captives against a sharpshooter from their own side. Smith has people secretly shelter the child of a chief after defeat. The Thin Leather version in Russell instead has a grandson found and later sold. Commentary describes Wooshkam and Hohokam survivors as mixed groups. The force expressly spared Hohokam who fled toward Big Mountain.

The story also has groups lose and regain an advantage in the hunt as they travel. A woman supplies arrows to a company short of arms, with many losses.
entries.unknown:
Siivan or Sivern appears in two death passages; whether these concern the same chief remains unclear. Child versus grandson and care versus capture and sale are separate versions. The captive passages need not concern one group throughout. Site and chief links are tentative, and survivor groups do not map straight onto modern peoples. Thin Leather is one narrator, even where his versions differ.

These different losses, new ties and refuge do not prove full replacement or safety for all. Local battle lengths do not fix an event calendar. Hayden gives an environmental account, and Bahr links sites; these remain their own views.
entries.next_step: Set bounds for the linked episodes at the named homes. Keep captive service, survivors who join other groups and spared refuge as explicit outcomes.

entries.name: Home choices after victory in the Dolores version
entries.place_and_era: The house of Siwani, river land and land below Baboquivari, North America. The event date and era are unknown. Dolores collected this version. Bahr presents it through the work of Saxton and Saxton, published in 1973.
entries.attested:
In this version, I'itoi gathered people to fight Siwani; others joined on the way. He promised the first killer a choice of land for a home. Rattlesnake killed first. The attackers wrecked the house of Siwani and destroyed his people. Rattlesnake chose Rattlesnake House.

Farmers from the far south took river land, while hunters took land below Baboquivari. The account calls them River People and Desert People from that time.
entries.unknown: Exact bounds, length of stay and the fate of all earlier residents are unknown. The link between Rattlesnake House and Snaketown is tentative. The source names do not give a full map of modern ancestry. This version and longer conquest accounts need not refer to separate events.
entries.next_step: Keep the linked home choices and different land uses together. Keep the link to longer conquest versions explicit.

entries.name: Homes and departure in the Font account
entries.place_and_era: Casa Grande, in what is now Arizona, North America. The event date and era are unknown. Font wrote down this account from a governor in 1775. Bahr published this version in 1994.
entries.attested:
The governor of Uturituc told Font that Bitter Man came with his daughter and son-in-law. Bitter Man built the great-house, got roof beams and grew crops there. Wind and Storm-cloud left his service, then came back and restored his crops. After many years, Bitter Man and his companions left.

In a separate story, the governor described people who spread upstream and downstream under the Drinker. They had different languages and relations.
entries.unknown: The last departure has no stated cause or named next residents. The separate Drinker story is not its stated cause. The link to later great-house accounts, archaeological Hohokam or modern groups remains unclear. The governor stopped the stories after the Spanish listeners laughed.
entries.next_step: Keep the last departure apart from the separate story of people who spread out. Trace their effects on homes and links to other great-house accounts.

entries.name: Homes and group separation near Komatke
entries.place_and_era: Near Komatke, glossed as Estrella Mountain in Arizona, North America. The event date and era are unknown. Smith told the account, and Allison translated it. It was written down in 1935.
entries.attested:
Smith says the Wooshkam made homes near Komatke after the war. A leader died, and his widow led the Horned Toad People. She fell ill while some people prepared to leave and others stayed. Her grandchildren cared for her. They buried her seated near the mountains. Those who stayed later moved toward a thicket.

Hendricks tells a different story about a grandmother. Two brothers ask her to agree to her death so they can keep pace with the people on the move. Tobacco later grows at her grave.
entries.unknown: The fate of earlier holders, length of stay and sole use of the new homes are unclear. The two grandmother stories do not give one combined cause of death. Smith was unsure of the state of the grave when he told the story. New homes and a split in the group do not by themselves prove a further loss of land for earlier residents.
entries.next_step: Keep the new homes and split in the group linked to the campaign and later movement. Keep the death versions distinct.

entries.name: Jackrabbit Eater escape and new homes
entries.place_and_era: Reported Jackrabbit Eater country and refuge to the south, North America. Exact places, event date and era are unknown. Smith told this account. Allison translated it, and Hayden wrote it down in 1935.
entries.attested:
Smith describes armed Wooshkam people on the move with families. They scout water, train and attack Sofch kah and Apaches on the way. A Jackrabbit Eater medicine woman called wind and rain, gathered her kin and escaped south. Pursuers failed to catch them. They destroyed another group they met. The last sentence describes new homes.

The next phase includes enemies spared for service and the capture, abuse and forced dance of Buzzard. Hendricks has Buzzard offer a scalp dance to survive. Thin Leather describes loss of the scalp, death and return to life. Hendricks also describes a wider circuit with battles and groups who left to settle. These include Papago in Sacaton Valley.
entries.unknown:
The last sentence has two possible senses. Wooshkam settled where defeated Jackrabbit Eaters lived, or Jackrabbit Eater refugees won land and made homes in Mexico. These are two ways to read one clause, not two proven outcomes. Earlier attacks lack a separate long-term effect on homes for each target.

Buzzard has different fates and choices in Hendricks and Thin Leather. Their routes and episodes cannot simply be added to Smith. A year of drills and four-day spans do not fix a calendar or modern route.
entries.next_step: Keep both senses of the clause about new homes open. Preserve escape, capture and survival as different outcomes within the movement.

entries.name: Pima and Apache war, visits and peace
entries.place_and_era: Reported Pima and Apache ties at farms, a shared place and Many-wells, glossed as Maricopa Wells, North America. The dates and eras of the episodes are unknown. This last part was written down with the Smith and Allison account in 1935.
entries.attested:
The last part describes peaceful visits in which Apaches shared food grown on Pima farms. War resumed after a mistake over a baby who cried. Chiefs met to stop the war.

The story then has a white man whose mules were stolen at Many-wells. A Pima attack on Apaches followed, and war resumed. The account ends when the Government stops the war and friendship returns.
entries.unknown: People in a conflict are not thereby proven to be displaced or new settlers. The passage does not state the effect of each episode on homes or land transfers, or its full course. No stated link ties the peace deals, mule incident or Government role to a named colonial campaign. They do not date the earlier conquest.
entries.next_step: Trace the shifts in visits, shared use and peace alongside war. Leave unstated effects on homes open.

entries.name: War and departure in the Manje account
entries.place_and_era: Casa Grande and other great-houses, North America. People reportedly left for the north, east and south. The event date and era are unknown. Manje wrote down this account from guides in 1694.
entries.attested: The guides told Manje that people came from the north and built great-houses under El Siba. They described bloody war with Apache and allied fighters. People died on both sides, and the war laid waste to their homes. Those who lost heart left: some went back north, while others went east and south. Bahr presents the account through a quote published by Fewkes.
entries.unknown: The guides do not name new settlers or give the later fate of each group that left. They do not say the attackers settled in the ruined places. Exact routes, modern identities and links to later revenge and conquest accounts remain unclear. The year 1694 dates the record, not the war.
entries.next_step: Define the linked war and departure account. Trace its link to the other great-house stories before it counts as a separate event.

entries.name: Antelope Creek: why people left
entries.place_and_era: Texas Panhandle and the Canadian River valley. The source reports departure by the late 1400s. This is not an attack date.
entries.attested: The National Park Service describes people who built homes, farmed and used flint quarries. It describes later settlement moves and departure from the region. It proposes drought, or pressure and attacks from groups it calls Apache ancestors, as possible causes.
entries.unknown: The source does not establish forced clearance or a group that took control. Exact move dates, destinations and later land use remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Test the proposed causes of the moves. Ask whether pressure or attacks forced people to leave homes, farms or quarries.

entries.name: Homes within the walls at Moundville
entries.place_and_era: Moundville is on the Black Warrior River in Alabama. The source dates this change to about 1200 to 1300.
entries.attested: The authors describe a new town with walls and a planned layout. Builders cleared earlier structures for it. They took Mound X out of use to clear a path for the wall. People moved inside the walls. The authors link this move to a need for defense.
entries.unknown: The account does not establish forced moves or the expulsion of prior users. The builders' authority and the residents' choices remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Examine who chose the new layout and the moves. Ask how those choices changed prior use of the site.

entries.name: Homes and graves at Moundville
entries.place_and_era: Moundville is on the Black Warrior River in Alabama. The authors date the move to after about 1300.
entries.attested: The authors say most residents left the center, probably for farms in the valley. Former home areas became grave sites. Some people stayed at the center, and farms remained in use. One possible cause is a choice by leaders to empty the center. The authors also propose soil depletion and a lack of wood, or less threat of attack. These causes can act together.
entries.unknown: The authors do not choose one cause. They do not establish that leaders forced people out. Exact routes and household choices remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Examine the three proposed causes together. Ask how they changed where people lived and used the site.

entries.name: War and the loss of valley residents
entries.place_and_era: The Black Warrior River valley is in Alabama. The authors date this loss to about 1650.
entries.attested: The authors say people lived in valley villages until about 1650. They link the loss of residents to war pressure across the region. They describe the valley as a buffer between proto-Creeks to the east and Choctaws to the west.
entries.unknown: The account does not show what happened to all residents. Exact moves, routes and later control remain unknown. The account does not establish a death toll or new settlers. The source does not name attackers for specific villages.
entries.next_step: Examine how war pressure changed homes and use of the valley. Keep this loss separate from the earlier moves at Moundville.

entries.name: Land grants in the Khadar
entries.place_and_era: The Khadar east of the mounds at Hastinapura. Lal calls the grants recent but gives no year.
entries.attested: Lal reports that the Uttar Pradesh government reclaimed this tract for crops. It allotted land to displaced people from West Panjab and to former servicemen. The report also describes new villages and a planned town.
entries.unknown: Lal does not name the prior owners or users of this tract. He gives no account of their consent or fate. The area, date, terms and number of grants remain open. The report does not say if the two groups overlap.
entries.next_step: Ask how the grants changed prior land use and the rights of those who used the tract.

entries.name: Fire and later use of the town
entries.place_and_era: At Hastinapura, a fire marks the end of Period III. Its exact year is unknown.
entries.attested: Lal reports burned walls, floors and roof material from the trenches. He describes fire on a large scale. Later residents built homes and used the town again after a gap.
entries.unknown: The cause of the fire remains unknown. The report gives no count of deaths or people who left. It does not identify the fire with the plot to burn the Pandavas in a house. The report does not establish a human attack.
entries.next_step: Ask what caused the fire and how it changed the lives and homes of the people there.

entries.name: New homes and old bricks at Hastinapura
entries.place_and_era: Hastinapura after a long gap in use. The report places new homes near the end of the eleventh century.
entries.attested: Lal describes new homes and the reuse of bricks from older structures. He thought Muslim conquerors brought the later craft of glazed pottery. He also notes local copies of foreign forms. The dates for the new homes and that craft differ.
entries.unknown: The report does not tie these changes to one local conquest. It does not identify a group of new arrivals or show that people lost their homes. The prior owners and their fate remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Keep the new homes and the later pottery craft as distinct questions about use of the site.

entries.name: Accounts of a town and a divided kingdom
entries.place_and_era: The area around Hastinapura in the accounts that Lal cites. Their event dates remain open.
entries.attested: Lal cites accounts in which Hastin founded the town or enlarged an older town. They describe Kuru rule over more land and branch kingdoms. They also describe Dhritarashtra as the king who split the kingdom between two related families.
entries.unknown: The report does not resolve whether Hastin founded the town or enlarged an older town. It does not give clear borders or explain the effect on prior residents. These accounts involve distinct rulers and acts. Pottery does not prove the named rulers or their control of land.
entries.next_step: Ask how each account describes a change in land control or use of the town.

entries.name: Exile and a request for a place to live
entries.place_and_era: The Pandavas in the accounts linked to Hastinapura. The village names vary, and the year is unknown.
entries.attested: Lal cites accounts of the Pandavas in exile and their request for at least five villages as a place to live. He also recounts a plot to burn them in a house, war, deaths and retaliation. These remain accounts of distinct acts in the conflict.
entries.unknown: The report does not establish that the Pandavas received the villages. It does not tell us if prior residents lost land or homes. A plot does not prove that the planned act took place. These accounts do not identify that plot with the fire in Period III.
entries.next_step: Ask how exile affected their homes and whether the request led to a grant of land.

entries.name: A flood account and a change of capital
entries.place_and_era: From Hastinapura to Kausambi in an account that Lal cites. The date and the route remain unknown.
entries.attested: Lal cites an account in which the king Nichakshu moved the capital to Kausambi after a flood at Hastinapura. He also reports flood damage in the trenches and proposes a link to that account. He thought the flood caused great loss of life and property, distress and a time when people left the town. Later homes mark a return to the town.
entries.unknown: The link between the flood and the capital move remains tentative. Lal gives no count of deaths or a full account of who left. The report does not establish a human attack, a forced move or loss of rights at either place.
entries.next_step: Ask who moved with the capital, while the link to the excavated flood remains open.

entries.name: The fort at Sisupalgarh changed access.
entries.place_and_era: Sisupalgarh lies near Bhuvanesvar in eastern India. Lal places its use at about 300 BCE to 350 CE. He dates the first fort walls to about 200 BCE.
entries.attested: Lal reports that people lived here before the fort walls. Builders made and repaired walls, gates, roads and homes. Cart tracks mark use of the gateway. A brick wall later closed a side passage. Homes and other uses continued through several phases.
entries.unknown: The builders, their aims and the reason for the closed passage remain unknown. The report does not establish that these acts forced people from their homes or land. Their effects on the rights of prior users remain open. A storm is one possible cause of damage at the gate. Continued use does not prove that every resident stayed.
entries.next_step: Ask how the fort walls and the closed side passage changed access for prior residents and other users.

entries.name: Moves from Jefferson County
entries.place_and_era: Jefferson County is in northern New York. The authors place the dispersal around 1500, but its exact date is unknown.
entries.attested: The authors propose that some groups built new communities north of the Saint Lawrence. They report that other groups joined communities in the Trent Valley or among eastern Haudenosaunee. Their pottery study traces changes in links between sites.
entries.unknown: The study does not establish what caused each move. Conflict is one proposed cause. Pottery links do not count migrants or prove that force made every resident leave.
entries.next_step: Trace the reported moves and changes in village use. Keep possible conflict and incorporation distinct from the network results.

entries.name: Later moves from the Saint Lawrence valley
entries.place_and_era: The account concerns communities in the Saint Lawrence valley. The authors place a move east around 1550. They report trade with Basque fishers until about 1580.
entries.attested: The authors report the move east and continued exchange. They propose that later groups joined Algonquian groups to the north and west. Other proposed moves led south to Abenaki groups.
entries.unknown: The authors suggest that warfare sped up the loss of residents. The study does not establish the cause of each move. It does not show that everyone died or that all use of the valley ended.
entries.next_step: Ask how people moved and whether they joined other groups. Keep this question separate from the earlier Jefferson County moves and the attack at Stadocona.

entries.name: Earlier moves from the Mesa Verde region
entries.place_and_era: The authors place these moves in the late 900s CE. They describe southwest Colorado and the northern edge of the Mesa Verde region. Possible destinations lie in New Mexico.
entries.attested: The authors report that many residents left the central Mesa Verde region. They describe earlier homes, farms and village growth. They report moves to its northern edge, and perhaps to the San Juan Basin and Chuska slopes.
entries.unknown: The source does not show why each group left or who went where. It does not establish forced moves or loss of land rights. A later chapter separates early departures, renewed use of some old villages, and the spread of household compounds. How these phases relate to the date in this study remains unresolved.
entries.next_step: Examine the cited studies for evidence of departure and later homes. Keep these earlier moves separate from later moves to the northern Rio Grande.

entries.name: Moves between Mesa Verde and the northern Rio Grande
entries.place_and_era: The study concerns southwest Colorado and north-central New Mexico. The authors place the later moves in the 1200s CE. Some early departures were possible before then.
entries.attested: The authors link departures from the Mesa Verde region with growth on the Pajarito Plateau. They argue that some early migrants returned with obsidian and knowledge of places where people already lived. They also cite warfare as the region lost residents.
entries.unknown: Objects do not identify each traveler or prove return visits. The cause of these moves and their effects on prior land use remain unknown. Counts of obsidian are not counts of migrants.
entries.next_step: Examine the cited settlement evidence for the proposed return visits. Ask how objects moved, and how new and prior residents used these places.

entries.name: A blind prince leaves his post and home
entries.place_and_era: The tale links Taxila with the royal capital of the father of Kunala. The event date is unknown.
entries.attested: In this tale, a forged order leads to the loss of the sight of Kunala. He leaves his post and travels with his wife as a beggar. They reach the capital of his father, who learns what took place.
entries.unknown: The order calls for the pair to be left in the hills. The tale does not confirm that every part of that order takes place.
entries.next_step: Distinguish the forged order from the acts that the tale reports. Keep the later exile of other people separate.

entries.name: A king loses his country and flees
entries.place_and_era: A shrine in Udyana marks this tale. It does not locate the country that the king lost. The event date is unknown.
entries.attested: Beal translates a tale of a king in a past life. He loses rule of his country and flees an enemy. He then offers himself bound as a captive so a poor man can claim a reward.
entries.unknown: The tale does not name the lost country or give the fate of its residents. It does not confirm the later delivery of the captive.
entries.next_step: Keep the lost country separate from the shrine. Trace the loss, flight and later offer as parts of one tale.

entries.name: A priest turns back at a river
entries.place_and_era: The tale concerns a priest on his way back to Kasmir. The event date is unknown.
entries.attested: In this relic tale, boatmen blame a sacred tooth for danger. Their master searches the goods of a priest. The priest gives the tooth to Nagas and turns back. He later returns and takes it to a home for priests.
entries.unknown: It is unclear whether people force him to stop or he turns back in response to sacred danger. The tale does not establish a wider expulsion.
entries.next_step: Distinguish the search by people from the role of Nagas in the tale. Ask what action stops his passage.

entries.name: A refugee takes rule in Udyana
entries.place_and_era: The tale concerns Udyana, in South Asia. The event date is unknown.
entries.attested: In this tale, hosts receive a Sakya refugee and offer him a home. A host gives him a hidden sword. He kills the local king, and the officials yield rule to him.
entries.unknown: The tale gives no general expulsion of residents. It does not establish a modern identity for the hosts, whom it calls Nagas.
entries.next_step: Keep the prior king and residents in view. Ask what changes for them when the refugee takes rule.

entries.name: A reported move toward Nepal
entries.place_and_era: Beal discusses people called Vrijji and a move toward the mountains of Nepal. The event date is unknown.
entries.attested: Beal relays an account in which a king checks this group and drives it northeast. His account also links the group to invaders. The group and its role remain uncertain.
entries.unknown: It is unclear whether residents lose their homes or an army retreats. A shared name or place does not establish a modern people.
entries.next_step: Ask who moves and what prior residence or use they lose. Keep the reported force without an assumed mass exile.

entries.name: A ruler tries to keep a pilgrim
entries.place_and_era: Beal places this episode at Kao-chang on the westward route of Hiuen Tsiang. The precise event date is unknown.
entries.attested: Beal reports that the ruler tries to keep the pilgrim at Kao-chang. The pilgrim then goes on. The account also describes aid, guides and obstacles along his route.
entries.unknown: It is unclear whether the ruler imposes a stay or fails in an attempt to retain him. The account does not establish a wider removal.
entries.next_step: Ask whether an actual loss of passage or choice of home occurs. Keep an attempt distinct from an imposed stay.

entries.name: A siege and loss of rule at Taxila
entries.place_and_era: Beal gives this account in a note about Taxila, in South Asia. The event date is unknown.
entries.attested: In a note, Beal reports a revolt and a failed siege. He says the people then submit to Asoka, who takes charge. The note later links a new revolt to the post of Kunala as governor.
entries.unknown: The note does not state that all residents lose their homes. Shared place names do not make this the same event as other conquests.
entries.next_step: Keep the siege and change of rule distinct from the later injury of Kunala. Compare the people, place and acts.

entries.name: An armed coup and return of priests
entries.place_and_era: The tale concerns a ruler from Himatala and people in Kasmir. The event date is unknown.
entries.attested: In this tale, armed men enter as guests under the guise of trade. Their king kills the local ruler and exiles ministers. He calls priests back, builds a home for them and gives them the country.
entries.unknown: The tale spares ordinary residents from blame. It does not give a total of exiles or later settlers. It also says the displaced rulers later regain power.
entries.next_step: Keep minister exile and priest return as distinct parts of one coup. Retain prior residents and the later change of rule.

entries.name: Beal reports a conquest in Gandhara
entries.place_and_era: Beal places this conquest in Gandhara, in South Asia. The event date is unknown.
entries.attested: Beal reports that a ruler of the Ye-tha takes Gandhara. He also reports wider conquests or tribute. The local claim concerns a change of rule in a place where people already live.
entries.unknown: A possible link to the other raid remains unclear. That raid names Mahirakula. The text does not prove a separate event or a general expulsion.
entries.next_step: Keep the reports distinct until the evidence links their actors and events. Do not merge them from the place name alone.

entries.name: Four defenders driven from home
entries.place_and_era: The tale concerns Sakya homes and a route toward Udyana. The event date is unknown.
entries.attested: In a tale that Beal translates, an army attacks the Sakyas. Their own clans drive four defenders from home. Each flees in a different direction. The tale follows one refugee to a new household.
entries.unknown: The attack and the expulsion have different actors. The tale does not identify all routes, later homes or the fate of each refugee.
entries.next_step: Keep the exile and the later seizure of rule distinct. One refugee later takes rule in Udyana.

entries.name: Monks move from Banaras to Kasmir
entries.place_and_era: Beal gives this account in a note about a monk and Kasmir. The event date is unknown.
entries.attested: In a note, Beal says people in Banaras resent the number of monks. A monk takes a large group to Kasmir by sacred flight. The note links this move with the spread of faith.
entries.unknown: The note does not establish whether residents force the monks out or the monks leave on a mission. The cause remains unclear.
entries.next_step: Ask what links the local resentment to the move. Retain the reported move without an assumed act of expulsion.

entries.name: Poor people bought to serve monks
entries.place_and_era: Beal gives this account in the origin history of Kasmir. The event date is unknown.
entries.attested: In the history that Beal translates, a monk founds homes for priests. He buys poor people from nearby countries to serve them. After his death, the text says these people take rule and face scorn from their neighbors.
entries.unknown: The text gives no count of the bought people or full terms of their service. It does not establish a modern group identity.
entries.next_step: Retain the bought service, later rule and prior use of the land. Keep the lake tale separate from claims about human groups.

entries.name: Priests flee a threat and receive land
entries.place_and_era: The tale links the Ganges with refuge in Kasmir. The event date is unknown.
entries.attested: The text says Asoka plans to drown priests. Some priests flee to Kasmir by sacred powers and refuse his call to return. He then builds homes for priests and gives them the country.
entries.unknown: The threat is not a count of people who die. The text does not define the land grant or show that prior residents leave.
entries.next_step: Keep the threat, refuge, refused return and grant distinct. Ask how priests and prior residents use the land.

entries.name: Rulers drive priests from Kasmir
entries.place_and_era: The text places this episode after the death of Kanishka. It gives no secure event date.
entries.attested: In the account that Beal translates, rulers called Kritiyas take power again. The text says they banish priests and overthrow their religion. A later tale recalls priests who disperse and choose new homes.
entries.unknown: The later tale can refer to the same exiles. The text does not give their number, full routes or later fate.
entries.next_step: Keep this expulsion linked to the later return of priests. Do not count the departure and return as new groups.

entries.name: Strife over rule at Taxila
entries.place_and_era: The text describes Taxila, in South Asia, as it pays tribute to Kasmir. The date of the change is unknown.
entries.attested: The text says nobles fight for power after a royal line ends. It reports changed tribute and ruined homes for priests. It also describes farms, residents and a few priests who remain.
entries.unknown: The text does not link a specific victor or act to loss of homes or land. Ruins do not identify an attacker.
entries.next_step: Ask what control or access changes as the nobles contest power. Keep the residents who remain and their land use in view.

entries.name: The king sends people into exile
entries.place_and_era: The tale concerns Taxila and a desert northeast of the Snowy Mountains. The event date is unknown.
entries.attested: In this tale, Asoka punishes those tied to the injury of Kunala. He sends some officials into exile and kills or removes others. He sends common people who took part into a desert.
entries.unknown: The text does not say that all Taxila residents leave. The numbers, routes and later homes of the exiles are unknown.
entries.next_step: Keep each affected group and form of punishment distinct. Keep this group distinct from Kunala and his wife.

entries.name: Two brothers seek refuge in China
entries.place_and_era: Beal places the refuge at Shingtu in China, during unrest at the end of Sui rule. The precise event date is unknown.
entries.attested: Beal reports that Hiuen Tsiang and his brother seek refuge because of political unrest. They find refuge at Shingtu. Their later study and travel are different moves.
entries.unknown: The account does not identify the fate of their former home or how long they remain. It does not establish a general expulsion.
entries.next_step: Keep the personal refuge distinct from later religious travel. Ask how unrest changes where the brothers can live.

entries.name: McPhee: deaths and the end of communal use
entries.place_and_era: McPhee Pueblo lay in the Dolores Valley in southwest Colorado. The chapter discusses these acts during regional depopulation near the end of the 800s CE. The exact date of the deaths and destruction is unknown.
entries.attested: The chapter reports violent deaths and paired burials in ritual pit structures. Roofs were taken apart and collapsed over the bodies. Other ritual and community structures were burned.
entries.unknown: The authors only suggest that roofs fell as people died. They do not identify the killers or show that every resident was forced to leave. Later use of parts of the village is reported.
entries.next_step: Keep the deaths and destruction of communal spaces in view. Ask how these acts changed use of those spaces and what happened to other residents.
source_citations: Kellam Throgmorton, Richard Wilshusen, Grant D. Coffey (2023). Bridging the Long Tenth Century. Chapter 11, printed pages 166, 170, 171. DOI: 10.5876/9781646424597.c011.

entries.name: Grass Mesa: people leave before the fire
entries.place_and_era: Grass Mesa lay in the Dolores Valley in southwest Colorado. The chapter places this move in the earlier regional decline. The village fire came months or years after people left.
entries.attested: The account describes temporary structures during a planned departure. The authors report that the village was burned later as a ritual act. These are separate stages in one local history.
entries.unknown: A planned move does not prove that people had a free choice. The later fire does not show an attack that caused the move. The effects on continued access and use are unknown.
entries.next_step: Trace the circumstances of departure and later use. Keep this account separate from the reported violence at McPhee.
source_citations: Kellam Throgmorton, Richard Wilshusen, Grant D. Coffey (2023). Bridging the Long Tenth Century. Chapter 11, printed pages 166, 168. DOI: 10.5876/9781646424597.c011.

entries.name: People use old villages again
entries.place_and_era: The chapter describes renewed use at selected villages in the Dolores Valley and central Mesa Verde region. It places much of this work in 925-975 CE. Construction dates differ between sites.
entries.attested: People rebuilt and lived in parts of earlier villages. Some reused old room plans. Other communities persisted while these places were used again.
entries.unknown: The source does not identify the new residents as the same families who left. Returns and possible places where people lived remain proposals. Changes in prior use are not established.
entries.next_step: Trace how the new residents related to those who left and those who stayed. Keep reuse of places separate from family identity and land control.
source_citations: Kellam Throgmorton, Richard Wilshusen, Grant D. Coffey (2023). Bridging the Long Tenth Century. Chapter 11, printed pages 169, 170, 171, 172. DOI: 10.5876/9781646424597.c011.

entries.name: Later compounds: local moves or arrivals?
entries.place_and_era: The chapter places this pattern of small homes in 975-1030 CE in central Mesa Verde. It describes compounds on mesa tops and in some old settlements.
entries.attested: More people used small post-and-adobe compounds across a wider range of places. Some homes resembled those in nearby regions. The authors propose local change and immigration as alternatives.
entries.unknown: Similar buildings do not establish that people arrived from elsewhere. Fallowed land does not show the absence of prior users or rights. The effects of these settlements on earlier users remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Seek evidence that distinguishes local moves from arrivals. Ask how compound residents and prior users shared or controlled these landscapes.
source_citations: Kellam Throgmorton, Richard Wilshusen, Grant D. Coffey (2023). Bridging the Long Tenth Century. Chapter 11, printed pages 173, 174, 175, 176. DOI: 10.5876/9781646424597.c011.

entries.name: Farm lands and an invited stay at Mesa Verde
entries.place_and_era: The account concerns Tawtaykya, or Mesa Verde. The exact date and farm parcels are unknown. Later dates for ceremonial roles do not date these acts.
entries.attested: Kuwanwisiwma describes Katsina and Badger leaders who assigned farm lands. Residents hosted and taught new arrivals. Residents welcomed Flute to perform and asked the group to stay.
entries.unknown: The account does not establish that these allocations took land from prior users. It does not say that Flute was held by force. Shared clan names do not identify one unchanged group across places.
entries.next_step: Trace how hosts and new residents shared or controlled farm use. Keep the reported land allocation separate from a forced loss of prior use.
source_citations: Leigh Kuwanwisiwma, Wesley Bernardini (2023). Place of the Songs. Chapter 5, printed pages 75, 76, 77, 80. DOI: 10.5876/9781646424597.c005.

entries.name: Rules for rites at Mesa Verde
entries.place_and_era: The account places this ban at Mesa Verde. The exact date is unknown. Later rites at Aztec have a separate context.
entries.attested: The account says Bow and its phratry were not allowed to perform rites at Mesa Verde. Greasewood received permission for a medicinal rite and four katsinam. Bow later held rites and built great kivas at Aztec.
entries.unknown: The ban is clear. Whether it barred use of a place or only set rules for rites remains unknown. The account does not link the ban to a later move.
entries.next_step: Ask whether the ban barred use of a place or set rules for rites alone. Keep the stated ban in view.
source_citations: Leigh Kuwanwisiwma, Wesley Bernardini (2023). Place of the Songs. Chapter 5, printed pages 76, 77, 80, 81. DOI: 10.5876/9781646424597.c005.

entries.name: Entry refusal, peace and travel
entries.place_and_era: The account describes territories encountered during journeys. The exact location and date of the refusal are unknown. It links the deniers and protectors with the Warrior Twins from Aztec.
entries.attested: Kuwanwisiwma describes territorial warriors whom he identifies as the Warrior Twins. They first deny some clans entry. The account then reports a peace pact and protection during travel.
entries.unknown: The human identity of these figures remains unknown. The exact travellers and territorial bounds are also unclear. The account does not show eviction from earlier homes or a permanent ban on entry. It identifies no modern ethnic people.
entries.next_step: Keep the refusal and later protection in one account. Ask what entry was denied and how the pact changed access.
source_citations: Leigh Kuwanwisiwma, Wesley Bernardini (2023). Place of the Songs. Chapter 5, printed pages 78, 81. DOI: 10.5876/9781646424597.c005.

entries.name: Greasewood receives aid and guidance to Mesa Verde
entries.place_and_era: The account follows Greasewood from Bears Ears to Fog Mountain and Mesa Verde. Fog Mountain is an unspecified Abajo peak. The exact calendar is unknown.
entries.attested: Greasewood approaches starvation and receives meat and pelts from people described as apparently Ute. At the request of Greasewood, guides lead the group to Mesa Verde. Settlement follows in the area now called Ute Mountain Tribal Park.
entries.unknown: The speaker reports a mountain visit. His visit does not make him a witness to the earlier encounter. The account does not establish a forced route, sole ownership or removal of prior residents.
entries.next_step: Ask how the guided settlers related to prior residents and later communities. Keep this aid account separate from reports of conflict among other clans.
source_citations: Leigh Kuwanwisiwma, Wesley Bernardini (2023). Place of the Songs. Chapter 5, printed pages 76, 78, 81. DOI: 10.5876/9781646424597.c005.

entries.name: Conflict near Chimney Rock
entries.place_and_era: Kuwanwisiwma places this conflict near Chimney Rock. The exact date and affected tract are unknown.
entries.attested: The account says some clans faced conflict there. The speaker contrasts this with the Ute aid in the account of his own clan.
entries.unknown: The speaker does not identify the other side. His guesses remain unconfirmed. The passage does not state a particular move, loss of home use or change in land control.
entries.next_step: Seek an account of what the conflict changed for residence, access or control. Do not supply the outcome from a different episode.
source_citations: Leigh Kuwanwisiwma, Wesley Bernardini (2023). Place of the Songs. Chapter 5, printed pages 78, 81. DOI: 10.5876/9781646424597.c005.

entries.name: Clans flee north after the loss of Palatkwapi
entries.place_and_era: The place called Palatkwapi is not fixed to one city. The note gives possible places from southern Arizona to Mesoamerica. The date is unknown.
entries.attested: A note that cites Yava reports the destruction of Palatkwapi after moral and social turmoil. Clans flee north. Some reach Hopi Mesas. The note also reports a break in rites and their later revival.
entries.unknown: The note does not identify a destroyer or a particular human removal process. It does not make every later Hopi arrival part of this flight. The cited Yava work was not newly read.
entries.next_step: Ask how destruction, flight and later settlement connect. Keep the moral frame of the account. Do not add an attacker or erase the reported acts.
source_citations: Leigh Kuwanwisiwma, Wesley Bernardini (2023). Place of the Songs. Chapter 5, printed pages 80, 81, 82. DOI: 10.5876/9781646424597.c005.

entries.name: A king's flight through Ceylon to Malabar
entries.place_and_era: The article places this flight in the reign of an earlier king of Ceylon. The exact date is unknown.
entries.attested: It says a Chola king drove the Pandya ruler out. He sought help in Ceylon, then went to Malabar. He left royal goods behind.
entries.unknown: The article does not name a group that went with him. His prior home, length of stay and later fate are unknown.
entries.next_step: Keep the first forced move distinct from the later trip. Ask what changed for the king at each place.
source_citations: E. Hultzsch, XV Contributions to Singhalese Chronology, Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 45(3), July 1913, pages 517–531; section V, printed pages 524–525 (Mahavamsa 53, as reported). DOI: 10.1017/S0035869X00045093. Public annual-volume scan.

entries.name: A king's flight to Rohana
entries.place_and_era: The article names Udaya as the king who fled to Rohana. Its date and the army's ruler are inferred, not fixed.
entries.attested: An army killed a commander. The king fled with royal goods. The troops could not reach him and went back without the goods.
entries.unknown: The text does not say that local people fled. It does not prove that the army took the goods or ruled the whole island.
entries.next_step: Keep the king's flight and the failed mission distinct. Ask what changed for his home and rule.
source_citations: E. Hultzsch, XV Contributions to Singhalese Chronology, Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 45(3), July 1913, pages 517–531; section V, printed pages 524–525 (Mahavamsa 53.44 translation correction and related account, as reported). DOI: 10.1017/S0035869X00045093. Public annual-volume scan.

entries.name: A later army sent to Ceylon
entries.place_and_era: The article places this mission after a king's death. It gives two dates for that death, not for the mission.
entries.attested: It reports that a general led an army to Ceylon. It does not state what land or homes were taken.
entries.unknown: The date and result of the mission are not fixed. A later murder report does not prove another taking of land.
entries.next_step: Keep the king's death and the later mission distinct. Ask what the force did and whose land or homes changed.
source_citations: E. Hultzsch, XV Contributions to Singhalese Chronology, Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 45(3), July 1913, pages 517–531; section IX, printed page 531 (Mahavamsa 90.47, as reported). DOI: 10.1017/S0035869X00045093. Public annual-volume scan.

entries.name: An army sent to South India
entries.place_and_era: The article places the mission in South India. It compares sources that give different clues to its date.
entries.attested: The article names Lankapura as the general who led the force. It says the force went against Kulasekhara of Madhura. It calls this an invasion of South India.
entries.unknown: This passage does not state which tract was taken or whose home changed. The fact that an army was sent does not show that it took all the land.
entries.next_step: Keep the reported mission visible. Ask what land or homes changed and which acts can form one clear question.
source_citations: E. Hultzsch, XV Contributions to Singhalese Chronology, Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 45(3), July 1913, pages 517–531; section I, printed pages 518–519 (Mahavamsa 76.7 and Arppakkam/twelfth-year references, as reported). DOI: 10.1017/S0035869X00045093. Public annual-volume scan.

entries.name: Cola rule and the capture of Mahinda
entries.place_and_era: The text names Rajarattha in Lanka. An editor dates the conquest to 1017. The text itself gives a year of the king's reign. The exact land bounds are unknown.
entries.attested: The text reports Cola rule over a named tract. The king was seized and sent to the Cola ruler. Temples lost wealth and buildings. His consort was seized. People kept the young prince safe.
entries.unknown: The text does not say the consort was sent abroad. It gives no count of local people made to leave. How rule changed their homes and rights is unknown.
entries.next_step: Keep rule, royal capture, temple harm and harm to local people distinct. Ask how each act changed use of land or homes.
source_citations: Geiger, Culavamsa, Part I. English translation from German by C. Mabel Rickmers (1929; AES reprint, 1998), chapter LV, verses 55.13–24 and 55.33–34, printed pages 187–189, including the colophon and cited notes (page 187 notes 2–3 continuing on 188, page 188 notes 1–3, page 189 note 3).

entries.name: Crowns taken from four named rulers
entries.place_and_era: The article compares a royal list with a chronicle. A record's date does not date each act.
entries.attested: A royal record lists crowns taken from four kings. The article also reports deaths. These do not prove a new taking of land for each name.
entries.unknown: Some names may match kings in other accounts. The article gives up one proposed match. The land and home effects are not clear.
entries.next_step: Keep the crowns and deaths as stated claims. Link the women already seized in the other questions. Do not add a new event for each crown.
source_citations: E. Hultzsch, XV Contributions to Singhalese Chronology, Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 45(3), July 1913, pages 517–531; sections II–III, printed pages 520–521 (the 1046 record, South Indian Inscriptions III 52, as reported). DOI: 10.1017/S0035869X00045093. Public annual-volume scan.

entries.name: Indraratha and his family were seized
entries.place_and_era: The text places the fight at Adinagar. It names Indraratha and his family. The exact date is unknown.
entries.attested: The text says the army seized the king and his family. It also says their treasures were carried away.
entries.unknown: The text does not say the people were sent elsewhere. We do not know their number, stay or later fate. Their homes and rights are not described.
entries.next_step: Keep the capture of people distinct from the removal of goods. Ask what happened to the people and their homes.
source_citations: E. Hultzsch, No. 31, Tirumalai Rock Inscription of Rajendra-Chola I, Epigraphia Indica IX, English translation, printed page 233, inscription lines 8–9; article printed pages 229–233.

entries.name: Mahinda's flight from the palace
entries.place_and_era: The text places Mahinda in Anuradhapura, then in Rohana. This is before the Cola attack. The exact year is unknown.
entries.attested: Unpaid troops blocked food from the palace. The king fled to Rohana with goods. He set up a camp and later a town.
entries.unknown: The text does not say who went with him. It does not show that local people lost homes or land. Later rights and return are unknown.
entries.next_step: Keep the king's move distinct from later capture. Ask who went with him and what changed for people at each place.
source_citations: Geiger, Culavamsa, Part I. English translation from German by C. Mabel Rickmers (1929; AES reprint, 1998), chapter LV, verses 55.1–12, printed pages 186–187; notes 1–3 on page 186 and note 4 on page 186.

entries.name: Other lands named in the conquest list
entries.place_and_era: The text names more lands and places. These are in the same royal list. The dates of each act are unknown.
entries.attested: The text says the army seized these lands. It names islands, towns, regions and a river. The claim of taking is positive.
entries.unknown: The text does not show which places were taken in one act. It does not state all local people's fate or the full bounds of each tract.
entries.next_step: Group the claims only where the source supports it. Keep each taking claim visible without making a new event for each name.
source_citations: E. Hultzsch, No. 31, Tirumalai Rock Inscription of Rajendra-Chola I, Epigraphia Indica IX, English translation, printed page 233, inscription lines 1–2, 4–7, 9, 11–12; article printed pages 229–233.

entries.name: The army took control of the land at Takkanaladam
entries.place_and_era: The text names Takkanaladam and its ruler Ranasura. The exact place and date are unknown.
entries.attested: The text says the army took control of the tract. It says this followed a strong attack on the ruler.
entries.unknown: The length of rule and the land's full bounds are unknown. The text does not say that local people fled or lost homes.
entries.next_step: Ask whose use of the tract changed. Keep the attack distinct from harm the text does not state.
source_citations: E. Hultzsch, No. 31, Tirumalai Rock Inscription of Rajendra-Chola I, Epigraphia Indica IX, English translation, printed page 233, inscription lines 10; article printed pages 229–233.

entries.name: The army took land in Vangala-desa
entries.place_and_era: The text names Vangala-desa and its ruler Govindachandra. The exact bounds and date are unknown.
entries.attested: The land is in the list of places the army took. The text says the ruler got down from his elephant and fled.
entries.unknown: The text does not say that all people fled. Their homes, rights and later fate are unknown. The length of rule is not stated.
entries.next_step: Keep the ruler's flight distinct from the land claim. Ask what changed for people who lived there.
source_citations: E. Hultzsch, No. 31, Tirumalai Rock Inscription of Rajendra-Chola I, Epigraphia Indica IX, English translation, printed page 233, inscription lines 10; article printed pages 229–233.

entries.name: The army took the land of Tandabutti
entries.place_and_era: The text names Tandabutti and its ruler Dharmapala. The exact place and date are unknown.
entries.attested: The text says the army took the tract. It links this to the destruction of its ruler in fierce battle.
entries.unknown: The text does not show that all people were made to leave. Their rights, homes and later fate are unknown. The ruler's name alone does not prove who he was.
entries.next_step: Keep the taking of land and the battle claim distinct. Ask what changed for those who used the tract.
source_citations: E. Hultzsch, No. 31, Tirumalai Rock Inscription of Rajendra-Chola I, Epigraphia Indica IX, English translation, printed page 233, inscription lines 9–10; article printed pages 229–233.

entries.name: The earlier claim to rule in Ilam
entries.place_and_era: The article names Rajaraja as an earlier ruler who took Ilam. It infers a range of years from dated records.
entries.attested: The article reports a royal claim to conquest of the named tract. It sets this before the later king's capture.
entries.unknown: This may overlap with part of the later conquest account. It does not prove that all residents lost homes. The full bounds and length of rule are unknown.
entries.next_step: Keep the earlier ruler's claim distinct from the later capture. Ask which parts of the two accounts overlap.
source_citations: E. Hultzsch, XV Contributions to Singhalese Chronology, Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 45(3), July 1913, pages 517–531; section IV, printed page 524 (comparison of South Indian Inscriptions III No. 52 and No. 6, as cited). DOI: 10.1017/S0035869X00045093. Public annual-volume scan.

entries.name: The flight of Manavamma from Ceylon to India
entries.place_and_era: The article places the first flight from Ceylon to India. The dates depend on its sources and sums of reigns.
entries.attested: It says Manavamma fled from Ceylon to India. He served a ruler there. His first bid to return failed, so he stayed abroad.
entries.unknown: The text does not say all the troops or their families were refugees. It does not state the fate of his prior home or who went with him.
entries.next_step: Keep the flight and first failed return distinct from the later victory. Ask how his place and role changed.
source_citations: E. Hultzsch, XV Contributions to Singhalese Chronology, Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 45(3), July 1913, pages 517–531; section VII, printed pages 527–529 (Mahavamsa 47 and comparative apparatus, as reported). DOI: 10.1017/S0035869X00045093. Public annual-volume scan.

entries.name: The forced move of a queen and her daughter
entries.place_and_era: The article names Jagatipala and his family in Ceylon. The exact date of their fate is unknown.
entries.attested: It reports that the king was killed. His queen and daughter were carried to Chola country.
entries.unknown: This may be the same event as the seizure of women in another account. The two kings' names differ. The women's later fate is unknown.
entries.next_step: Keep the forced move as a positive claim. Keep the possible match open without joining the people or counting them twice.
source_citations: E. Hultzsch, XV Contributions to Singhalese Chronology, Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 45(3), July 1913, pages 517–531; section III, printed page 521 (Mahavamsa 56.13–15, as reported). DOI: 10.1017/S0035869X00045093. Public annual-volume scan.

entries.name: The later attack in Rohana and local rewards
entries.place_and_era: This is a later attack in Rohana. The text says the young prince was twelve. The exact year is unknown.
entries.attested: Troops sought the prince and plundered the region. Two leaders fought them for six months. The troops who lived went back to their base. The prince gave a village reward and relief from dues.
entries.unknown: The text does not show that the prince was caught. It does not show that local people lost homes or that troops left a settled home. Prior rights in the village and later use are unknown.
entries.next_step: Keep troop retreat, the village award and relief from dues distinct. Ask whose access to land changed and how.
source_citations: Geiger, Culavamsa, Part I. English translation from German by C. Mabel Rickmers (1929; AES reprint, 1998), chapter LV, verses 55.23–32, printed pages 188–189; page 189 notes 1–2 and the note to 55.33 (note 3).

entries.name: The later return and rise to rule
entries.place_and_era: This is Manavamma's later return to Ceylon. The exact date is not fixed.
entries.attested: He returned with aid, beat the ruler and took rule. The defeated ruler was killed and his head was shown.
entries.unknown: The text does not prove that all people lost homes. The land's full bounds and length of control are unknown. Troops are not all a new settler group.
entries.next_step: Keep this success distinct from the first failed trip. Ask who ruled, stayed or lost access after the return.
source_citations: E. Hultzsch, XV Contributions to Singhalese Chronology, Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 45(3), July 1913, pages 517–531; section VII, printed pages 527–529 (Mahavamsa 47 second expedition and reign comparison, as reported). DOI: 10.1017/S0035869X00045093. Public annual-volume scan.

entries.name: The loss of rule in Irattapadi
entries.place_and_era: The text names Irattapadi and Musangi. It comes from the king's thirteenth year. The dates of the acts are unknown.
entries.attested: The text says the king's army took the land from Jayasimha. It says he fled and hid.
entries.unknown: We do not know the land's full bounds or how long rule changed. The text does not say that local people fled or lost homes.
entries.next_step: Keep the ruler's flight and the loss of rule distinct. Ask how the taking changed local use of land.
source_citations: E. Hultzsch, No. 31, Tirumalai Rock Inscription of Rajendra-Chola I, Epigraphia Indica IX, English translation, printed page 233, inscription lines 5–6; article printed pages 229–233.

entries.name: The taking of Odda-vishaya
entries.place_and_era: The text names Odda-vishaya. This is a tract in the conquest list. The exact date is unknown.
entries.attested: The text says the army took control of the tract in close fights.
entries.unknown: The bounds and length of rule are unknown. The text does not say that local people fled. How the taking changed homes and rights is unknown.
entries.next_step: Keep this tract distinct from nearby names in the list. Ask whose use of land changed and how.
source_citations: E. Hultzsch, No. 31, Tirumalai Rock Inscription of Rajendra-Chola I, Epigraphia Indica IX, English translation, printed page 233, inscription lines 9; article printed pages 229–233.

entries.name: The taking of the city of Madhura
entries.place_and_era: The article links Madhura to a war under Parantaka. It compares dates of records with a proposed date for the war.
entries.attested: It reports that the city and elephants were taken. It praises the slaying of a large army. A chronicle says the force sent to help went back without success.
entries.unknown: No exact death count is shown. The text does not say that all city people left or lost homes. The length of rule is unknown.
entries.next_step: Keep the city claim, battle and failed return distinct. Ask what changed for people who used the city.
source_citations: E. Hultzsch, XV Contributions to Singhalese Chronology, Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 45(3), July 1913, pages 517–531; section VI, printed pages 525–526 (Mahavamsa 52.70–78; Udayendiram, South Indian Inscriptions II 387, verses 9–11; Annual Reports on Epigraphy, as cited). DOI: 10.1017/S0035869X00045093. Public annual-volume scan.

entries.name: The taking of the city of Vatapi
entries.place_and_era: The article links Vatapi to a war led by Narasiha. Exact dates and land bounds are not fixed.
entries.attested: It reports that Vatapi was taken. It links this claim to a ruler's defeat.
entries.unknown: The text does not say that all city people fled or lost homes. The length of control and later rights are unknown.
entries.next_step: Keep this city claim distinct from the two island missions. Ask what changed for people who used the city.
source_citations: E. Hultzsch, XV Contributions to Singhalese Chronology, Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 45(3), July 1913, pages 517–531; section VII, printed pages 528–529 (South Indian Inscriptions II 343 and Fleet, as cited). DOI: 10.1017/S0035869X00045093. Public annual-volume scan.

entries.name: Two royal sons seized by an army
entries.place_and_era: The article reports an attack in Ceylon. It names the sons' father as Manabharana. A dated record reports the acts, not their exact dates.
entries.attested: The article reports that a king was killed. It says two sons of another king were seized.
entries.unknown: We do not know where the sons were kept or for how long. The text does not show what happened to their homes.
entries.next_step: Keep the sons' capture distinct from harm to other people. Ask what happened to them after capture.
source_citations: E. Hultzsch, XV Contributions to Singhalese Chronology, Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 45(3), July 1913, pages 517–531; section II, printed pages 519–520 (South Indian Inscriptions III 59 and local III 39, as cited). DOI: 10.1017/S0035869X00045093. Public annual-volume scan.

entries.name: Women seized after a king's defeat
entries.place_and_era: The article reports Vira-Salamegha's defeat in Ceylon. Its cited record may list acts from more than one year.
entries.attested: His elder sister and daughter, or wife, were seized. His mother's nose was cut off. He was killed in battle.
entries.unknown: The text does not say where the seized women went. This may be the same event as another account. The kings' names differ, so the match is not proved.
entries.next_step: Keep the named kin and their harms distinct. Do not count this and the other account as two separate events.
source_citations: E. Hultzsch, XV Contributions to Singhalese Chronology, Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 45(3), July 1913, pages 517–531; section III, printed pages 520–521 (South Indian Inscriptions III 52, as cited). DOI: 10.1017/S0035869X00045093. Public annual-volume scan.

entries.name: Women seized after the king fled
entries.place_and_era: The text names Mahipala in a battle claim. The exact place and date of this act are unknown.
entries.attested: The text says the army put the king to flight. It then seized women and elephants. The women are people, not part of the goods.
entries.unknown: The women's names, number and ties to the king are unknown. The text does not say where they went or what happened to their homes.
entries.next_step: Keep the seizure of women distinct from the king's flight and goods. Ask what happened to the women after capture.
source_citations: E. Hultzsch, No. 31, Tirumalai Rock Inscription of Rajendra-Chola I, Epigraphia Indica IX, English translation, printed page 233, inscription lines 10–11; article printed pages 229–233.

entries.name: An attack and expulsion in the Great Prairie account
entries.place_and_era: Great Prairie, by the Arkansas River. The account record dates to 1827. The attack date is unknown.
entries.attested: Hoffman quotes a Quapaw account of an attack on a camp. It says the people resisted, then lost. The attackers drove them away and claimed control of the area.
entries.unknown: The source links the name Intouka to Illinois. That link, the date and the extent of control remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Study the people at the camp and the land they used. Keep this attack distinct from the earlier Tonnika encounter.
source_citations: Michael P. Hoffman (1993), The Depopulation and Abandonment of Northeastern Arkansas in the Protohistoric Period. Chapter 15 in James B. Stoltman (ed.), Archaeology of Eastern North America: Papers in Honor of Stephen Williams. Archaeological Report 25, printed pages 261–275; cited printed pages 268. One consulted chapter; underlying accounts and reports not independently consulted.

entries.name: Survivors and new homes by the Arkansas River
entries.place_and_era: By the Arkansas River. Hoffman places the likely moves in the late 1500s or early 1600s. The exact dates remain unknown.
entries.attested: Hoffman argues that survivors from the Old Town, Kent and Walls phases moved to the Arkansas River. He uses pottery evidence for this view.
entries.unknown: The cause and terms of these moves remain unclear. Pottery does not prove that people left under force or took land from others.
entries.next_step: Study the groups and their new homes. Keep other proposed routes distinct.
source_citations: Michael P. Hoffman (1993), The Depopulation and Abandonment of Northeastern Arkansas in the Protohistoric Period. Chapter 15 in James B. Stoltman (ed.), Archaeology of Eastern North America: Papers in Honor of Stephen Williams. Archaeological Report 25, printed pages 261–275; cited printed pages 269–272. One consulted chapter; underlying accounts and reports not independently consulted.

entries.name: The loss of homes in northeast Arkansas
entries.place_and_era: Northeast Arkansas. Hoffman compares regional reports from the 1540s and 1673. The gap in permanent homes does not date one forced move. It does not prove that all land use stopped.
entries.attested: Hoffman contrasts towns in use in the 1540s with a later lack of permanent homes. He reviews disease, drought and conflict as possible causes.
entries.unknown: The chapter does not establish one cause or one forced move. The fates of many residents remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Keep local departures and new homes distinct. Study how each proposed cause relates to the loss of permanent homes.
source_citations: Michael P. Hoffman (1993), The Depopulation and Abandonment of Northeastern Arkansas in the Protohistoric Period. Chapter 15 in James B. Stoltman (ed.), Archaeology of Eastern North America: Papers in Honor of Stephen Williams. Archaeological Report 25, printed pages 261–275; cited printed pages 261–263, 265–269, 272–273. One consulted chapter; underlying accounts and reports not independently consulted.

entries.name: Tunica and Tonnika accounts of flight
entries.place_and_era: Near the lower Mississippi River. Hoffman argues that the Tunica left before 1699. The exact date and earlier home remain unknown.
entries.attested: Hoffman recounts a Tunica tradition of conflict and a move downstream. A Quapaw account claims an attack that drove Tonnika away.
entries.unknown: It is unclear if both accounts describe the same departure. The exact date and place remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Study the earlier home area and the new settlement. Keep each account and its source clear.
source_citations: Michael P. Hoffman (1993), The Depopulation and Abandonment of Northeastern Arkansas in the Protohistoric Period. Chapter 15 in James B. Stoltman (ed.), Archaeology of Eastern North America: Papers in Honor of Stephen Williams. Archaeological Report 25, printed pages 261–275; cited printed pages 267–269, 272–273. One consulted chapter; underlying accounts and reports not independently consulted.

entries.name: Nulliak stayed in use under pressure
entries.place_and_era: Nulliak is on the north coast of Labrador. Spiess uses the term Late Maritime Archaic for the site. His text gives no exact date for the pressure.
entries.attested: Spiess says people kept Nulliak in use under pressure. He says the pressure came from immigrant groups. He calls them Paleoeskimo.
entries.unknown: The form of pressure is unclear. The source does not show that people lost homes or land.
entries.next_step: Read the cited reports on Nulliak. Study the pressure and whether people lost access to land.
source_citations: Arthur E. Spiess (1993), Caribou, Walrus and Seals: Maritime Archaic Subsistence in Labrador and Newfoundland. Chapter 7 in James B. Stoltman (ed.), Archaeology of Eastern North America: Papers in Honor of Stephen Williams. Archaeological Report No. 25, Mississippi Department of Archives and History, printed pages 73–100; claim at printed page 74, physical PDF page 87, right-column Nulliak paragraph. This note reports Spiess’s account; his citations are not separate confirmation.

entries.name: Homes lost at Cambabe II
entries.place_and_era: Cambabe II was a camp in Bengo, Angola. Police burned homes there in September and October 2002. The later eviction date is unknown.
entries.attested: Human Rights Watch reports that police burned homes and crops. Most residents fled. People who stayed in a compound were later forced out.
entries.unknown: The full number of people forced out is unknown. The later fate of the land is unclear.
entries.next_step: Trace the first flight and the later eviction as one sequence. Check where residents went and what happened to their homes.
source_citations: Human Rights Watch; Nadejda Marques. Struggling Through Peace: Return and Resettlement in Angola. August 2003, Vol.15, No.16(A). Printed pages: 9, 10; PDF pages: 13, 14; notes: 28-31. One consulted Human Rights Watch report; testimony, staff interviews and cited correspondence as specified in the shared source genealogy.

entries.name: Some residents left Bengo II under pressure
entries.place_and_era: Bengo II was a camp near Negage in Uige, Angola. The report covers pressure in 2002 and 2003.
entries.attested: Human Rights Watch reports that some residents left under pressure. Others stayed with aid worker support. Some kept homes, crops and school ties.
entries.unknown: The number who left is unclear. The source does not show that all residents lost their homes.
entries.next_step: Trace those who left and those who stayed. Separate the state orders from the food aid cutoff.
source_citations: Human Rights Watch; Nadejda Marques. Struggling Through Peace: Return and Resettlement in Angola. August 2003, Vol.15, No.16(A). Printed pages: 10, 11, 12, 13, 14; PDF pages: 14, 15, 16, 17, 18; notes: 32-49. One consulted Human Rights Watch report; testimony, staff interviews and cited correspondence as specified in the shared source genealogy.

entries.name: Families forced to move from home
entries.place_and_era: The report names Calala and Luvuei in Angola. Luvuei is in Moxico. The date of the transfer is unknown.
entries.attested: Human Rights Watch reports a forced move. About 18 families of former fighters went from Calala to Luvuei.
entries.unknown: The report does not name who moved the families. Their exact home sites, later rights and links to other groups are unknown.
entries.next_step: Trace this forced transfer and its effects on homes and land. Keep families distinct from people in any count.
source_citations: Human Rights Watch; Nadejda Marques. Struggling Through Peace: Return and Resettlement in Angola. August 2003, Vol.15, No.16(A). Printed pages: 22, 23; PDF pages: 26, 27; notes: 98. One consulted Human Rights Watch report; testimony, staff interviews and cited correspondence as specified in the shared source genealogy.

entries.name: A woman taken from shelter at Cazombo
entries.place_and_era: The assault took place at Cazombo in Angola. The report gives the date as January 14, 2003.
entries.attested: Human Rights Watch reports that soldiers took a woman from a school used as shelter to the bushes. They raped her and beat men. She later received medical care.
entries.unknown: The exact place in the bushes is unknown. The effect on use of the shelter remains an open question.
entries.next_step: Study how the assault affected use of the shelter. Compare it with the Catofe market question under the same rule.
source_citations: Human Rights Watch; Nadejda Marques. Struggling Through Peace: Return and Resettlement in Angola. August 2003, Vol.15, No.16(A). Printed pages: 19, 20, 21; PDF pages: 23, 24, 25; notes: 78-83, 90-91. One consulted Human Rights Watch report; testimony, staff interviews and cited correspondence as specified in the shared source genealogy.

entries.name: Aid pressure at Bengo and Feira
entries.place_and_era: The report places these camps near Negage in Uige, Angola. It describes pressure in 2002 and 2003.
entries.attested: Human Rights Watch reports orders to leave and threats to cut aid. Food aid also stopped at Bengo II. Some residents lacked transport.
entries.unknown: It is unclear who left because of each form of pressure. Camp names and household overlap need checks.
entries.next_step: Link this wider pressure question to the Bengo II departures. Keep food aid decisions separate from state orders.
source_citations: Human Rights Watch; Nadejda Marques. Struggling Through Peace: Return and Resettlement in Angola. August 2003, Vol.15, No.16(A).
