Printed pages: 10, 11; PDF pages: 14, 15; notes: 32-37. One consulted Human Rights Watch report; testimony, staff interviews and cited correspondence as specified in the shared source genealogy.

entries.name: A blocked family journey from Negage to Luanda
entries.place_and_era: The report describes a woman near Negage in Uige, Angola. She sought to join family in Luanda in 2003.
entries.attested: Human Rights Watch reports that barriers kept the woman from Luanda. Mines blocked land routes, and the state controlled air access.
entries.unknown: The precise role of each barrier is unclear. The source does not establish a permanent ban.
entries.next_step: Trace the barriers and their effect on her choice of home. Check how the state controlled access to Luanda.
source_citations: Human Rights Watch; Nadejda Marques. Struggling Through Peace: Return and Resettlement in Angola. August 2003, Vol.15, No.16(A). Printed pages: 11, 12; PDF pages: 15, 16; notes: 38-40. One consulted Human Rights Watch report; testimony, staff interviews and cited correspondence as specified in the shared source genealogy.

entries.name: The market burned at Catofe
entries.place_and_era: Catofe was a camp in Kuanza Sul, Angola. The report gives no exact date for the act.
entries.attested: Human Rights Watch reports that the Angolan army burned the camp market at Catofe.
entries.unknown: The full extent of the damage is unknown. How long the loss of use lasted is unknown. Later access is unclear.
entries.next_step: Trace the damage and later use of the market. Check how the loss affected its users.
source_citations: Human Rights Watch; Nadejda Marques. Struggling Through Peace: Return and Resettlement in Angola. August 2003, Vol.15, No.16(A). Printed pages: 22, 23; PDF pages: 26, 27; notes: 98. One consulted Human Rights Watch report; testimony, staff interviews and cited correspondence as specified in the shared source genealogy.

entries.name: A threat to burn homes at Amboiva
entries.place_and_era: Amboiva was a camp in Angola. The report gives no exact date for the threat.
entries.attested: Human Rights Watch reports that troops threatened to burn homes at Amboiva.
entries.unknown: The source does not establish that troops burned the homes or that residents left. A link to the Calala transfer is unknown.
entries.next_step: Trace what happened after the threat. Check for any loss of homes or use of land.
source_citations: Human Rights Watch; Nadejda Marques. Struggling Through Peace: Return and Resettlement in Angola. August 2003, Vol.15, No.16(A). Printed pages: 22, 23; PDF pages: 26, 27; notes: 98. One consulted Human Rights Watch report; testimony, staff interviews and cited correspondence as specified in the shared source genealogy.

entries.name: Reports of violence and questions about homes
entries.place_and_era: These are separate reports from the border and from Bengo II in Angola. They concern different acts and dates.
entries.attested: Human Rights Watch reports a fatal attack at the border and deaths in a river. It also reports rape and abduction at Bengo II. These are separate reports, not one event.
entries.unknown: The effect of each incident on homes or land use is unclear. The reports do not establish forced departure in every case.
entries.next_step: Trace each incident and its effect on residence separately. Keep the victims and dates distinct.
source_citations: Human Rights Watch; Nadejda Marques. Struggling Through Peace: Return and Resettlement in Angola. August 2003, Vol.15, No.16(A). Printed pages: 13, 14, 18; PDF pages: 17, 18, 22; notes: 46-49, 71-73. One consulted Human Rights Watch report; testimony, staff interviews and cited correspondence as specified in the shared source genealogy.

entries.name: Pressure and village moves near Lake Ontario
entries.place_and_era: Western north shore of Lake Ontario, in the late 1500s and early 1600s. These are broad study dates, not the dates of one attack.
entries.attested: Birch and Hart link the loss of village residence in western valleys to pressure from a conflict frontier. Their study uses site dates, settlement patterns and pottery. They note that some village moves had other causes.
entries.unknown: The study does not trace each family or each move. Exact dates, routes and later access to the old village lands are unclear. Refuge at sites farther east is a linked proposal.
entries.next_step: Assess this bounded withdrawal for the atlas. Keep its limits and its possible links to other village moves clear.
source_citations: Jennifer Birch, John P. Hart (2021). Conflict, Population Movement, and Microscale Social Networks in Northern Iroquoian Archaeology. American Antiquity 86(2):350–367. DOI: 10.1017/aaq.2021.5.

entries.name: Health and burial treatment at Harappa
entries.place_and_era: Harappa, in present-day Pakistan; burial groups from about 2550 to 1700 BCE. These dates describe the study, not a removal event.
entries.attested: A study reports disease and unequal burial treatment at Harappa. It cites earlier injury findings and discusses population decline. The original dig report describes mixed human and animal remains with burial pottery in Area G.
entries.unknown: The dig report names several possible causes: massacre, raid, accident or epidemic. These sources do not establish that a group lost its homes or use of land. The burial samples do not show rates of disease or violence among people alive at the time.
entries.next_step: Compare the Area G burial context with evidence for where people lived. Check whether a specific process changed access to homes or land for a group.
source_citations: Gwen Robbins Schug and colleagues, Infection, Disease, and Biosocial Processes at the End of the Indus Civilization, PLOS ONE 8(12), e84814 (2013), pp.4–11 and16–17; Tables1–2. DOI:10.1371/journal.pone.0084814.
Madho Sarup Vats, Excavations at Harappa (1940), vol. I, Chapter V, pp. 192–202; especially pp. 197–202. PDF pages 219–229.
Vats, Excavations at Harappa (1940), vol. II, plates XXXIX–XLII and LVIII(a). PDF pages 89, 90, 92, 94 and 124.

entries.name: Fire and departure at a Mitchell house
entries.place_and_era: Mitchell, in present-day South Dakota, United States. The ancient date is not known.
entries.attested: Meleen describes burned posts, pots and other finds at House 1. He interprets them as signs of a partial fire and a hurried departure. His report also describes village defenses.
entries.unknown: The cause and date are not known. This report does not show that people were forced out or that the whole village was left. The link between the village and nearby burial mounds is unclear.
entries.next_step: Check excavation records and later studies of the site. Look for evidence of what caused the departure and what happened to the use of this house.
source_citations: Elmer E. Meleen, A Preliminary Report of the Mitchell Indian Village and Burial Mounds on Firesteel Creek, Mitchell, Davison County, South Dakota (Museum of University of South Dakota, December1938), PartI, pp.4,9,14.

entries.name: The earlier Yueh-chih flight
entries.place_and_era: An ancient movement before Kushan rule. The homeland and date are unknown. The account names northern Bactria as a later home.
entries.attested: Puri says Hsiung-nu pressure drove the Great Yueh-chih from their homeland. They later settled in northern Bactria.
entries.unknown: The route and the size of the group are unknown. The account does not link every later leg to the same people.
entries.next_step: Assess the reported departure and later settlement as one bounded question. Keep later Kushan acts separate.
source_citations: B. N. Puri, The Kushans, History of Civilizations of Central Asia, volume II, chapter 11 (first publication 1994; held impression 1996), pp. 239, 240.

entries.name: Kujula defeats four rival rulers
entries.place_and_era: The early Kushan realm. The four domains and the exact date remain unknown.
entries.attested: Puri says Kujula defeated four other yabghu and made himself king. Their separate rule ended in this account.
entries.unknown: The account does not name the four rulers or fix their domain bounds. The fate of residents is unknown.
entries.next_step: Assess one collective loss of rule. Do not turn the four rulers into four separate capture events.
source_citations: B. N. Puri, The Kushans, History of Civilizations of Central Asia, volume II, chapter 11 (first publication 1994; held impression 1996), pp. 240.

entries.name: Kujula takes Kabul
entries.place_and_era: Kao-fu, which Puri calls Kabul. The date and exact tract bounds are unknown.
entries.attested: Puri identifies Kao-fu as Kabul and says Kujula took it. The account describes a loss of Indo-Parthian control.
entries.unknown: Kapisa is related context, but its exact link to Kabul is not settled. Household removal and the duration of rule remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Assess the Kabul control claim. Keep the place-name link open and do not add a separate Kapisa capture.
source_citations: B. N. Puri, The Kushans, History of Civilizations of Central Asia, volume II, chapter 11 (first publication 1994; held impression 1996), pp. 240, 247.

entries.name: Kujula takes P'u-ta
entries.place_and_era: P'u-ta, which Puri calls Pushkalavati. This ancient account gives no fixed date or city boundary.
entries.attested: Puri says Kujula overthrew prior rule and annexed P'u-ta. The city came under his control in this account.
entries.unknown: The source does not state what happened to residents. The duration of control and exact date remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Assess this loss of city control. Keep it separate from the older account of Alexander at the same city.
source_citations: B. N. Puri, The Kushans, History of Civilizations of Central Asia, volume II, chapter 11 (first publication 1994; held impression 1996), pp. 240, 241.

entries.name: Kujula takes Chi-pin
entries.place_and_era: Chi-pin, which Puri calls Kashmir. The date and exact extent of rule remain unknown.
entries.attested: Puri says Kujula overthrew prior rule and annexed Chi-pin. The account states a change of control.
entries.unknown: The fate of residents and priests is unknown. The exact place-name match and duration of rule remain open.
entries.next_step: Assess the reported control loss. Keep later Kashmir priest and court stories separate.
source_citations: B. N. Puri, The Kushans, History of Civilizations of Central Asia, volume II, chapter 11 (first publication 1994; held impression 1996), pp. 240, 241.

entries.name: Vima and T'ien-chu
entries.place_and_era: T'ien-chu is the broad source name for India. Its exact extent and the conquest date are unknown.
entries.attested: Puri says Vima conquered T'ien-chu and put a general in control.
entries.unknown: Its link to the Indus conquest is unresolved. The account does not map a conquest of the whole subcontinent.
entries.next_step: Assess the tract and its link to the Indus claim. Resolve whether both describe the same conquest.
source_citations: B. N. Puri, The Kushans, History of Civilizations of Central Asia, volume II, chapter 11 (first publication 1994; held impression 1996), pp. 240.

entries.name: Vima takes the Indus valley
entries.place_and_era: The Indus valley to Sind. This ancient account gives no exact date or boundary.
entries.attested: Puri says Vima seized this tract as Indo-Parthian power weakened. The claim describes a change of rule.
entries.unknown: The link to T'ien-chu is unresolved. The account does not state that households left their homes.
entries.next_step: Assess the Indus control claim and its overlap with T'ien-chu. Keep Vima separate from Kujula.
source_citations: B. N. Puri, The Kushans, History of Civilizations of Central Asia, volume II, chapter 11 (first publication 1994; held impression 1996), pp. 247.

entries.name: Kanishka and the Parthian war
entries.place_and_era: Former Indo-Parthian lands in Iran. The war site and date remain unknown.
entries.attested: Puri cites a Buddhist war story. Ghirshman links it to a possible Parthian bid to regain lost lands.
entries.unknown: The account does not fix the land won or lost. The proposed cause of war remains uncertain.
entries.next_step: Assess what the reported war changed in land control or use. Keep its proposed cause separate from its outcome.
source_citations: B. N. Puri, The Kushans, History of Civilizations of Central Asia, volume II, chapter 11 (first publication 1994; held impression 1996), pp. 247.

entries.name: Begram: destruction and abandonment questions
entries.place_and_era: The New Royal City at Begram, Afghanistan. The dates and links between its occupation layers remain disputed.
entries.attested: Puri reports destruction at Begram. Later studies question the dates and links between layers; Morris argues for continued occupation, then abandonment.
entries.unknown: The cause of abandonment and its effect on residents are not established. The studies may refer to different layers.
entries.next_step: Compare the excavation records to identify which layers each account describes and what ended their use.
source_citations: B. N. Puri, The Kushans, History of Civilizations of Central Asia, volume II, chapter 11 (first publication 1994; held impression 1996), pp. 243.
Osmund Bopearachchi, Les données numismatiques et la datation du bazar de Begram, Topoi 11/1 (2001; published 2003), pp. 411–435.

Lauren Morris, Revised dates for the deposition of the Begram hoard and occupation at the New Royal City, Parthica 19 (2017), pp. 75–104; consulted manuscript, physical pp. 1–30, with five figures omitted.

entries.name: Ardashir takes three eastern tracts
entries.place_and_era: Margiana, Carmania and Sistan. Each tract has its own control claim. Exact dates remain unknown.
entries.attested: Puri says Ardashir conquered Margiana. He also names conquests of Carmania and Sistan.
entries.unknown: The order of events and the fate of residents are unknown.
entries.next_step: Assess each tract claim within this linked question. Keep later submission and Shapur phases separate.
source_citations: B. N. Puri, The Kushans, History of Civilizations of Central Asia, volume II, chapter 11 (first publication 1994; held impression 1996), pp. 248.

entries.name: Kushans regain lost territory
entries.place_and_era: Former Kushan lands before Shapur II came of age. Exact tracts and dates remain unknown.
entries.attested: Puri says the Kushans regained lost lands amid disorder in Iran.
entries.unknown: The account does not name each recovered tract or the power that lost it. Whether any household returned is unknown.
entries.next_step: Identify the recovered tract and earlier holder of control. Keep this phase separate from the earlier conquests.
source_citations: B. N. Puri, The Kushans, History of Civilizations of Central Asia, volume II, chapter 11 (first publication 1994; held impression 1996), pp. 248.

entries.name: Shapur II defeats the Kushans
entries.place_and_era: The Kushan conflict under Shapur II. The battle site and exact date are unknown.
entries.attested: Puri says Shapur II renewed war and decisively defeated the Kushans.
entries.unknown: The effects on land or homes are unknown. Defeat does not by itself show that a whole people left.
entries.next_step: Assess any stated change in control or use after this defeat. Keep this war separate from the wars of Shapur I.
source_citations: B. N. Puri, The Kushans, History of Civilizations of Central Asia, volume II, chapter 11 (first publication 1994; held impression 1996), pp. 248.

entries.name: Kanishka and eastern rule
entries.place_and_era: Mathura, Kausambi and Sarnath have inscriptions. Coins occur as far as Patna and Gaya. These are ancient sites of rule or finds.
entries.attested: Puri links inscriptions, coin finds and written accounts to wider Kushan rule.
entries.unknown: The finds do not fix one conquest or a prior holder of control. The extent and dates remain open.
entries.next_step: Separate evidence of rule from evidence of a specific conquest. Assess its link to the Pataliputra story.
source_citations: B. N. Puri, The Kushans, History of Civilizations of Central Asia, volume II, chapter 11 (first publication 1994; held impression 1996), pp. 249, 252.

entries.name: Ashvaghosha in a war payment
entries.place_and_era: Pataliputra in a religious story. The date and any later home for Ashvaghosha remain unknown.
entries.attested: Puri retells the defeat of its king. Kanishka demanded payment. He accepted Ashvaghosha, the alms bowl of the Buddha and a cock.
entries.unknown: Whether Ashvaghosha consented or moved is unknown. The story does not state that Kanishka annexed the city.
entries.next_step: Assess whether the payment changed control of his life or his residence. Keep the person distinct from the two objects.
source_citations: B. N. Puri, The Kushans, History of Civilizations of Central Asia, volume II, chapter 11 (first publication 1994; held impression 1996), pp. 249.

entries.name: Lost eastern lands after Huvishka
entries.place_and_era: Some distant eastern Kushan lands after Huvishka. The lost tracts and dates remain unknown.
entries.attested: Puri says the Kushans lost some eastern lands. They kept Mathura under their rule.
entries.unknown: The account does not name the new rulers of each lost tract. It does not give one date for all losses.
entries.next_step: Assess each lost tract and its change of rule. Keep Mathura apart from the lost lands.
source_citations: B. N. Puri, The Kushans, History of Civilizations of Central Asia, volume II, chapter 11 (first publication 1994; held impression 1996), pp. 249.

entries.name: Further losses after Vasudeva
entries.place_and_era: Kushan lands after Vasudeva. Exact tracts and dates remain unknown.
entries.attested: Puri says new dynasties and republican states took more Kushan territory after a period of stable rule.
entries.unknown: The account does not name all new rulers or fix each transfer. It does not give one date for all losses.
entries.next_step: Assess the tract and prior rule in each claimed loss. Keep the Huvishka and Vasudeva phases separate.
source_citations: B. N. Puri, The Kushans, History of Civilizations of Central Asia, volume II, chapter 11 (first publication 1994; held impression 1996), pp. 250.

entries.name: A proposed move from the Tensas Basin to Jordan
entries.place_and_era: Kidder places this movement in northeast Louisiana, roughly 1550 to 1680. These are broad source dates.
entries.attested: Kidder proposes that people moved west from the Tensas Basin and gathered at Jordan. He suggests disease and political change as possible causes.
entries.unknown: Who moved, how pressure shaped the move, and what happened at the places they left are unresolved. The chapter does not establish an expulsion.
entries.next_step: Examine the proposed move and changes in residence as separate questions. Keep the possible causes and group identities open.
source_citations: Kidder 1993, chapter 14, printed p. 256

entries.name: People gather near the lower Ouachita river junctions
entries.place_and_era: Kidder places this change near the lower Ouachita river junctions between 1682 and about 1700. It follows the earlier Tensas-to-Jordan movement.
entries.attested: He proposes that villages joined near the Ouachita and Bayou Bartholomew. He links this change to the collapse at Jordan and new trade conditions. He suggests that people from several groups joined.
entries.unknown: The groups, household choices and changes in land use are not fully known. When villages join, this does not prove that earlier residents lost their homes.
entries.next_step: Keep the decline at Jordan and the new settlements distinct. Clarify whose residence changed. Do not treat pottery styles as peoples.
source_citations: Kidder 1993, chapter 14, printed pp. 255–257

entries.name: Reported armed attacks on northeast Louisiana communities
entries.place_and_era: Kidder discusses northeast Louisiana in the early 1700s. He does not give one exact attack date or a complete list of affected places.
entries.attested: He reports that armed incursions were blamed for severe losses among Native communities. He names Chickasaw and Choctaw in this account. He also discusses a wider loss of local residents.
entries.unknown: The specific attacks, communities, numbers and resident outcomes remain unclear. The report does not show that all earlier residents were killed or expelled.
entries.next_step: Clarify the reported attacks and their effects on residence. Keep death, flight and fusion with other groups distinct.
source_citations: Kidder 1993, chapter 14, printed p. 257

entries.name: French policy and encouraged Native settlement
entries.place_and_era: Kidder describes settlement on the Yazoo River and near Natchitoches in the early 1700s. These are separate areas for settlement, not one mapped route.
entries.attested: He reports that French policy encouraged Native groups to settle in these areas. The aim included defense against rival powers and their Native allies. French resources also shifted toward the Red River.
entries.unknown: The groups, origins, terms and household choices are unresolved. Encouragement does not by itself establish forced transport or loss of home rights.
entries.next_step: Clarify the terms of settlement and any change in residence or land control. Keep the two areas and their groups separate.
source_citations: Kidder 1993, chapter 14, printed p. 257

entries.name: A decline in Lower Ohio Valley settlement
entries.place_and_era: The Lower Ohio Valley and the Wabash river mouth. The later study covers a broad period from about 1400 to 1700. These are context dates, not the date of one move.
entries.attested: Muller describes a large decline in settlement. He rejects a sudden departure of every resident. Pollack and Munson describe a move downstream from Angel toward the Wabash. They report that settlement density and outside exchange continued.
entries.unknown: The causes, people who left, routes and exact sequence remain unclear. The accounts cover different places and scales. Neither establishes forced removal. Continued settlement density does not prove that the total number of people stayed the same.
entries.next_step: Trace where people stayed or moved after Angel was left. Keep that local history separate from wider decline. Test the proposed causes. Do not treat decline as proof of expulsion.
source_citations: Muller 1993, chapter 10, printed p. 132 (context pp. 131–132)

David Pollack and Cheryl Ann Munson, Caborn-Welborn Ceramics: Intersite Comparisons and Extraregional Interaction, Current Archaeological Research in Kentucky, Volume Five (1998), printed pp. 163, 165.

entries.name: Possible upland moves away from demands by chiefs
entries.place_and_era: The question comes from a Lower Ohio Valley study. The places and dates of these possible upland moves remain unclear.
entries.attested: Muller suggests that some upland sites reflect moves away from harsh demands by chiefs. This is a proposed cause.
entries.unknown: The sites and people remain unclear. Their prior homes, new homes and changes in residence are not known. This view does not explain all regional decline.
entries.next_step: Find out which sites and moves fit this view. Keep it separate from the wider decline in settlement.
source_citations: Muller 1993, chapter 10, printed p. 140 (context pp. 138–140)

entries.name: People from Balkh settle in an Indian city
entries.place_and_era: People from Balkh in a city in India. The city and date remain unclear.
entries.attested: Litvinsky cites a literary work. It reports that people from Balkh settled in a city.
entries.unknown: The cause, number of people and changes in land use remain unclear. The report does not establish forced removal.
entries.next_step: Clarify where people settled and what changed in residence or land use. Keep the cause open.
source_citations: Litvinsky 1994, held 1996 impression, chapter 13, printed p. 296, note 33 (context pp. 295–296)

entries.name: An artist goes to work at a monastery
entries.place_and_era: An artist goes from Pushkalavati to Asmaka. Asmaka is probably in Central Asia. The place and date are not certain.
entries.attested: Litvinsky reports a story about an artist from Pushkalavati who went to Asmaka. He went there to work at a monastery.
entries.unknown: The author of the Sutralamkara is uncertain. The exact date, location and changes in residence remain unclear. The story does not establish forced labor.
entries.next_step: Clarify what the journey changed in residence or land use. Do not assume that the work was forced.
source_citations: Litvinsky 1994, held 1996 impression, chapter 13, printed p. 300, Sutralamkara IV.21 story

entries.name: An attack and a question about homes
entries.place_and_era: The McCutchan-McLaughlin site. The date of the reported attack is unknown.
entries.attested: Schambach reports violent deaths at the site. Leith reports possible homes near the mound that held graves. Excavation exposed part of one possible home, with a floor and possible posts. His study also uses earlier work on the deaths and proposes a boundary between groups.
entries.unknown: The accounts do not establish who used the tested home when the attack took place. They do not show whether the attack caused loss of homes or land. The attack date remains unknown. He did not excavate the other possible homes at this site.
entries.next_step: Check whether the people killed lived at the site. Ask what the attack changed in the use of homes or land.
source_citations: Schambach 1993, chapter 13, printed pp. 191–192 (PDF physical pp. 204–205)

Luther J. Leith, A Re-Conceptualization of the Fourche Maline Culture: The Woodland Period as a Transition in Eastern Oklahoma (PhD dissertation, University of Oklahoma, 2011), printed pp. 37–39 and 140–177. Selected site context and settlement/territoriality chapters; figures, other chapters and cited originals not verified.

entries.name: A proposed trader settlement at Sanders
entries.place_and_era: Sanders in the Red River Valley. The date and the homes of the proposed traders remain unclear.
entries.attested: Schambach proposes that traders from the Arkansas Valley settled at Sanders. He compares objects and human remains. Other explanations exist.
entries.unknown: The report does not establish a forced move or a loss of local land. A proposed link to child adoption, slavery and disease remains a guess.
entries.next_step: Clarify who settled at Sanders and on what terms. Ask what changed for those who arrived and for people already there.
source_citations: Schambach 1993, chapter 13, printed pp. 203–207 (PDF physical pp. 216–220)

entries.name: A proposed trader settlement at Nagle
entries.place_and_era: Nagle is near Oklahoma City. The date and the homes of any proposed traders remain unclear.
entries.attested: Schambach proposes that traders settled at Nagle. He compares burial objects and human remains with finds from other sites.
entries.unknown: These comparisons do not establish a forced move or a loss of local land. Modern damage to graves does not describe an ancient removal.
entries.next_step: Clarify who used Nagle and whether traders settled there. Ask what changed in residence, land use or access.
source_citations: Schambach 1993, chapter 13, printed pp. 207–208 (PDF physical pp. 220–221)

entries.name: A report of war between Tanico and Tula
entries.place_and_era: Tanico and Tula in a report from the sixteenth century. The exact places, groups and dates remain unclear.
entries.attested: Schambach relays a report through Quinn. In this account, a leader described war and said the groups did not understand each other.
entries.unknown: The report does not establish a loss of homes or land. The identity of Tula and the extent of the war remain uncertain.
entries.next_step: Clarify which groups the account names and how they used the area. Ask whether the reported war changed residence or access to land.
source_citations: Schambach 1993, chapter 13, printed pp. 222–223 (PDF physical pp. 235–236)

entries.name: Did people linked to Spiro move to Tanico?
entries.place_and_era: Spiro and proposed later settlements along the Arkansas River. The places, groups and dates in this proposed sequence remain unclear.
entries.attested: Schambach asks whether people linked to Spiro moved to Tanico. He also asks whether Wichita later entered a western area.
entries.unknown: These ideas do not establish a forced move, a cause of decline or a transfer of land. They do not prove that the named groups were the same people.
entries.next_step: Clarify which settlements continued and which people moved, if any. Treat each proposed stage as a separate question about residence and land use.
source_citations: Schambach 1993, chapter 13, printed pp. 221–224 (PDF physical pp. 234–237)

entries.name: Water duties and pressure at Vargsar
entries.place_and_era: Vargsar and Samarkand. The chapter places the duties in an early medieval context. The dates of the attacks remain unknown.
entries.attested: The chapter reports dam guard duties and land-tax relief at Vargsar. It also says invaders tried to destroy the dam and force Samarkand to yield.
entries.unknown: The account does not fix each attack, its date or its result. Changes to homes, land use and control remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Keep dam duties separate from attacks. Clarify who acted, who used the land and what changed.
source_citations: Mukhamedjanov 1994, chapter 12, printed p. 263 (PDF physical p. 264)

entries.name: A duty to guard the Samarkand water supply
entries.place_and_era: Samarkand. The exact date of the reported duty is unknown.
entries.attested: The chapter says magi had to maintain and guard an aqueduct. It also reports land revenue for this duty.
entries.unknown: The account does not show a transfer of land ownership or a move from home. The people and land involved need clearer bounds.
entries.next_step: Clarify who owed the duty and how they used the land. Ask what the duty changed for them.
source_citations: Mukhamedjanov 1994, chapter 12, printed p. 264 (PDF physical p. 265)

entries.name: Slaves in the Toprak-kala records
entries.place_and_era: Toprak-kala. The chapter describes household records. This question has no settled date.
entries.attested: The chapter lists enslaved people in wealthy households. It refers to records seven and eight.
entries.unknown: The chapter does not explain how each person entered a household. Their origins and later homes remain unclear. The cited Tok-kala title needs a clearer link.
entries.next_step: Clarify the people and status in the records. Ask what changed in residence, land use or access.
source_citations: Mukhamedjanov 1994, chapter 12, printed pp. 280–281 (PDF physical pp. 281–282)

entries.name: India and the trade in enslaved people
entries.place_and_era: India in this account. The specific groups, dates and routes remain unknown.
entries.attested: The chapter reports imports and exports of enslaved people. It cites Pigulevskaya for the export list.
entries.unknown: The account does not identify a specific group, capture route or land outcome. It does not establish the later homes of those traded.
entries.next_step: Clarify which people the trade reports describe. Ask where they lived and what the trade changed for them.
source_citations: Mukhamedjanov 1994, chapter 12, printed p. 277 (PDF physical p. 278)

entries.name: Sogdians who lived at Tun-huang
entries.place_and_era: Tun-huang. The letter dates differ: late second or early fourth century CE. These are not dates of a move.
entries.attested: The chapter describes free Sogdian residents at Tun-huang. An estimate also includes slaves and families. The account notes ties with Samarkand.
entries.unknown: The account does not show that all residents arrived by force. An estimate does not give the size of a forced group.
entries.next_step: Clarify who lived at Tun-huang and how they came to live there. Keep slave status separate from claims about how all residents arrived.
source_citations: Mukhamedjanov 1994, chapter 12, printed p. 278 (PDF physical p. 279)

entries.name: A Han campaign in Ferghana
entries.place_and_era: Ferghana and the eastern Silk Route. This question has no settled campaign date.
entries.attested: The chapter reports Han control along the Silk Route and a campaign in Ferghana.
entries.unknown: A campaign does not by itself show that local people lost homes or land. Other Han cases do not fix the date here.
entries.next_step: Clarify the reported campaign, affected people or tract, and result. Keep the mission, campaign and later outposts separate.
source_citations: Mukhamedjanov 1994, chapter 12, printed p. 279 (PDF physical p. 280)

entries.name: Land and revenue at Old Nisa
entries.place_and_era: Old Nisa. The chapter draws on records from the first century BCE. That is context, not a date for a new land seizure.
entries.attested: The chapter describes royal estates and types of land revenue. It names uzbar, dastkirt and patbazik.
entries.unknown: The chapter does not show how these holdings began. It does not establish a new seizure of land or a move by its users.
entries.next_step: Clarify who controlled and used the land. Ask what the revenue terms show about property and duties.
source_citations: Mukhamedjanov 1994, chapter 12, printed p. 281 (PDF physical p. 282)

entries.name: Did landholders try to bind people to land?
entries.place_and_era: The chapter discusses communes and land. It does not fix a date, actor or tract for this proposed change.
entries.attested: The author thinks the state and large landholders tried to bind commune members to the land. He presents this as probable.
entries.unknown: The account does not establish one change for all communities. It leaves the process and its effects on homes and land unresolved.
entries.next_step: Clarify which people and land the claim concerns. Ask what evidence supports a change in their duties or freedom to move.
source_citations: Mukhamedjanov 1994, chapter 12, printed pp. 281–282 (PDF physical pp. 282–283)

entries.name: A condition to keep estates
entries.place_and_era: Kharagpur in Bengal is the reported place. The account links the claim to Akbar, but gives no event year.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that defeated Kharagpur rulers accepted Islam to keep their family estates. He cites a census report.
entries.unknown: The account does not show whether they kept the estates or lost any land. The terms and effects remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Trace the report and define the estates at issue. Ask what the condition changed for the rulers and other users.
source_citations: Eaton 1993, chapter 5, note 23

entries.name: A report of attacks on the Noakhali coast
entries.place_and_era: The complaint dates from 1638. It concerns the Noakhali coast in Bengal.
entries.attested: Eaton cites a complaint by the governor. It reports Portuguese attacks on Muslims along the coast.
entries.unknown: The account does not establish that people left their homes or lost land. The people and places affected remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Trace the complaint and its source. Ask what the attacks changed for homes, land or local control.
source_citations: Eaton 1993, chapter 5, note 62

entries.name: Jessore comes under Mughal rule
entries.place_and_era: The source names Jessore in Bengal. It gives no year for this loss of rule.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that Mughal forces defeated Pratapaditya and put him in prison. Mughal officers then took control of the lands under his rule. They assessed the revenue from those lands.
entries.unknown: The source does not show that residents lost homes or land rights. The date and the harm to residents remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Assess this reported loss of rule. Keep the earlier promise of retained lands separate from the later loss of control.
source_citations: Eaton 1993, chapter 6, notes 71–73

entries.name: Sand Canyon Pueblo: attack and loss of residence
entries.place_and_era: Sand Canyon Pueblo, southwest Colorado. The attack was after 1277 CE. The report estimates that use of the site as a home ended around 1280 CE.
entries.attested: The site report links a lethal attack to the end of residence at Sand Canyon Pueblo.
entries.unknown: The report does not establish who attacked, where survivors went, or how many people died.
entries.next_step: Review this record for atlas admission. Keep the earlier departures separate from the final attack.
source_citations: Kuckelman 2007, chapter 9, paragraphs 9-16, 51-62, 65-66

entries.name: Mahmud cedes territory to Sher Khan
entries.place_and_era: Eaton places the cession west of Rajmahal in 1535.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that Sher Khan forced Mahmud to give up territory west of Rajmahal. Mahmud also had to pay tribute.
entries.unknown: The exact area and changes to local rights remain unclear. The source does not establish that residents lost homes.
entries.next_step: Assess the reported change in control. Keep the later overthrow separate.
source_citations: Eaton 1993, chapter 6, notes 2 and 3

entries.name: Bengal: seizure and sale of wives and children
entries.place_and_era: Bengal, South Asia. The account has seventeenth-century context. The dates of the practice are unknown.
entries.attested: Manrique reports that tax officials seized wives and children from families he called "heathens". He says they enslaved them and sold them at auction when families lacked the means to pay tax. An editor's note discusses non-Muslim debtors as a broader group.
entries.unknown: The chapter does not establish a change of home or land control. Destinations and numbers are unknown.
entries.next_step: Check whether this practice forced a move or changed land use or access. Names, counts and later land titles are not required.
source_citations: Manrique, Travels of Fray Sebastien Manrique 1629-1643, volume I, chapter VI. Routledge 2016 reflow of the Luard/Hosten translation: physical page 119, sections [20/2]-[21/1]; editorial note 5, physical page 123. Original printed-page-53 crosswalk unverified.

entries.name: East Tennessee: moves into walled towns
entries.place_and_era: East Tennessee, late 1200s to early 1300s. The study links the Hiwassee Island and Dallas periods.
entries.attested: The authors report that turmoil led people from scattered farms and small villages into Dallas towns with wooden walls.
entries.unknown: The kind of pressure on these moves is unclear. The account does not show that every move was forced. Safety, imposed moves and agreed moves remain possible.
entries.next_step: Examine how turmoil changed where people lived and what choices they had.
source_citations: Lynne P. Sullivan, Kevin E. Smith, Scott C. Meeks and Shawn M. Patch (2024), "Tracking Mississippian Migrations from the Central Mississippi Valley to the Ridge and Valley with a Unified Absolute Chronology," American Antiquity 89(2): 221-237. DOI: 10.1017/aaq.2024.1. Relevant pages: 225, 226, 228 and 231.

entries.name: Middle Cumberland to Ridge and Valley: possible migration
entries.place_and_era: Middle Cumberland and Ridge and Valley regions, from the mid-1200s into the 1400s.
entries.attested: The authors propose a gradual movement between these regions. They compare dates, objects and studies of human remains.
entries.unknown: The migration model does not establish one forced route or one cause for all moves.
entries.next_step: Identify a bounded move and the pressure, loss of residence or change in land use involved.
source_citations: Lynne P. Sullivan, Kevin E. Smith, Scott C. Meeks and Shawn M. Patch (2024), "Tracking Mississippian Migrations from the Central Mississippi Valley to the Ridge and Valley with a Unified Absolute Chronology," American Antiquity 89(2): 221-237. DOI: 10.1017/aaq.2024.1. Relevant pages: 226 and 228-232.

entries.name: Hixon mound: possible refuge from northern Georgia
entries.place_and_era: Hixon mound, southeast Tennessee, in the 1200s and 1300s.
entries.attested: The authors report differences between people buried at Hixon and three nearby groups. They suggest refuge from northern Georgia, perhaps Etowah, as one explanation.
entries.unknown: The authors call the refuge idea speculative. The comparison does not prove an Etowah origin or a forced move. The study identifies no living area linked to the mound.
entries.next_step: Examine whether the people buried at Hixon came from northern Georgia and what caused any move.
source_citations: Lynne P. Sullivan, Kevin E. Smith, Scott C. Meeks and Shawn M. Patch (2024), "Tracking Mississippian Migrations from the Central Mississippi Valley to the Ridge and Valley with a Unified Absolute Chronology," American Antiquity 89(2): 221-237. DOI: 10.1017/aaq.2024.1. Relevant pages: 227-228 and 230.

entries.name: Etowah: later use by about 1400
entries.place_and_era: Etowah, northern Georgia, by about 1400, after the earlier violent collapse.
entries.attested: The study reports that people used Etowah again. It became one of several towns of moderate size in the region.
entries.unknown: The later residents are not matched to those who left. The study does not establish a new taking of land or forced move into the site.
entries.next_step: Keep the later use linked to the earlier loss. Examine whether later use involved a separate taking or forced move.
source_citations: Lynne P. Sullivan, Kevin E. Smith, Scott C. Meeks and Shawn M. Patch (2024), "Tracking Mississippian Migrations from the Central Mississippi Valley to the Ridge and Valley with a Unified Absolute Chronology," American Antiquity 89(2): 221-237. DOI: 10.1017/aaq.2024.1. Relevant pages: 225 and 232.

entries.name: A Christian farm community at Bhallua
entries.place_and_era: Bhallua; observed in 1713
entries.attested: A priest visited the village. He described a local leader, his sons and workers in a farm community.
entries.unknown: The start date and any loss of earlier land use are unknown. The source does not establish the origin of the leader.
entries.next_step: Trace how the village formed and who used its land before.
source_citations: Eaton (1993), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 9, notes 98, 99, 100.

entries.name: A disputed market on shrine land
entries.place_and_era: Satkania; grant in 1734, complaint date unknown
entries.attested: A shrine trustee said Tej Singh set up a market on shrine land without right. The trustee asked for its removal.
entries.unknown: The passage does not give the judgment or say that the market was removed.
entries.next_step: Find the outcome of the complaint and its effect on land use.
source_citations: Eaton (1993), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 9, notes 51.

entries.name: A gap in residence at Strawberry Island
entries.place_and_era: Strawberry Island, lower Snake River, Washington. Early homes predate European contact. The date of any departure is unknown.
entries.attested: The report records two groups of homes built at different times. The author suggests a long gap in residence, followed by later use of the site.
entries.unknown: The cause of the gap is unknown. Some homes had several floors, so the evidence does not show that all people left.
entries.next_step: Check the dates and layers for each group of homes. Look for evidence of why residence ended or changed.
source_citations: Randall F. Schalk (editor; Chapter 7 author), The 1978 and 1979 Excavations at Strawberry Island in the McNary Reservoir, Project Report 19 (1983), Chapter 7, printed pp. 137–148.

entries.name: A general transfers control under Sena V
entries.place_and_era: Sri Lanka during Sena V's reign, in the tenth century. The source reports the second regnal year.
entries.attested: Codrington describes a general's retaliation after the king killed his brother. Control changed before reconciliation and the king's return.
entries.unknown: The account calls the treatment oppressive but does not specify all acts. It does not establish mass expulsion.
entries.next_step: Identify the acts and affected places. Keep this episode separate from Mahinda's later flight.
source_citations: H. W. Codrington, A Short History of Ceylon, chapter III, Sena V (web transcription).

entries.name: A grant and settlement at Pingla
entries.place_and_era: Midnapur; a later account places the grant during the reign of Taj Khan Karrani, 1564–65.
entries.attested: A tradition links Khondkar Shah Ala to a grant from Taj Khan Karrani. Local people helped clear forest.
entries.unknown: The account does not establish the grant boundary, earlier land rights or any forced move.
entries.next_step: Check what rights the grant changed and who used the land.
source_citations: Eaton (1993), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 8, note 44.

entries.name: A Kalinga ruler seeks refuge in Lanka
entries.place_and_era: Kalinga and Sri Lanka, probably the early seventh century. The date is not secure.
entries.attested: Codrington reports that a ruler left Kalinga because of war and became a monk in Lanka.
entries.unknown: The ruler is unnamed. The link to Pulakesin's conquest and its date is tentative. No wider group of refugees is established.
entries.next_step: Identify the chronicle passage and assess the reported departure. Keep its cause open.
source_citations: H. W. Codrington, A Short History of Ceylon, chapter III, Kalinga ruler flight (web transcription).

entries.name: A kazi settlement in Gaurnadi: record 696
entries.place_and_era: Gaurnadi, Bakarganj; recorded in surveys from 1902–1913. The settlement date is unknown.
entries.attested: A survey links the community to a kazi who was among the early settlers.
entries.unknown: The account does not establish earlier land rights or a taking. This village has a separate survey record.
entries.next_step: Trace this community and its land history without merging the two records.
source_citations: Eaton (1993), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 8, note 91.

entries.name: A lama and part of his flock in refuge
entries.place_and_era: From Sikkim to Puraniya district. Hamilton published the account in 1819. He gives no exact year for the flight.
entries.attested: Hamilton says a lama fled with part of his flock to escape Gorkhalese violence. The lama was his main source on Sikkim.
entries.unknown: Hamilton reports what an informant told him. The home village, group size and ethnic identity remain unknown. The account does not establish permanent settlement or a later return.
entries.next_step: Trace this group and its former homes. Keep this earlier flight separate from the letter of 1827.
source_citations: Francis Buchanan Hamilton, An Account of the Kingdom of Nepal (1819). Hamilton1819 Introduction printed1–2, with entire introduction1–6 read for method; Country of Sikim118–128 for bounded context. HTML transcription with print anchors; no scanned-page verification. Informant account, not an eyewitness claim about flight.

entries.name: A land grant and settlement at Mithapur
entries.place_and_era: Mithapur in Bengal; an eighteenth-century settlement account.
entries.attested: Eaton links settlement at Mithapur to a revenue grant and cooperation between Janaki Ballav Roy and Shaikh Ghazi.
entries.unknown: The account does not establish prior rights or show that anyone had to leave. Forest does not mean vacant land.
entries.next_step: Identify the land rights before and after the grant, and any earlier residents.
source_citations: Eaton (1993 archive context), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 8, notes 94.

entries.name: A leader leaves Saiyidpur
entries.place_and_era: Saiyidpur in Bengal; an account from 1906 about the eighteenth century.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that a captain got a holy man to leave after local farmers withheld rent. The captain then gained revenue rights.
entries.unknown: How the man left and where he went are unknown. The account does not establish a violent attack.
entries.next_step: Define the change in control. Keep the unknown means of departure explicit.
source_citations: Eaton (1993 archive context), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 8, notes 97.

entries.name: A possible refuge at Cerro de en medio
entries.place_and_era: Aguascalientes, Mexico. The study concerns the Late Classic period, 500 to 900 CE. This does not date a known flight.
entries.attested: The study records hilltop homes, walls and food stores. The authors suggest that people used the site as a refuge.
entries.unknown: The study does not show who sought shelter or why people later left. The authors also consider other uses for the food stores and hilltop.
entries.next_step: Look for evidence of when people lived at the site, why they came and why they left.
source_citations: Manuel de Jesús Dueñas-Garcia, Miriam Selene Campos-Martinez and Nicola Lercari, Evaluating settlement defensibility during the late classic (2022), author-uploaded version: internal pp. 17–24; methods/results pp. 7–16. Final pagination not mapped.

entries.name: A possible temporary move at Consol
entries.place_and_era: Consol, in the Upper Ohio Valley. The study compares the earlier village with sites occupied in the 1300s. It does not give the date of a temporary move.
entries.attested: Two village layouts overlap. The authors infer that residents had to live elsewhere for a time between the two occupations. They think that the same community built both villages.
entries.unknown: The place where people stayed, the length of the gap and its cause remain unknown. The source does not establish force or loss of land rights. It leaves the cause of later village growth open.
entries.next_step: Check the dates and order of construction. Look for evidence of where people lived during the gap and why they moved.
source_citations: John P. Hart and Bernard K. Means, The Monongahela tradition in “real time”: Bayesian analysis of radiocarbon dates (2022), PLOS ONE 17(10): e0276014, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0276014. Discussion, paragraph beginning Consol’s two components represented discrete occupations; temporary relocation and same-community inference remain qualified.

entries.name: A southward village shift near the Spoon River
entries.place_and_era: Central Illinois River Valley, near the Spoon and Illinois river junction. Wilson links the shift to Oneota arrival around 1300.
entries.attested: Wilson reports that villages shifted south as Oneota people arrived in the area. He suggests conflict as a cause. He gives alliances and captivity as possible explanations for mixed pottery.
entries.unknown: The cause of the move is not established. The source does not name every community or identify the attackers at Orendorf. Mixed pottery alone does not prove captive movement.
entries.next_step: Check the link between the reported move and conflict. Keep alliance, captive and other accounts distinct.
source_citations: Greg D. Wilson, Incinerated Villages in the North (2015), printed pp. 104. Original author-hosted chapter; full eight-page text layer and selected published images read. Underlying excavation reports not independently read.

Gregory D. Wilson, Mallory A. Melton, Amber M. VanDerwarker, Reassessing the chronology of the Mississippian Central Illinois River Valley using Bayesian analysis (2017), ahead-of-print physical pp. 4. Consulted author-archived ahead-of-print version; physical pages1–4 and13–15 read. No full model audit or crosswalk to2018issue22–38. Overlapping author, not independent attack confirmation.

entries.name: Afghan refuge in Sylhet
entries.place_and_era: Southern Sylhet; late sixteenth-century context
entries.attested: Eaton says Afghan chiefs fled Mughal forces as they advanced. The chiefs found refuge in southern Sylhet.
entries.unknown: The passage does not name their home tracts. It does not show what changed for people already in Sylhet.
entries.next_step: Trace this flight and its effects. Keep it distinct from earlier Afghan arrivals.
source_citations: Eaton (1993), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 9, Religious Gentry of Sylhet opening narrative.

entries.name: Ahom defeat of sultanate forces
entries.place_and_era: Kuch Bihar and Kamrup, in 1533.
entries.attested: A note by Eaton reports that Ahom forces defeated the sultanate army. The sultanate then withdrew from Kuch Bihar and Kamrup.
entries.unknown: This does not show that the wider population was deported. The account does not define the later control of every part of the region.
entries.next_step: Compare this reversal with the earlier sultanate conquest. Keep it distinct from the broad history of Ahom settlement.
source_citations: Eaton (1993 archive context), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 7, section s1.7.6, notes 75.

entries.name: Altamaha and Ocute withdrawal
entries.place_and_era: Coastal South Carolina toward Guale and Florida, after the 1715 war.
entries.attested: Smith traces Altamaha and Ocute as Lower Yamassee towns. He reports their later withdrawal toward Guale and Florida.
entries.unknown: The order of events does not establish whether or how people were forced to move. It does not show that they took others’ land on arrival.
entries.next_step: Keep these groups and their destinations separate from the Lower Creek return.
source_citations: Smith (1992), Historic Period Indian Archaeology of Northern Georgia, p. 36.

entries.name: An order to take back land grants
entries.place_and_era: Sylhet; order in 1672-1673
entries.attested: Eaton reports an order to take back Hindu rent-free grants. He also records further grants to Hindus in Sylhet after that order.
entries.unknown: The order does not prove that each grant was taken back. Later grants do not prove that no one lost rights.
entries.next_step: Find evidence of how the order was applied to particular grants.
source_citations: Eaton (1993), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 9, notes 93, 94.

entries.name: An unexplained departure from Daimabad
entries.place_and_era: Daimabad, Maharashtra, India. This question concerns the end of the Late Harappan phase and the later Daimabad phase. The departure date is unresolved.
entries.attested: Sali reports a gap between occupations and weathered deposits. He says the reason that the Late Harappan residents left is unknown.
entries.unknown: The report does not establish why people left or where they went. Later occupation does not show that the new residents forced them out.
entries.next_step: Check the layers and dates of the gap. Look for evidence of the cause of departure and later use.
source_citations: S. A. Sali, Daimabad 1976–79, Memoirs of the Archaeological Survey of India 83 (1986), printed pp. 21, 24, 26.

entries.name: Apalachee settlement near Savannah Town
entries.place_and_era: From the Tallahassee area to near former Savannah Town, 1704.
entries.attested: Smith reports Apalachee settlement near former Savannah Town. Barnwell’s map marks the Apalatachee town as deserted in 1715.
entries.unknown: The riverbank and local land relations are unclear. The account does not show that all arrivals were captives. Later copies of maps do not prove continued residence.
entries.next_step: Keep this place of arrival separate from the attacks in Florida. Check the local land relations.
source_citations: Smith (1992), Historic Period Indian Archaeology of Northern Georgia, pp. 34, 35, 36.

entries.name: Birbhum under Mughal rule
entries.place_and_era: Birbhum, in the early Mughal period described by Eaton.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that Birbhum submitted to Mughal rule without resistance. He places this in a western region where much local administration continued.
entries.unknown: The account does not establish eviction of the people who lived there. Continued local rule does not mean there was no change in power.
entries.next_step: Assess the change in rule and keep local continuity visible. Do not require expulsion for a land-control question.
source_citations: Eaton (1993 archive context), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 7, section s1.7.5, notes 67.

entries.name: Blue Mesa: death and a burned house
entries.place_and_era: Blue Mesa, Colorado, site 5LP379, in the early Pueblo I regional study. The event date is unresolved.
entries.attested: Potter reports an interpretation of a woman’s death as violence followed by destruction of the house.
entries.unknown: He also allows burial followed by ritual burning. The source does not settle which process occurred.
entries.next_step: Read Fritz and Honeycutt’s report to check the remains, fire and residential context.
source_citations: James M. Potter, The Community, Animas–La Plata Project, Volume XVI: Final Synthetic Report, chapter 13 (2010), pp. 253, 255.

entries.name: Bodo Canyon: a house fire
entries.place_and_era: Bodo Canyon, Colorado, site 5LP481, in the early Pueblo I regional study. The event date is unresolved.
entries.attested: Potter reports two people interpreted as trapped when a pit house burned.
entries.unknown: The cause of the fire is unclear. Accidental fire remains possible; deliberate removal is not established.
entries.next_step: Read Fuller’s report to check the fire context and the end of residential use.
source_citations: James M. Potter, The Community, Animas–La Plata Project, Volume XVI: Final Synthetic Report, chapter 13 (2010), pp. 253, 256.

entries.name: Burned homes and departure at Orendorf
entries.place_and_era: Central Illinois River Valley. Wilson places the final village fire around 1250. This is an estimate.
entries.attested: Wilson says fire destroyed the final village. People left in haste and left valuable goods in their homes. He says warfare was the most likely cause.
entries.unknown: The attackers, exact year and places where survivors went are unknown. The account does not prove that a man found in a burned house died in that fire. Regional grave counts do not give a death count for this event.
entries.next_step: Assess this village destruction and departure under the atlas rules. Keep the likely cause and estimated date clear.
source_citations: Greg D. Wilson, Incinerated Villages in the North (2015), printed pp. 102, 103. Original author-hosted chapter; full eight-page text layer and selected published images read. Underlying excavation reports not independently read.

entries.name: Burned homes at Buckeye Bend
entries.place_and_era: Central Illinois River Valley. Wilson places this village in his account of village fires in the late 1200s. No exact year is set.
entries.attested: Wilson names Buckeye Bend as a village with burned rows of homes around a plaza. His account treats warfare as the most likely cause of the village fires.
entries.unknown: The cause is likely, not certain. The account gives less detail on departure here than at Orendorf. The attackers, deaths and places where residents went are unknown. We do not copy details from Orendorf.
entries.next_step: Assess the probable wartime destruction of these homes. Keep any departure and its date separate from what the evidence shows.
source_citations: Greg D. Wilson, Incinerated Villages in the North (2015), printed pp. 103. Original author-hosted chapter; full eight-page text layer and selected published images read. Underlying excavation reports not independently read.

entries.name: Burned homes at Star Bridges
entries.place_and_era: Central Illinois River Valley. Wilson places this village in his account of village fires in the late 1200s. No exact year is set.
entries.attested: Wilson names Star Bridges as a village with burned rows of homes around a plaza. His account treats warfare as the most likely cause of the village fires.
entries.unknown: The cause is likely, not certain. The account gives less detail on departure here than at Orendorf. The attackers, deaths and places where residents went are unknown. We do not copy details from Orendorf.
entries.next_step: Assess the probable wartime destruction of these homes. Keep any departure and its date separate from what the evidence shows.
source_citations: Greg D. Wilson, Incinerated Villages in the North (2015), printed pp. 102, 103. Original author-hosted chapter; full eight-page text layer and selected published images read. Underlying excavation reports not independently read.

entries.name: Captives settled as farmers in Arakan
entries.place_and_era: Arakan; dates unresolved
entries.attested: Eaton reports that captives taken by the Arakanese were settled on land as farmers.
entries.unknown: The particular raids, places where captives settled and overlap with other capture accounts remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Trace the places where captives settled and their links to the reported raids.
source_citations: Eaton (1993), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 9, notes 19.

entries.name: Capture raids in Lower Bengal
entries.place_and_era: Lower Bengal waterways and islands; Bernier was there in 1665, but raid dates are unclear.
entries.attested: Eaton quotes Bernier on Portuguese raiders under Arakanese protection. The account reports capture, slavery, burning and deserted islands.
entries.unknown: The passage does not identify each raid, island or number of people. It does not show that Arakanese forces joined the raids.
entries.next_step: Assess the reported removal practice without merging it with other attacks or tax seizures.
source_citations: Eaton (1993), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 8, note 83.

entries.name: Chickasaw settlement and river crossing
entries.place_and_era: Near Fort Moore, around 1722–1723, with a move across the river in 1737.
entries.attested: Smith reports a Chickasaw settlement and a later move across the river.
entries.unknown: The account does not establish force or a taking of land. Residence until the Revolution is only a possibility.
entries.next_step: Trace the reasons for the moves and the land relations at each place.
source_citations: Smith (1992), Historic Period Indian Archaeology of Northern Georgia, p. 36.

entries.name: Coastal guards bar entry under Sena II
entries.place_and_era: The coast of Sri Lanka during Sena II's ninth-century reign. Sites and exact dates are unknown.
entries.attested: Codrington reports guards placed on the coast to bar entry by members of suppressed religious groups.
entries.unknown: The account does not identify prior residents among those barred. Expulsion and blocked return are not established.
entries.next_step: Identify the groups and whether the restriction prevented entry, return, or both.
source_citations: H. W. Codrington, A Short History of Ceylon, chapter III, Sena II: coastal guards (web transcription).

entries.name: Conquest of Bhallua
entries.place_and_era: Bhallua in eastern Bengal, around 1611.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that Mughal forces took a fort and raided the countryside. They killed or imprisoned peasants who refused to submit. Ananta Manik left his lands, which the Mughals took over. His minister accepted Mughal rank.
entries.unknown: The account does not show that all peasants fled. It does not give their destinations or the share killed or held captive.
entries.next_step: Keep the peasants, the ruler who left and the minister distinct. Assess the land takeover without a claim that later religious change had one cause.
source_citations: Eaton (1993 archive context), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 7, section s1.7.7, notes 93, 94, 95.

entries.name: Coosa and nearby chiefdoms
entries.place_and_era: Southeastern North America, in accounts from 1540 and 1560.
entries.attested: Hally reports that up to six chiefdoms acknowledged Coosa rule. He cites Spanish accounts from 1540 and 1560.
entries.unknown: The chapter does not show how this rule began or establish a change in local land use. The two dates do not prove continuous rule.
entries.next_step: Check the cited accounts for how control changed and what it meant for the land.
source_citations: Hally (1993), The Territorial Size of Mississippian Chiefdoms, pp. 163–164.

entries.name: Deaths of family members near Dhaka
entries.place_and_era: Near Dhaka, in 1617.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that Qasim Khan killed his chief wives when he faced defeat. Some comrades also killed members of their families.
entries.unknown: The account does not establish a change in land or residence from these deaths. It does not give a share of all families harmed.
entries.next_step: Trace the relation of the event to land or residence. Keep the reported deaths visible. Do not invent a removal.
source_citations: Eaton (1993 archive context), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 7, section s1.7.1, notes 20.

entries.name: Defeat and service at Shahzadpur
entries.place_and_era: Shahzadpur, in 1609.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that Tuqmaq Khan defeated the local ruler. He then employed and converted the son of the ruler. The governor disapproved and moved Tuqmaq Khan from his assigned estate.
entries.unknown: The account does not show that the son was forced to migrate or was enslaved. It does not define the land outcome of the defeat.
entries.next_step: Trace what changed at the defeated estate. Keep service, conversion and movement distinct.
source_citations: Eaton (1993 archive context), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 7, section s1.7.3, notes 60.

entries.name: Disputed rent at Panam Dulalpur
entries.place_and_era: Panam Dulalpur in Bengal; an account set in the early eighteenth century.
entries.attested: Eaton describes gifts to a holy man that became compulsory rent. Some villagers appealed and lost. Officials then recognized him as the landholder.
entries.unknown: The exact date and the former land rights are unclear. The account does not establish that villagers left.
entries.next_step: Define the change in land rights and the people it affected.
source_citations: Eaton (1993 archive context), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 8, notes 95.

entries.name: Enslaved artisans in Pepiliyana grants
entries.place_and_era: Pepiliyana Vihara, Sri Lanka, in the fifteenth century. Specific grant dates remain unchecked.
entries.attested: Codrington describes documents that grant enslaved people with land. Many were artisans.
entries.unknown: The cited documents were unpublished in his account. A change of ownership does not establish that people moved.
entries.next_step: Read the grant terms and distinguish control of people from forced movement and changes in residence.
source_citations: H. W. Codrington, A Short History of Ceylon, chapter III, Pepiliyana grants (web transcription).

entries.name: Families forced from homes near Jhalakati
entries.place_and_era: Jhalakati in Bengal; departure before a survey in 1906.
entries.attested: Eaton quotes a survey that reports pressure forced several Namasudra families to leave. Other villagers then held their land and homes.
entries.unknown: The departure date and village name are unclear. The survey date does not date the departure.
entries.next_step: Resolve the date range and village location. These gaps do not disprove the reported loss.
source_citations: Eaton (1993 archive context), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 8, notes 99.

entries.name: Farming leases at Swarupkati
entries.place_and_era: Bakarganj; a 1906 survey recalls leases from about 220 years earlier, around 1686.
entries.attested: The account says the Pals, Dasses and Chandras settled under farming leases from Nayerkaleri landlords.
entries.unknown: Earlier occupants and any pressure remain unclear. This is separate from the thirteenth-century refuge story.
entries.next_step: Trace the lease terms and earlier rights, linked to the broader Bakarganj question.
source_citations: Eaton (1993), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 8, note 82.

entries.name: Flight and killing at Cakradhara
entries.place_and_era: Kashmir. The account follows a royal return dated to 1121. The date of the fire is not yet settled.
entries.attested: Kalhana's account says families from Vijayuksetra and nearby towns and villages fled to a shrine. Royal soldiers also went there. Bhiksu's forces besieged the refuge. A man set fire to it to kill an enemy inside. The text describes deaths within and the killing of people who escaped. It then says homes stood empty because householders and their families died.
entries.unknown: Errors remain possible in the online text. We did not check the printed pages or the Sanskrit. The account gives no reliable count of deaths or lost homes. It does not establish a single ethnic group or an order to start the fire. Later control of the empty homes is unknown.
entries.next_step: Assess this bounded case under the atlas rules. Keep the date, numbers and later ownership unknown where the evidence does not resolve them.
source_citations: Kalhana, Kalhana’s Rajatarangini: A Chronicle of the Kings of Kasmir, translated by M. A. Stein, volume II (1900), Book VIII 971–995, printed pp. 76–78; context VIII 947–1008, printed pp. 75–79. Unproofread online translation OCR; page images and Sanskrit not verified.

entries.name: Four Chattahoochee towns burned
entries.place_and_era: Coweta, Kasihta, Tuskegee and Kolimi on the Chattahoochee, December 1685.
entries.attested: Smith reports that Matheos burned the four towns after failing to capture English traders.
entries.unknown: The burning does not show that all residents left for good. This Tuskegee is not the Overhill Cherokee town of the same name.
entries.next_step: Trace what the burning did to residence in each town. Keep the later 1690 move separate.
source_citations: Smith (1992), Historic Period Indian Archaeology of Northern Georgia, p. 29.

entries.name: Gilimale changes from dedicated land to a royal village
entries.place_and_era: Gilimale, Sri Lanka. The earlier dedication is linked to Vijaya Bahu I; the later change is not dated.
entries.attested: Codrington lists Gilimale as land once dedicated to feed pilgrims and later held as a royal village.
entries.unknown: The account does not date the resumption or explain its effect on cultivators and former beneficiaries.
entries.next_step: Locate the act of resumption and establish whose rights changed. Do not infer eviction from the title change.
source_citations: H. W. Codrington, A Short History of Ceylon, chapter III, Authorities: Gilimale (web transcription).

entries.name: Guale missions destroyed
entries.place_and_era: Guale coastal missions, late 1680s.
entries.attested: Smith links the destruction of coastal missions to conflict between English and Spanish powers.
entries.unknown: The passage does not tie all regional captives or moves to this episode. Links to the people and settlements attacked in 1702–1706 remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Keep this earlier episode distinct from the later Florida attacks. Trace the loss of the mission settlements.
source_citations: Smith (1992), Historic Period Indian Archaeology of Northern Georgia, p. 34.

entries.name: Hidden Valley: burned houses
entries.place_and_era: Hidden Valley near Durango, Colorado. House construction dates cluster in 760–761 CE; the departure date is not established.
entries.attested: Potter reports that the excavated houses burned at abandonment and had not been salvaged.
entries.unknown: The account does not establish an attack, a single fire across the settlement, or a forced departure.
entries.next_step: Read Carlson’s excavation report to trace how and when use of the houses ended.
source_citations: James M. Potter, The Community, Animas–La Plata Project, Volume XVI: Final Synthetic Report, chapter 13 (2010), pp. 237.

entries.name: Hijli under Mughal rule
entries.place_and_era: Hijli, in the early Mughal period described by Eaton.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that Hijli submitted to Mughal rule without resistance. Its ruler paid tribute and kept control of local administration.
entries.unknown: The account does not establish eviction of the people who lived there. Continued local rule does not mean there was no change in power.
entries.next_step: Assess the change in rule and keep local continuity visible. Do not require expulsion for a land-control question.
source_citations: Eaton (1993 archive context), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 7, section s1.7.5, notes 67.

entries.name: Kazi families in Gaurnadi: record 717
entries.place_and_era: Gaurnadi, Bakarganj; recorded in surveys from 1902–1913. The settlement date is unknown.
entries.attested: A survey describes kazi families as the original settlers of this village.
entries.unknown: Earlier land rights remain unclear. The later population count does not count people harmed or first settlers.
entries.next_step: Check this village and its earlier land use as a separate question.
source_citations: Eaton (1993), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 8, note 92.

entries.name: Kendangamuwa becomes a royal village
entries.place_and_era: Kendangamuwa, Sri Lanka. An earlier grant is linked to Parakrama Bahu VI; the later change is not dated.
entries.attested: Codrington lists land given to Aramanapola Vihara that later appeared as a royal village.
entries.unknown: The date, act and effect on residents remain unclear. Royal control does not by itself prove their removal.
entries.next_step: Locate the resumption and distinguish changes in revenue rights from loss of residence or use.
source_citations: H. W. Codrington, A Short History of Ceylon, chapter III, Authorities: Kendangamuwa (web transcription).

entries.name: Khan Jahan at Bagerhat
entries.place_and_era: Bagerhat; Khan Jahan died in 1459, and traditions were collected in 1870.
entries.attested: Eaton describes a tomb title and public works, alongside a later account of a revenue grant and cultivation.
entries.unknown: These sources support different claims. They do not establish forced labor or empty land.
entries.next_step: Keep the claims separate and trace the grant and earlier land use.
source_citations: Eaton (1993), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 8, notes 50–56.

entries.name: Land assigned to the Chittagong garrison
entries.place_and_era: Chittagong; from 1666, later change undated
entries.attested: Troops received rent-free plots. Eaton reports that the government later took the lands back. The troops or their descendants became landlords who collected revenue.
entries.unknown: The later date and the rights lost or retained are unclear. The account does not say the troops left.
entries.next_step: Identify what rights changed in the later repossession.
source_citations: Eaton (1993), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 9, notes 29.

entries.name: Land grant to Firuzpuri near Malda
entries.place_and_era: Near Malda, in the Mughal period described by Eaton.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that Shah Nimat Allah Firuzpuri received a grant of land from the governor. His servants and descendants later gained wealth from it.
entries.unknown: The account does not identify prior holders or changes in their access to the land. The exact tract of the grant is not given.
entries.next_step: Trace what the grant changed for people on the land. Do not count the size of the grant as a number of displaced people.
source_citations: Eaton (1993 archive context), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 7, section s1.7.2, notes 30, 31.

entries.name: Land grants for Muhammad Rabi
entries.place_and_era: Sylhet; grants in 1753 and 1756
entries.attested: Grants supported Muhammad Rabi, his workers, family and religious institutions. The later grant set terms for cultivation and use of the harvest.
entries.unknown: The passage does not establish all prior land uses, actual clearance or the workers' conditions.
entries.next_step: Trace earlier use and what changed when the grants took effect.
source_citations: Eaton (1993), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 9, notes 95, 96.

entries.name: Land grants to Ikundā
entries.place_and_era: The frontier between Nepal and Sikkim. The commentary describes events in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The grant dates remain unknown.
entries.attested: The commentary on the letter cites grants to Ikundā of land and rights to rule or collect revenue. It also cites land for resettlement.
entries.unknown: The grant texts remain unread in this review. A grant does not prove that settlement occurred or that prior residents lost land.
entries.next_step: Read the cited grants. Distinguish the rights they granted from actions on the ground and effects on prior residents.
source_citations: Julia Shrestha with Martin Gaenszle (editors and translators), A letter from Subba Jayanta Khatri reporting on the killing of Limbus and Lepchas at the Nepal-Sikkim frontier (DNA_0001_0109; VS1883) (2023). DNA_0001_0109 commentary paragraphs on Ikundā; cited RRC_0040_0442 and RRC_0006_0858/RRC_0036_0251/RRC_0036_0252; Hamilton1819 printed123,126. Edition translation and commentary in accepted review. No facsimile or independent translation verification. Commentary is not a separate witness to the letter. English edition/translation/commentary CC BY-SA4.0. Document date1827 is distinct from edition metadata; no facsimile reproduced and no DOI verified.

Francis Buchanan Hamilton, An Account of the Kingdom of Nepal (1819). Hamilton1819 printed123,126: reported civil administration/revenue context; does not establish execution of the cited grants. HTML transcription with print anchors. Earlier administration account is not proof of grant execution or the1827violence.

entries.name: Limbu and Lepcha families in forest refuge
entries.place_and_era: The frontier between Nepal and Sikkim. A letter reports this flight in 1827. The exact flight dates are unknown.
entries.attested: Khatri relays a plea from five messengers. They report that descendants and nephews of Ikundā captured and killed Limbu and Lepcha residents. Some families fled to forest camps. Other families planned to leave.
entries.unknown: Five is the number of messengers, not the total who fled or died. The homes, camp sites and later fate of the families remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Trace the flight that already occurred. Keep plans for later moves separate. Examine whether officials granted the request for protection.
source_citations: Julia Shrestha with Martin Gaenszle (editors and translators), A letter from Subba Jayanta Khatri reporting on the killing of Limbus and Lepchas at the Nepal-Sikkim frontier (DNA_0001_0109; VS1883) (2023). DNA_0001_0109, translation [1r], paragraphs beginning Uprānta and Some family groups; diplomatic line references 6–10,16–23,34–35 supplied by edition; commentary and notes3–9,12–16. Edition translation and commentary in accepted review. No facsimile or independent translation verification. Commentary is not a separate witness to the letter. English edition/translation/commentary CC BY-SA4.0. Document date1827 is distinct from edition metadata; no facsimile reproduced and no DOI verified.

entries.name: Loss and retention of land in Bakla
entries.place_and_era: Bakla in eastern Bengal, about the time of the Bhallua campaign around 1611.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that Ram Chandra was defeated and detained in Dhaka. He kept enough land to support a naval fleet. Mughal tax collectors and other holders received the rest of his lands.
