entries.unknown: This was not the loss of all his land. The account does not show that the peasants were expelled. The date is given by its link to the nearby campaign.
entries.next_step: Keep both the lost and retained lands visible. Do not turn the detention of the ruler into a mass removal.
source_citations: Eaton (1993 archive context), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 7, section s1.7.7, notes 96.

entries.name: Lower Cherokee burnings and westward refuge
entries.place_and_era: Northeastern Georgia and the Coosa valley, from 1776 through the end of the Revolution.
entries.attested: Smith reports town burnings in 1776 and later movement west. He describes Willstown as a settlement of refugees from the Savannah area.
entries.unknown: Not all departures occurred in 1776. The account does not establish that arrivals displaced earlier Coosa residents.
entries.next_step: Trace the moves and receiving settlements. Keep the 1760 burnings and later nineteenth-century removal separate.
source_citations: Smith (1992), Historic Period Indian Archaeology of Northern Georgia, pp. 37, 38.

entries.name: Lower Cherokee towns burned in 1760
entries.place_and_era: Lower Cherokee towns in northeastern Georgia and northwestern South Carolina, 1760.
entries.attested: Smith reports that Montgomery’s forces burned the towns. Towns remained in the region afterward.
entries.unknown: The burning does not establish a permanent departure in 1760.
entries.next_step: Trace the loss of homes even where people stayed or rebuilt. Keep this episode separate from the 1776 burnings.
source_citations: Smith (1992), Historic Period Indian Archaeology of Northern Georgia, p. 37.

entries.name: Lower Creek movement east
entries.place_and_era: Chattahoochee towns and the Ocmulgee and Towaliga valleys, 1690.
entries.attested: Smith reports that many towns moved east after continued conflict with Spain. They moved toward English allies. Some towns stayed.
entries.unknown: Some town names in the account are only suggestions. The account does not establish that arrivals took land from earlier residents.
entries.next_step: Keep each town’s move and the places of arrival distinct. Separate this move from the 1685 burnings and later return.
source_citations: Smith (1992), Historic Period Indian Archaeology of Northern Georgia, pp. 29, 33.

entries.name: Lower Creek return after the Yamassee War
entries.place_and_era: Oconee, Ocmulgee and Chattahoochee valleys, after the 1715 war.
entries.attested: Smith reports that many groups returned to the Chattahoochee. Earlier Oconee and Ocmulgee sites were left. Lower Cherokee Tugalo was an exception to the wider Savannah valley abandonment pattern.
entries.unknown: The cause of each move and the exact returning groups remain unclear. Copied maps do not prove continued occupation.
entries.next_step: Trace the groups and causes of return. Do not infer forced removal from the order of events alone.
source_citations: Smith (1992), Historic Period Indian Archaeology of Northern Georgia, pp. 35, 36, 39.

entries.name: Madura is taken and a ruler installed
entries.place_and_era: Madura in southern India, during Sena II's reign in the ninth century. The exact year is uncertain.
entries.attested: Codrington reports that Sena's general took and sacked Madura, then placed another ruler on its throne.
entries.unknown: The account does not establish civilian expulsion. A Pandyan accession date does not securely date this intervention.
entries.next_step: Assess the reported capture and change of rule. Keep the fate of residents open.
source_citations: H. W. Codrington, A Short History of Ceylon, chapter III, Sena II: Madura (web transcription).

entries.name: Mehr Ali at Mehrpur
entries.place_and_era: Jessore; an early Mughal tradition recorded in 1982.
entries.attested: Eaton reports a tradition that Mehr Ali arrived and helped local people grow rice.
entries.unknown: The account does not establish earlier land rights, a taking or a forced move.
entries.next_step: Trace the settlement and earlier land use in this area.
source_citations: Eaton (1993), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 8, note 42.

entries.name: Migrants in Mughal Bengal
entries.place_and_era: Bengal, in the Mughal period described by Eaton.
entries.attested: Eaton describes soldiers, merchants, clerks and artisans who moved into Bengal from North India. These arrivals formed part of the imperial social order.
entries.unknown: This regional account does not identify one land takeover by all the migrants. Claimed ancestry does not establish a route or a forced move.
entries.next_step: Trace distinct communities and their links to land. Do not treat religion or elite insults as proof that people were displaced.
source_citations: Eaton (1993 archive context), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 7, section s1.7.2, notes 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36.

entries.name: Mughal annexation of Sylhet
entries.place_and_era: Sylhet; reported in 1612
entries.attested: Eaton reports that the Mughals annexed Sylhet in 1612.
entries.unknown: The passage does not describe effects on residents or private land rights. It does not say that the earlier refugees were expelled.
entries.next_step: Trace the change in rule and its local effects.
source_citations: Eaton (1993), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 9, Religious Gentry of Sylhet opening narrative.

entries.name: Mughal conquest of Kuch Bihar and Kamrup
entries.place_and_era: Kuch Bihar and Kamrup, in 1613.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that Mughal forces took forts and drove the ruler into Kamrup. He later submitted and was sent to Dhaka. The Mughals took control of both regions and imposed a new land tax system.
entries.unknown: The account does not show that all farmers left. It does not give a full area of land lost or a permanent end date.
entries.next_step: Keep the moves of the ruler distinct from the changes imposed on farmers. Compare this conquest with the later revolts.
source_citations: Eaton (1993 archive context), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 7, section s1.7.6, notes 82, 83, 84, 85, 86.

entries.name: Nasir al-Din at Murarbond
entries.place_and_era: Sylhet; a Mughal-period tradition recorded in 1982.
entries.attested: The account says Nasir al-Din arrived and taught local people to grow rice.
entries.unknown: These changes do not by themselves show that land was taken.
entries.next_step: Check how land use and control changed at Murarbond.
source_citations: Eaton (1993), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 8, note 43.

entries.name: New revenue collectors at Ambarabad
entries.place_and_era: Ambarabad in Bengal; a revenue district formed in 1734.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that small landholders said they requested revenue collectors. He argues that pressure from Mughal power better explains their agreement.
entries.unknown: The landholders described a request. Eaton instead infers pressure. The earlier land rights and any eviction remain unclear.
entries.next_step: Compare the reported request with the evidence for pressure and changes in land rights.
source_citations: Eaton (1993 archive context), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 8, notes 57, 58.

entries.name: Oconee River village burned
entries.place_and_era: An Oconee River village, 1767.
entries.attested: Smith reports that an occupied village was burned.
entries.unknown: Its exact identity is unclear. A town shown on a 1774 map may be the same place, but that link is uncertain.
entries.next_step: Trace the destruction and possible later residence. A village name or casualty count is not needed to examine the loss.
source_citations: Smith (1992), Historic Period Indian Archaeology of Northern Georgia, p. 37.

entries.name: Okfuskenena burned and Creek towns left
entries.place_and_era: Middle Chattahoochee and the modern West Point Lake area toward Alabama, 1793.
entries.attested: Smith reports that Georgians attacked and burned Okfuskenena. He links the attack to Creek towns in the area moving to Alabama.
entries.unknown: The number of towns attacked is uncertain. The broad destination does not establish an exact route or receiving site.
entries.next_step: Trace the attack and departures using the boundaries of the time. Georgia then ended farther east, at the Oconee.
source_citations: Smith (1992), Historic Period Indian Archaeology of Northern Georgia, pp. 38, 39.

entries.name: Overhill departures and loss of land
entries.place_and_era: The lower Little Tennessee valley, in the Revolutionary and Federal periods. The account includes the treaties of 1798 and 1819.
entries.attested: Davis says settler pressure forced Cherokee families south. Many moved to the Hiwassee valley and beyond. He says the treaties transferred land to the United States and opened it to settlers. Some families stayed or moved nearby. The 1819 treaty allowed some to stay on reserved land.
entries.unknown: The account does not link each move to one treaty or each treaty to one riverbank. The 31 people or family heads who received reserved land lived in a wider area. They are not a count of all who lost homes.
entries.next_step: Keep the two land transfers distinct. Check how these earlier moves relate to the wider removal case. Keep the families who stayed visible.
source_citations: Davis (1986), Stability and Change in Aboriginal Settlement within the Lower Little Tennessee River Valley, printed pp. 419, 420, 427, 428, 429.

entries.name: Overhill towns as places of refuge
entries.place_and_era: Tomotley, Tuskegee and Mialoquo in the lower Little Tennessee valley. Eighteenth century.
entries.attested: Davis says these towns probably grew as places of refuge. People came from Lower, Middle and possibly Valley Towns. He also reports that later refugees joined the towns. They came from other Cherokee and southeastern groups.
entries.unknown: The cause and date of each move remain unclear. The account does not show that these arrivals took land from people who lived there.
entries.next_step: Trace why people left and what happened to land at each end. Refuge alone does not show that the new arrivals took land.
source_citations: Davis (1986), Stability and Change in Aboriginal Settlement within the Lower Little Tennessee River Valley, printed pp. 424, 425, 428.

entries.name: Pachet under Mughal rule
entries.place_and_era: Pachet, in the early Mughal period described by Eaton.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that Pachet submitted to Mughal rule without resistance. He places this in a western region where much local administration continued.
entries.unknown: The account does not establish eviction of the people who lived there. Continued local rule does not mean there was no change in power.
entries.next_step: Assess the change in rule and keep local continuity visible. Do not require expulsion for a land-control question.
source_citations: Eaton (1993 archive context), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 7, section s1.7.5, notes 67.

entries.name: Pir Qutb at Kutubpur
entries.place_and_era: Narayanganj, Dhaka; the settlement date is unknown.
entries.attested: A survey links the village name to Pir Qutb and recalls no homesteads when he arrived.
entries.unknown: No homesteads does not mean no earlier land use or rights.
entries.next_step: Trace the settlement and earlier uses of the land.
source_citations: Eaton (1993), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 8, note 93.

entries.name: Possible captivity at Crable
entries.place_and_era: Central Illinois River Valley. Wilson places this account in the later Mississippian period. The burial has no exact date here.
entries.attested: Wilson reports a young woman buried in an abandoned storage pit at Crable. He infers low status from how her body was treated. He offers captivity as a possible explanation.
entries.unknown: Captivity is not established. Her prior home, origin and any forced move are unknown. The burial does not by itself show forced work or loss of her former home.
entries.next_step: Check what the burial evidence can establish about captivity and residence. Keep a possible captive identity separate from a proven forced move.
source_citations: Greg D. Wilson, Incinerated Villages in the North (2015), printed pp. 104. Original author-hosted chapter; full eight-page text layer and selected published images read. Underlying excavation reports not independently read.

entries.name: Possible Coosa movement downstream
entries.place_and_era: Ridge and Valley area and the later Weiss Reservoir area; after the mid-sixteenth-century Spanish expeditions.
entries.attested: Smith suggests that people left the Ridge and Valley area and moved downstream.
entries.unknown: Gaps in known occupation do not by themselves prove a departure or forced move.
entries.next_step: Check the proposed movement. Keep it separate from Coosa rule and the medieval Etowah site.
source_citations: Smith (1992), Historic Period Indian Archaeology of Northern Georgia, p. 32.

entries.name: Possible new groups at Reckner
entries.place_and_era: Reckner, in the Allegheny Mountains. The study places the village in the 1300s. It does not date the proposed arrivals.
entries.attested: The authors interpret village growth as the possible addition of groups. One suggestion is that the groups asked to join. They state that the wall pattern does not reveal membership.
entries.unknown: The source does not establish the groups' origins or moves. It does not establish force, exclusion or loss of former homes. These are not shown by the lack of a new wall.
entries.next_step: Check the original site study and the proposed addition of groups. Trace prior residence if the evidence permits.
source_citations: John P. Hart and Bernard K. Means, The Monongahela tradition in “real time”: Bayesian analysis of radiocarbon dates (2022), PLOS ONE 17(10): e0276014, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0276014. Discussion, paragraph beginning A second example is the Reckner site; fourteenth-century context and paragraph discussion of group petitions/palisade visibility.

entries.name: Possible new households at Peck No. 1
entries.place_and_era: Peck No. 1, in the Allegheny Mountains. The study compares village date ranges that overlap around 1270 to 1310. It does not date the proposed arrivals.
entries.attested: The authors interpret two village expansions as possible additions of small groups. One proposed explanation is that the groups were families or lineages. The proposed checks on new members and role of a leader rely on comparisons with other societies.
entries.unknown: The source does not identify an origin village or prove a move. It does not show whether force caused anyone to leave a former home. A larger village plan is not a count of people.
entries.next_step: Check the original site study. Test the proposed arrival of groups. Keep their origin and former home questions open.
source_citations: John P. Hart and Bernard K. Means, The Monongahela tradition in “real time”: Bayesian analysis of radiocarbon dates (2022), PLOS ONE 17(10): e0276014, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0276014. Discussion, paragraph beginning Peck1 represented growth by the addition; inference and ethnographic analogies attributed to Means/reference46.

entries.name: Possible Oconee movement to coastal missions
entries.place_and_era: Oconee valley and coastal missions; the proposed move has no fixed date.
entries.attested: Smith suggests that people moved to coastal missions. He offers this as a possible cause of the valley’s population decline.
entries.unknown: The passage does not establish that this move occurred or that people were forced to leave.
entries.next_step: Check whether the move occurred and what happened to land in the valley.
source_citations: Smith (1992), Historic Period Indian Archaeology of Northern Georgia, p. 28.

entries.name: Possible potter residence near the Wabash
entries.place_and_era: Slack Farm and other sites near the Ohio and Wabash rivers. The study covers a broad period from about 1400 to 1700. The date of any household move is unknown.
entries.attested: Pollack and Munson compare local pottery with vessels linked to Oneota traditions. They propose two explanations: traded vessels or resident potters. They suggest household moves, marriage or kinship as possible ways to support exchange.
entries.unknown: The source does not establish that households moved. It does not show force or a loss of local homes. The political reasons for the exchange remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Test trade and local production as explanations for the vessels. If evidence supports resident potters, trace how residence began and its effects on prior residents.
source_citations: David Pollack and Cheryl Ann Munson, Caborn-Welborn Ceramics: Intersite Comparisons and Extraregional Interaction, Current Archaeological Research in Kentucky, Volume Five (1998), printed pp. 192–194; conditional exchange context p. 195.

entries.name: Refuge and settlement in Bakarganj
entries.place_and_era: Bakarganj in Bengal; early thirteenth-century refuge and later accounts of settlement.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that Hindu chiefs fled to Bakarganj. He also describes local groups who caught fish and later became farmers.
entries.unknown: The departure sites and changes in local land rights are unclear. Refuge alone does not prove that arrivals took land from others.
entries.next_step: Keep flight, arrival and changes for local residents as separate questions.
source_citations: Eaton (1993 archive context), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 8, notes 81, 82.

entries.name: Reported deaths at Saunaktuk
entries.place_and_era: Saunaktuk in Arctic Canada. The article dates use of the site to about 1370. This does not date the attack.
entries.attested: The authors link injuries on human bones from a house site to a local account of an attack. They suggest that the residents were Inuit. The reported deaths meant loss of homes for those residents.
entries.unknown: The link between the bones and the account remains uncertain. The attackers and the fate of other residents remain unknown.
entries.next_step: Examine how the house context supports the link to residents. Keep the local account and its later retellings distinct.
source_citations: Jerry Melbye and Scott I. Fairgrieve, A Massacre and Possible Cannibalism in the Canadian Arctic: New Evidence from the Saunaktuk Site (NgTn-1) (1994). Printed page 58 (dwelling and occupation context); pages 73–75 (discussion, transmitted attack account and interpretation). One consulted article, in saved web-returned context and discussion windows only. Arnold 1990 and LeMeur 1984 are secondhand here, not independently consulted sources. Page images, complete methods and lesion catalogue remain unchecked.

entries.name: Reported displacement before Malwa occupation at Daimabad
entries.place_and_era: Daimabad, Maharashtra, India. Sali places Malwa arrival around 1600 BCE. That is not a verified date for the claimed forced departure.
entries.attested: Sali suggests that Malwa arrivals first shared the site with earlier residents, then forced them out. He bases this account on an overlap of remains.
entries.unknown: The link between these remains and forced departure needs further study. The phase names do not by themselves identify separate peoples.
entries.next_step: Check the overlap and the claim of shared residence. Look for evidence of how the earlier residents lost their homes.
source_citations: S. A. Sali, Daimabad 1976–79, Memoirs of the Archaeological Survey of India 83 (1986), printed p. 28; structural limits pp. 92–93.

entries.name: Reported loss of homes at Daimabad
entries.place_and_era: Daimabad, Maharashtra, India. The report places this change between the Savalda and Late Harappan phases. The date of the claimed departure is unresolved.
entries.attested: Sali says Late Harappan arrivals forced out earlier residents and replaced their village. The report describes later deposits above the earlier settlement.
entries.unknown: The evidence behind the forced departure needs further study. A change in pottery does not by itself show that another group took the site.
entries.next_step: Check the layers, homes and dates behind the claim. Look for evidence of what happened to the earlier residents.
source_citations: S. A. Sali, Daimabad 1976–79, Memoirs of the Archaeological Survey of India 83 (1986), printed pp. 23–25; structural limits pp. 88, 92–93.

entries.name: Reviews of rent-free land grants
entries.place_and_era: Chittagong; hearings from 1819 to 1848
entries.attested: Company officials reviewed land grants and sought to reclaim those they judged invalid. Eaton describes these hearings as the reason many grant records survived.
entries.unknown: This passage does not identify which rejected holders lost rights or whether people had to leave.
entries.next_step: Trace specific rejected grants and what happened to their holders.
source_citations: Eaton (1993), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 9, notes 32.

entries.name: Revolt and reconquest in Kamrup
entries.place_and_era: Rangamati and Gilah, in 1614.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that rebels overpowered Rangamati and besieged Gilah. Mughal forces then recovered the sites. The revolt followed the new tax and service system.
entries.unknown: The account does not show that all local people fled. This recovery does not prove permanent control of the region.
entries.next_step: Keep this change of control distinct from the defeat of Sanatan in 1615.
source_citations: Eaton (1993 archive context), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 7, section s1.7.6, notes 87, 88.

entries.name: Ridges Basin: a death in a burned house
entries.place_and_era: Ridges Basin, Colorado, site 5LP237, in the early Pueblo I regional study. The event date is unresolved.
entries.attested: Potter reports a possible killing and house burning associated with Burial 137.
entries.unknown: Burial followed by ritual burning remains possible. A separate pit deposit is not established as part of the same event.
entries.next_step: Read the site report to distinguish the deposits and establish what ended use of the house.
source_citations: James M. Potter, The Community, Animas–La Plata Project, Volume XVI: Final Synthetic Report, chapter 13 (2010), pp. 255.

entries.name: Royal and military retreats in Sikkim
entries.place_and_era: Sikkim and nearby areas. Hamilton describes events from 1788 to 1809. He casts doubt on some dates and claims.
entries.attested: Hamilton describes retreats by rulers and troops, relief of a siege and a later royal return. He also reports changes in political control.
entries.unknown: These moves do not by themselves prove that local families lost their homes. The account does not show one continuous flight by civilians.
entries.next_step: Examine each retreat separately. Ask whether local families or the royal household lost their homes.
source_citations: Francis Buchanan Hamilton, An Account of the Kingdom of Nepal (1819). Hamilton1819 Country of Sikim printed120–124; settlement/geographic context118–119,124–128. HTML transcription with print anchors; no scanned-page verification. Informant account, not an eyewitness claim about flight.

entries.name: Rule in the Oconee valley
entries.place_and_era: The Oconee River in Georgia, in the mid-sixteenth century.
entries.attested: Hally cites Spanish accounts of chiefdoms on the Oconee River under one chief. He treats rule by a senior chief as probable.
entries.unknown: The chapter does not show how this rule began or what changed for local land use. The extent of direct control remains unclear.
entries.next_step: Check the cited accounts for how control changed and what it meant for the land.
source_citations: Hally (1993), The Territorial Size of Mississippian Chiefdoms, pp. 163–164.

entries.name: Tax pressure and departure from Cossimbazar
entries.place_and_era: Cossimbazar, in the context of the tax imposed in 1679 and its later enforcement in Bengal.
entries.attested: A note by Eaton reports forced tax demands on Hindu silk workers. It says the disruption drove the "little people" of the city into the interior.
entries.unknown: The people who left are not shown to be the same group as the silk workers. Early 1681 dates tax collection in Dhaka, not every departure from Cossimbazar. The number and routes are unknown.
entries.next_step: Keep the two towns distinct. Retain the reported forced departure without an invented exact date or a new land claim at the destination.
source_citations: Eaton (1993 archive context), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 7, section s1.7.3, notes 58.

entries.name: The Bhanja rulers lose land and move to Ganjam
entries.place_and_era: Upper Orissa and Ganjam, eastern India, probably in the late tenth century. The date is uncertain.
entries.attested: Sircar reads the land grants as evidence that the Bhanja rulers lost territory and were driven to Ganjam.
entries.unknown: The grants do not directly describe the move. Its date and full extent are unclear. The account does not show that other residents were expelled.
entries.next_step: Check how the cited grants support the loss of territory and the move. Keep the rulers distinct from other residents.
source_citations: Dines Chandra Sircar, The Bhañjas of Khiñjali-Maṇḍala, Indian Historical Quarterly 28(3) (1952), pp. 225–231; placing discussion pp. 225–229, especially 227.

entries.name: The capture of Chittagong
entries.place_and_era: Chittagong; reported in 1666
entries.attested: Eaton reports that Mughal forces took the citadel after a siege. They then made the city a district centre under Mughal rule.
entries.unknown: The account does not establish whether residents were removed or which private land rights changed.
entries.next_step: Trace the effects on residents and earlier landholders.
source_citations: Eaton (1993), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 9, notes 27, 28.

entries.name: The defeat of Sanatan and flight
entries.place_and_era: Dhamdhama in Kamrup, in 1615.
entries.attested: Eaton reports that Sanatan led armed resistance to Mughal rule. His demands included tax changes and the withdrawal of troops. Mughal forces destroyed the stockades and forced him to flee.
entries.unknown: Eaton presents Sanatan as a probable paik leader. His flight does not show that all his supporters left. The account does not give their share of the local population.
entries.next_step: Keep the forced flight and loss of the defended place visible. Do not infer a route for all the people who took part.
source_citations: Eaton (1993 archive context), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 7, section s1.7.6, notes 87, 89, 90, 91.

entries.name: The rise of landlords at Fatulla
entries.place_and_era: Dhaka; a 1912 survey recalls arrival in the reign of Jahangir.
entries.attested: The account says descendants of Shah Fateh Allah became landlords and remained so into the twentieth century.
entries.unknown: The source does not say when or how they gained control.
entries.next_step: Trace the change in land rights and the people it affected.
source_citations: Eaton (1993), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 8, note 96.

entries.name: The sack of Anuradhapura under Sena I
entries.place_and_era: Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka, during Sena I's reign in the ninth century. Exact dates remain uncertain.
entries.attested: Codrington reports a Pandyan attack and sack. He then records peace and the king's return.
entries.unknown: The effects on other residents are unclear. The later move to Polonnaruwa is not shown to be forced. The author doubts the story of stolen relics.
entries.next_step: Assess the attack and loss of control separately from the king's later change of residence.
source_citations: H. W. Codrington, A Short History of Ceylon, chapter III, Sena I (web transcription).

entries.name: The settlement tradition at Kazi Abad
entries.place_and_era: Barahanuddin, Bakarganj; recorded in surveys from 1902–1913. The settlement date is unknown.
entries.attested: A survey says the settlement took its name from a kazi who settled there first.
entries.unknown: That claim does not show that earlier people had no use of, or rights to, the land.
entries.next_step: Check the settlement history and earlier land rights.
source_citations: Eaton (1993), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 8, note 90.

entries.name: The settlement tradition at Pail
entries.place_and_era: Sylhet; an undated tradition recorded in 1982.
entries.attested: A tradition recalls a teacher of rice farming and Islam. His sons later settled in Comilla and Sylhet and taught there too.
entries.unknown: The account does not say the sons founded new settlements or forced anyone to move.
entries.next_step: Trace earlier land use and the settlements named in the tradition.
source_citations: Eaton (1993), The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, chapter 8, note 43.

entries.name: The Upper Ohio dispersal question
entries.place_and_era: Southwestern Pennsylvania and nearby areas. The question concerns villages often dated from about 1050 to 1635. That range does not date a move.
entries.attested: Hart and Means call for tests of the view that local communities left by 1635. They say the date lacks independent support. They also call for tests of the proposed roles of Seneca attacks and drought.
entries.unknown: It is not clear which communities left, when they left, or where they went. The source does not establish an attack, forced movement or the loss of homes. The shared archaeological label does not establish one people.
entries.next_step: Read the earlier site and dispersal studies. Test each place and departure on its own. Keep drought, conflict and other causes open.
source_citations: John P. Hart and Bernard K. Means, The Monongahela tradition in “real time”: Bayesian analysis of radiocarbon dates (2022), PLOS ONE 17(10): e0276014, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0276014. Conclusions, paragraph beginning Contemporary practice calls for multiple radiocarbon measures; proposed1635 dispersal and causes expressly require testing.

entries.name: Ustanali and Etowah towns attacked in 1793
entries.place_and_era: Ustanali and the historical town of Etowah, 1793.
entries.attested: Smith reports that Sevier burned Ustanali and destroyed Etowah town. Ustanali was later rebuilt.
entries.unknown: Etowah’s exact site is uncertain here. This is the historical town, not the medieval mound center. Permanent abandonment is not established.
entries.next_step: Trace the loss of residence at both towns. Keep rebuilding and the separate 1782 attack visible.
source_citations: Smith (1992), Historic Period Indian Archaeology of Northern Georgia, p. 38.

entries.name: Ustanali destroyed in 1782
entries.place_and_era: Ustanali, 1782, with later residence.
entries.attested: Smith reports the town’s destruction. Later residence and its role as a capital show that the account does not end with the attack.
entries.unknown: Permanent exile is not established. The actor in the separate 1793 attack cannot be assigned to this event.
entries.next_step: Keep this destruction distinct from the 1793 attack. Trace the loss in place and later residence.
source_citations: Smith (1992), Historic Period Indian Archaeology of Northern Georgia, p. 38.

entries.name: War pressure and defended villages in central Illinois
entries.place_and_era: Central Illinois River Valley, in the early 1200s and after. A later study revises the earlier phase dates.
entries.attested: Wilson links warfare to a shift from scattered homes to compact villages with walls. He also describes limits on access to fields and other food sources. The later study supports war-related settlement change.
entries.unknown: The accounts do not name all earlier homes or define one displaced people. The regional process is not one village attack. Revised phase dates do not give the date of each fire.
entries.next_step: Define the place, period and households for this settlement change. Keep it distinct from each village fire and from later regional departure.
source_citations: Greg D. Wilson, Incinerated Villages in the North (2015), printed pp. 102, 103. Original author-hosted chapter; full eight-page text layer and selected published images read. Underlying excavation reports not independently read.

Gregory D. Wilson, Mallory A. Melton, Amber M. VanDerwarker, Reassessing the chronology of the Mississippian Central Illinois River Valley using Bayesian analysis (2017), ahead-of-print physical pp. 4, 14. Consulted author-archived ahead-of-print version; physical pages1–4 and13–15 read. No full model audit or crosswalk to2018issue22–38. Overlapping author, not independent attack confirmation.

entries.next_step: Trace the loss of residence and the places of refuge. Keep survival distinct from loss of a group name.
source_citations: Smith (1992), Historic Period Indian Archaeology of Northern Georgia, pp. 28, 32, 33.
